item.title: I'm sorry, but you still have to think
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
I'm sorry, but you still have to think

Piotr Sarnacki

8 minutes by Piotr Sarnacki Piotr argues that AI-generated code is not automatically reliable. Comparing Rust and Elixir rewrites of a chat application reveals important differences in performance, message delivery, and resource usage. He highlights the limits of benchmarks and shows how design choices affect real-world behavior. Developers still need to understand their systems, evaluate trade-offs, and test carefully to build reliable software, even when AI does most of the coding.
item.description: I'm sorry, but you still have to think

item.title: Let's build a compressor from scratch
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
Let's build a compressor from scratch

Adolfo Ochagavía

5 minutes by Adolfo Ochagavía Compression shrinks files by rewriting data more efficiently without losing any information. A common method called Huffman coding works by giving shorter codes to bytes that appear often and longer codes to rare ones. Building a basic compressor with this approach takes only a few hundred lines of code and can cut a book's file size nearly in half.
item.description: Let's build a compressor from scratch

item.title: Good interfaces make good neighbors
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
Good interfaces make good neighbors

Andrew Bosworth

2 minutes by Andrew Bosworth Andrew points out that clashing teams often have an interface problem, not a relationship problem. Good collaboration needs three things: clear ownership so anyone can find who is accountable, an honest priority list that includes what was left out, and a defined process for handling new requests. With those in place, disagreements stay manageable and escalation becomes rare.
item.description: Good interfaces make good neighbors

item.title: The lightbulb computer
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
The lightbulb computer

Guillaume Ardaud

7 minutes by Guillaume Ardaud Projecting information onto surfaces around your home could be a better future for computing than smart glasses or small screens. A lightbulb-shaped device combining a projector with computer vision could let you view recipes, maps, and photos on any surface, control smart home devices by pointing, and get answers to questions hands-free. Unlike eyewear, it works socially, requires no face-mounted hardware, and blends naturally into everyday spaces.
item.description: The lightbulb computer

item.title: I love software rendering
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
I love software rendering

James Mackenzie

4 minutes by James Mackenzie Software rendering in old DOS games means the CPU draws every pixel, with no graphics card involved. This produces sharp, gritty visuals that many prefer over the smoothed look of early 3D card acceleration. Running these games on fast modern hardware lets you push resolutions that were impossible in the 1990s, and doing it on real hardware rather than emulation keeps performance solid. And the most popular article from the last issue was: * How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code
item.description: I love software rendering

item.title: Aspect-oriented programming with Metalama in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
Aspect-oriented programming with Metalama in .NET

Aram

Repeated code for logging, validation, and timing spreads across .NET projects and becomes hard to maintain. Metalama brings Aspect-Oriented programming to C# by generating that surrounding code at compile time, so each method stays focused on its actual purpose. You define a behavior once in an aspect, then apply it broadly using attributes or fabric queries. The result is less repeated code, consistent behavior, and easier-to-read business logic. Agents write the code. You own what ships. Run and review them
item.description: Aspect-oriented programming with Metalama in .NET

item.title: Adding properties with extension methods in C# 14
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
Adding properties with extension methods in C# 14

Steven Giesel

C# 14 extensions let you add properties to existing types in two creative ways. The first uses ConditionalWeakTable with StrongBox to attach data to objects without affecting garbage collection or losing null distinction. The second abuses Unsafe.As to treat objects as a mirrored subclass with extra fields, though this requires matching field layouts exactly. Both approaches are clever experiments, not production solutions.
item.description: Adding properties with extension methods in C# 14

item.title: A practical guide to API versioning in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
A practical guide to API versioning in ASP.NET Core

Yogi Hosting

Yogi's guide explains how to implement API versioning in ASP.NET Core for Controllers and Minimal APIs. It covers generating version-specific OpenAPI documents, integrating Swagger UI and Scalar, and controlling which model properties appear in each version. Yogi also introduces automated API linting to detect breaking changes and maintain consistency, helping developers evolve their APIs safely and document them effectively.
item.description: A practical guide to API versioning in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Querying Roslyn syntax trees with XPath
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
Querying Roslyn syntax trees with XPath

Gérald Barré

MA0240 is a generic Roslyn analyzer rule that lets teams ban C# language constructs without writing custom analyzers. You add XPath queries to a BannedSyntaxes.txt file, and the rule reports violations using those patterns. The queries work against the syntax tree, semantic model, or compiler operation tree, so you can match things like implicit boxing or calls inside loops, not just code shapes. This turns what would normally be a new analyzer project into a single line in a text file.
item.description: Querying Roslyn syntax trees with XPath

item.title: An introduction to compact binary object representation in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.content:encoded:
An introduction to compact binary object representation in .NET

Andrew Lock

Compact binary object representation is a binary data format that works like JSON but produces smaller output, especially for numbers, booleans, and raw binary data. It is an official internet standard and supports streaming, unlike similar formats such as MessagePack. The .NET package System.Formats.Cbor provides low-level reading and writing tools, meaning you handle each field manually rather than converting whole objects automatically. It suits cases where payload size matters or binary data is common, though JSON remains the better default for most APIs. And the most popular article from the last issue was: * Upgrading to .NET 10: The breaking changes that don't show up
item.description: An introduction to compact binary object representation in .NET

This week’s system design refresher:

  • RAG vs Agentic RAG

  • Understanding the Linux Directory Structure

Top 5 AI Building Blocks Every Engineer Should Know

RAG vs Agentic RAG

RAG is a technique that combines information retrieval with an LLM to generate answers. Here is how RAG works at a high level:

  • A user asks a question to the application.

  • The retrieval system fetches the relevant information from a knowledge base.

  • The application adds that information to the prompt.

  • The LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

RAG usually follows a predefined retrieval process. The quality of its results depends on the accuracy of the retrieved context.

Agentic RAG follows a different approach. Instead of retrieving once, an agent can repeatedly fetch and evaluate information until it has enough evidence to generate an answer. Here is how it typically works:

  • An agent selects the right tools based on the task.

  • Those tools can search documents, APIs, databases, or the web.

  • The fetched evidence is then checked if it is sufficient for the task.

  • If it is not, the agent can adjust its search or choose a different tool.

  • Once sufficient evidence is achieved, LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

OAuth (authorization) + OIDC (authentication layer)

If you want to show Google Calendar events inside your Slack channel, it will require permission to read your calendar. How would you let Slack access your calendar without giving Slack your Google password?

This is where OAuth 2.0 comes into the picture. Slack basically never sees your Google password. It lets an app access a protected resource on your behalf without knowing your credentials.

Basically OAuth 2.0 handles authorization. In Slack’s case, it will send you to Google’s authorization server, where you will login and give Slack permission to access your calendar. Google gives you the authorization code, and Slack will exchange that code for access_token.

If Slack also wants to authenticate the identity of the person requesting the access to Google Calendar, you will need OIDC for that. The OIDC handles authentication and sits on top of OAuth 2.0.

OAuth answers what you’re allowed to touch, while OIDC answers who you are. In addition to the access_token returned by the authorization server, this time, it will also send an id_token, a signed JWT which basically tells Slack who just signed in.

Understanding the Linux Directory Structure

The linux directory structure starts with the root directory "/". Let’s navigate to the directory structure of linux.

The kernel image and bootloader files are stored in the "boot" directory. Your hard disk partitions and device related files are located in the “dev” directory.

All your programs and libraries are stored in "bin", "sbin", "usr", and "lib" directories. Like, your installed software is located in the "usr" directory. Ever wondered where ls, cp, and cat commands are? "bin" is the directory that holds those essential commands.

System-wide configuration goes in "etc", and "var" holds data that changes as the system runs, which is where you'll find your logs.

If you have a USB drive, it gets mounted in “bin” folder. For any external drive that you want to mount temporarily on your linux machine, "media" is the directory for it. If you have multiple user accounts, "home" is the directory for each user in your linux system.

Why Distributed Systems Prefer Independence over Coordination

ByteByteGo
Oct 22
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

In a distributed system, you have components running in separate processes or machines. These components could be application services, database replicas, or even background workers.

Since in distributed systems, we divide the system into so many components, it’s pretty common that one component may need to talk to another component to get something done. It may also have to wait for the other component’s response. You can think of coordination as this talking between components. For example, you may have one service waiting for another service to approve a request. Or a database waits for acknowledgment from its replicas. Or a worker waits for a lock.

In this article, we’ll look at why coordination is a challenge for distributed systems. Here’s what we will cover.

  • Why coordination becomes a challenge

  • How coordination increases in a system

  • How to reduce coordination

  • Strategies to handle coordination

The Pulse: Time to rethink software security because of AI?

A month’s worth of security breaches in a single day – will things get worse before they improve? Also: Anthropic accused of version control “rip off”, and more

Gergely Orosz
Oct 22
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

  1. Time to rethink software security because of AI? A series of high-profile security incidents and breaches took place in a single day, many fueled by AI. Attackers gain advantage by using AI, and defenders will have to respond.

  2. Is Anthropic’s new version control system “a rip off”? The creator of an open source, high-throughput version control server accuses Anthropic for ripping off their design, and presenting their product as novel by not giving credit to the pre-existing one. It’s not a good look for the leading AI lab.

  3. Industry Pulse. Saudi Arabia made a “problematic” offer to pay alleged OpenAI spy’s bail, Shopify builds tooling for self-healing software, Foursquare’s sale disappoints, Claude Code gets a major speed boost with gzip, and more.

  4. Predictions for the future of software development. Some bold calls by software engineer and Amp cofounder Thorsten Ball, such as that open source no longer makes sense.

The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. Read the full article uninterrupted, online.

Read the full article online

1. Time to rethink software security because of AI?

It’s been an absolutely wild few days, with security breaches and major security vulnerabilities being exposed worldwide across tech. Many incidents took place on Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. We’ll start with a brief summary, then look closer at three of them:

  1. Intermediate CA certificate compromised: eight private 384-bit keys issued by eMudhra – which is an intermediate Certificate Authority (CAs) – leaked, meaning that servers in server-to-server communication can face man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. Any internet communication not going through modern browsers (that already patched this) could be risky.

  2. PHP: Unpatched servers risk remote code execution (RCE) and opening up access for attackers. Around 70% of all websites run on PHP and unpatched systems are at risk. Two critical security patches have been released.

  3. Railway: customer secrets stored on the service were leaked and some have been decrypted. Secrets exposed can include access to production systems, enabling attackers to potentially access customer systems.

  4. GitLab: Unpatched GitLab servers are at risk of an attacker gaining full access. A critical security patch for RCE has been released.

  5. Node.js: Unpatched servers are vulnerable to remote execution attacks. A new release fixes 10 critical vulnerabilities (CVEs), including one that allows for RCE, and another fix revokes the compromised eMudhra intermediate certificate.

  6. Go: a new release is out, adding a mitigation for the compromised eMudhra intermediate certificate.

  7. TiDB: attackers gained near-total access to the complete control plane systems of the managed TiDB provider, PingCAP, for a whole month (!!). The attacker released 10TB of customer-sensitive data, including from Booking.com, Airbnb, Pinterest, Databricks, and more such as SQL queries that customers ran, billing, contacts, and source code for PingCAP’s systems The breach lasted from 9 Sept until 7 Oct, but was only disclosed this week. PingCAP claims no customer data stored inside TiDB was accessed, but I find it hard to see how the company will avoid losing security-conscious customers. This incident shows that the absence of adequate access monitoring and alerting can be an open invitation for attacks lasting weeks.

With that, let’s get into the first three incidents in the list.

eMudhra CA compromise

Certificate authorities (CAs) are organizations that vouch for identity on the internet. When a browser, phone, or server pings a site like chase.com or revolut.com, intermediate CAs and digital signatures verify that you really are talking with the bank’s server, and not a fake one set up by an attacker with the purpose of stealing users’ credentials. This is where the HTTPS protocol comes into play, with root CAs, intermediate CAs and the TLS handshake.

The whole system is built on a chain of trust and verification: we trust the root CAs and their certificates, and so we can trust the signatures of the intermediate CAs. The assumption is that both the root CA and intermediate CAs are trustworthy and verifiable.

But eMudhra broke this trust in the most blatant way: its private keys turned out to be single-digit numbers. A private key is a 384-bit key, which means that it would be a number between 0 and 2^384, (a number with 116 digits!)

Except, the key turned out to be the number “4.” Yes, that’s right: the number four. What on earth was eMudhra doing?! It’s as if they chose random numbers between 0 and 384, not 0 and 2^384! It is quite literally comical: in 2007, an XKCD comic described exactly this choice:

And the other keys were also not that much better: 56, 66, 115, 156, 230 and 237! It’s as if eMudhra generated an 8-bit private key, not a 384-bit one.

eMudhra explaining how these keys were generated (emphasis mine):

“We have done some preliminary assessment, there appears to be a flaw in the KGC [Key Generation Ceremony] script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys [elliptic-curve cryptography key pairs], our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM [Hardware Security Module] keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the CSR [Certificate Signing Request] (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo)

The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted.

Some additional context - these issuers were meant for export to our US and European data centers to solve data sovereignty issues for some of our customers (but never ended up operationally in production except for one).

We are still assessing the code to see steps where this process went wrong.”

I have so many questions:

  • How does eMudhra test generated keys? There seems to have been no automated testing of the key in place at all, in order to discover that these numbers were not “random” from a flaw in the key generation ceremony

  • How did eMudhra not notice this on day one, when the Key Generation Ceremony went wrong? If this was an automated process, the script would’ve changed from one day to the next, which would raise questions. If the process was fully manual, it explains how the mistake would be missed. And if it was manual, then why? Also, where are the detailed audits for such an important process?

  • The certificates with the easy-to-guess private keys were generated on 30 April 2025, so why did eMudhra not spot the mistake for 18 months?

Carelessness in the creation of intermediate certificates risks reputational damage to eMudhra’s business as a certificate authority. Google Chrome announced it is evaluating whether to continue with the company:

“Due to the seriousness of this incident, the Chrome Root Program is closely investigating the ongoing inclusion of eMudhra’s remaining CA certificates in the Chrome Root Store and will share further updates in public forums (e.g., the Common CA Database Public list) as our evaluation progresses.”

Given eMudhra’s sole business is in issuing digital certificates, being dropped by Chrome as a CA could be crippling. eMudhra is a publicly traded company on the Indian stock market, and two days before the breach was revealed its market cap was close to $500M. After details of its incompetence in creating certificates emerged, the company lost 40% of its value in two days.

PHP exploit: AI model beats attackers to finding critical vulnerability

The PHP situation is interesting because the “good guys” in this case (the security researchers) found a critical vulnerability in the framework before attackers did. From OpenAI:

“Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif [a respected security team] identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz [a security company] also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.”

On the surface, this is great news! Critical vulnerabilities were found and can now be patched, thereby closing the door before attackers can exploit them. Right..?

The problem of critical vulnerabilities for open source software is that systems which aren’t immediately patched can be exploited. When the PHP team released the fix for these two vulnerabilities, attackers got details about the vulnerabilities: the code itself shows where the attack can be inititiated! In the case of PHP, that means attackers can now easily execute remote code on any PHP server that is as yet unpatched.

Around 70% of all websites run PHP servers, which is a massive attack surface. We can be confident that many sites won’t update their PHP versions for days, weeks, months, or even years.

This particular vulnerability was so severe that before the security patch, the National Security Agency (NSA) in the US issued guidance urging websites to immediately patch upon release, or take applications fully offline until patched.

Exploits began hours before the fix was announced. It was known in advance that a major vulnerability fix was coming for PHP, and somehow, the vulnerability leaked from the group that disclosed and fixed it. Cloudflare was in the group that worked on this problem and created tooling to monitor and block exploit attempts. From Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince:

Amazon detected exploit attempts days before the fix. From AWS:

“Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.”

Attackers now have AI agents to automate and speed up attacks. Now that the vulnerability is known, attackers can simply spin up agents, instructing them to attempt to exploit servers that have not applied the patch. This probably explains why Cloudflare saw millions of exploit attempts just a few hours after the patch was released.

Railway’s customer secrets leak

Elsewhere on the same day, developer-first cloud provider Railway was hacked and the environment variables (secrets) of its customers were exposed. From the company:

“Our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.”

Immediately after detecting the breach, Railway took decisive action by notifying customers and the public, and pausing all deployments.

Pausing deployments created a huge headache for customers, who could not rotate their keys without crashing their systems running on Railway. Also from Railway:

“We strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.

All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.”

This is contradictory: rotating environment variables – say, a database access token – means that the application using the old variable stops working until a redeploy. However, Railway has paused deploys! So, customers of Railway had two choices:

  • Rotate keys (the responsible step) and deliberately crash their application or take it offline (irresponsible)

  • Don’t rotate and hope their key was not leaked – (irresponsible) – and let their application continue to operate (responsible)

Of course, it’s clear why Railway is pausing deployments after the environment variables leaked, and the team must ensure that new variables added by customers do not leak.

In the end, it took Railway close to 20 hours to resolve the problem and allow deployments again. During that time, they unfortunately gave security-conscious customers an impossible choice of bricking their service while rotating keys, or ignoring security best practices to keep services running.

Can we expect future ‘deluges’ of security incidents?

AI labs did warn of a looming “security tsunami” fueled by the technology in May 2026, as per CNBC:

“Dario Amodei warned Tuesday [5 May 2026] that artificial intelligence has created a narrow window for the world’s tech firms, governments and banks to fix tens of thousands of software vulnerabilities found by his company’s latest model.

That AI model, Mythos, was previewed last month along with the disclosure that it had unearthed decades-old vulnerabilities in crucial software.

“The danger is just some enormous increase in the amount of vulnerabilities, in the amount of breaches, in the financial damage that’s done from ransomware on schools, hospitals, not to mention banks,” Amodei said.

Anthropic has limited Mythos to a few partner companies because of concerns about what criminals or adversarial nations could do with it.”

Around that time, I talked with “AI-pilled” devs – some with access to the Mythos model – who told me the same: they expect the security landscape to become very bad in the coming months, with record numbers of systems being breached. One engineer said he’s moving many of his secrets like 2FA backup phrases off cloud storage services and onto paper because he expects cloud storage services to also be breached.

This week, it has seemed like the prediction in May has come to fruition, much of it done with AI’s help. A few days ago, on 17 October, OpenCode was breached and its customer secrets – AI API keys – stolen. Cofounder, Dax Raad, shared that the company has been under constant attack, in his reply to Railway:

Attacks much easier & defense much harder with AI

I sense the balance of power between the good and bad actors in this space is shifting because of AI. Let’s see what it took for an attacker to get access to a system before AI existed, via a critical vulnerability exposure (CVE) – disclosed or not:

With AI, finding critical vulnerabilities is easier for everybody, including bad actors who can automate attacks as well, and do so easily. The change:

It gets worse: before AI, it took quite some skill to be an effective attacker: you needed to be a good-enough coder, understand concepts like buffer overflows, and also learn techniques for executing remote code execution attacks. With AI, none of that applies. Venture capitalist, Deedy Das, described it as scary that nontechnical people now have the tools to easily exploit known CVEs like the PHP one:

So, let me update the diagram to account for the drastic lowering of the bar to becoming an effective attacker:

And we see all of this playing out in practice, starting with publicly disclosed CVEs skyrocketing:

We may need to urgently rethink software security for all systems:

  • Automated patching: manual monitoring for patches on a daily/weekly basis will become as irresponsible as applying patches months or years after release. Of course, automatic patching has its own risks, such as if a vendor providing a patch is breached, or a patch causes an outage, etc.

  • Expect attackers to use day-zero CVEs. Attackers will increasingly have access to undisclosed vulnerabilities and will access systems externally, or even execute code remotely.

  • Ongoing automated security monitoring to be non-negotiable. To detect security breaches, you need a decent level of automated logging and monitoring. This needs to be in place sooner rather than later. The TiDB incident this week shows what happens when a company allows an attacker to freely access their system for a month.

  • Defenders will have to use more AI. Attackers are gaining advantage by using AI agents, so defenders will have to do the same. There are no best practices in this field, but there are likely to be lessons in how companies like OpenCode, Railway, and PingCAP are responding – if they share their approaches.

  • Securing services and software will become more expensive. Continuously running AI agents to monitor for and mitigate breaches costs money, as do security engineers who are “AI-native.” This all increases the cost of security engineering. We previously covered security engineering basics and did a podcast on code security.

How are you approaching securing your services and systems in light of incidents this week? Leave a comment below.

Leave a comment

2. Is Anthropic’s new version control system “a rip off”?

Last week, I wrote about Anthropic’s new source control system, ‘Scion.’ The AI lab detailed how the system works, but kept it closed source. In the comments below the story, Nick Pleatsikas alerted us to a controversy around the AI giant’s new system.

There are accusations from the creator of Mononoke (an open source server built to scale to thousands of commits per hour) which accuse Anthropic of ripping off their work. From the creator of Mononoke:

“This [Scion] was a ripoff. My post yesterday was trying to be as charitable as possible given what I knew, and in particular that the similarity to Mononoke was mostly unintentional and the lack of credit was the result of not doing due diligence. However, after publishing the post I privately received confirmation that Scion intentionally and blatantly ripped off Mononoke, and in particular that there was overlap in personnel. There is no chance that this was an unintentional homage. This is something I had a hunch about but was not comfortable saying yesterday, given what I knew back then.

The resemblance is much deeper than just the notion of derived data. Some people pointed out that derived data is just an index, which is a well-known concept. I want to clarify that derived data was merely the most striking resemblance. It goes much deeper than that, and extends to the entire data model, as well as a number of the structures built around it.”

Anthropic does not credit Mononoke in its original post, but added a small attribution after the complaint.

To be clear, the point of open source is that you can do what you want with the software without much limitation, except for what the license states. However, it’s poor that it took a public complaint for Anthropic to admit that the clever data structure presented in the AI lab’s blog post is heavily derived from an existing, open source data structure.

3. Industry Pulse

Saudi Arabia in “problematic” offer to pay alleged OpenAI spy’s bail

The involvement of the Saudi Arabian government in the case of the alleged spy at OpenAI was raised in court this week, after the Saudi government reportedly offered to pay the suspect’s bail. Previously, a Saudi official booked the flights that Abdulrahman Alfozan intended to take from the US to the kingdom.

Also, prosecutors claim the arrested engineer was in frequent communication with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp, including as recently as October 5.

Shopify builds tooling for self-healing software

Shopify’s Head of Mobile, Mustafa Ali shared:

“We’re making Shopify’s mobile apps self-healing.

Agents watch production 24x7 for new crashes, reproduce them, write and verify a fix, then generate a short video explaining the root cause and the fix. Much faster to digest than the usual wall of text.

An engineer then just reviews and ships it.”

This reminds me of OpenAI’s Perf Factory agent, except that at OpenAI the agent continuously monitors for performance regressions. I’m expecting many more companies to build the same loop, as it seems like a natural part of the new “software factory” which most tech companies are putting together.

Foursquare’s sale disappoints

Location startup Foursquare was founded in 2009 and was valued at $650 million in 2014. The service remains popular, but the business has been struggling. It was sold last month to the adtech company Infillion, but it was not a happy transaction. Foursquare co-founder Dennis Crowley explained in a post:

“The Foursquare acquisition was a $0 outcome for equity holders – $0 for preferred, $0 for common. It’s bittersweet to see these details surface publicly – at least now there’s an opportunity to comment on them.

I was heartbroken by this ending. There are so many people who put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare – the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1,600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth… nothing?”

Foursquare is a reminder that startups are risky and equity’s value can shrink to zero. Employees who exercised their stock options (spending money on exercising them and paying taxes on paper gains) have lost money as a result.

Claude Code’s speed increases threefold with gzip

Claude has shortened its time to first token by 3x, by compressing data sent over the network with gzip:

There’s a slight irony here: modern browsers handle gzip automatically – and gzipping text content is common for modern servers – but this new optimization technique was not employed for more than a year after Claude Code’s release. It suggests there’s plenty of “low-hanging fruit” to be had in performance optimization tricks – many of which may already be widespread.

DeepSeek banned from US federal agencies

The Department of Homeland Security published a notice on Tuesday (20 October) instructing civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek products and ‘any third-party services developed using DeepSeek implementations,’ and to stop buying them.

It feels like the first step in an attempt to regulate open-weight models. Then again, given the Pentagon also labelled Anthropic a ‘national security risk’ – and still maintains this label to this day – it’s hard to read a lot into this ban. It’s ironic that Anthropic, a US company, is still classified as a national security risk, when many other candidates for that label are not.

Linus Torvalds: “banning AI-written messages is stupid”

On the Linux mailing list, it was clear that Linus Torvalds had had enough of a discussion about banning AI in commit messages. His response (emphasis mine):

“I don’t understand this whole idiotic concept of “don’t use AI for X”.

Here’s a new rule just for you: don’t use compilers for any of your kernel submissions.

Because if you can’t show that you really understand what the machine is actually doing by writing your code in assembler, then I don’t want to see your code contribution. You clearly aren’t competent if you can’t write it that way.

And btw, you had better not use an editor to write that commit message either.

Because I need you to show me that you can actually write a good commit message without using tools that make it easy to backspace and hide the mistakes you made while typing.

Ok?

Because otherwise those tool-assisted commits of yours clearly aren’t showing that you know what you are doing.

Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be?

So no. We’re not going to make stupid rules that say “you can’t use tools for X”.

The kind of expectations I have is that people do their best and I expect people to understand what they are doing.

But that understanding has very little to do with what tools they use.

And quite honestly, in my experience, the people I respect and call intelligent are not the ones that shy away from using new and interesting tools.”

4. Predictions for the future of software development

Software engineer and Amp cofounder Thorsten Ball recently made a series of predictions about the future of software development, including some bold ones:

Open source in its current form doesn’t make sense anymore. “Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow” is still true, but now we have artificial eyeballs.

Tokens are the new computing paradigm. Everything will be re-made on top of it. We’ve had deterministic computers for 80 years, so we confuse “how computers have worked” with “how computers must work.” We’re entering the post-binary era.

The terminal is dead. Most developer tooling will be washed away by tokens. Shells, text editors, CLI tools won’t be used by humans anymore. There’s no need to know command line flags and jq invocations anymore. It’ll be seen as arcane as knowing how to write everything as a Perl one-liner. (I’m saying this as a lover of the terminal & dev tools.)

There’s no proof that “good code” will matter in the future. The notion of “good code” itself is mostly based on the idea that it’s easy/cheap/efficient for humans to work with. But humans won’t modify the majority of code. Think of how dumb it is to assume that “...only 80 columns wide” or “but newlines here and there” matters for agents. Now, consider all the other properties you have in mind for “good code”. Yes.

The differences between software engineering at large corporations and small ones will increase. Start-ups adopting the practices of Google will look even sillier than before because they can now build so much faster and with so many fewer constraints.

The craft of building software will be more important than ever. Knowing how to solve business problems with software, how other software did it and why and why not, when and how to ship it, how to get feedback on it – that’s the new game.

Thorsten’s final prediction:

“It’ll take a while for this to play out. It’ll take a generation for the “new software” to replace the “old software”. Just like there are people happily employed as ASP developers today, there will be people employed to write code in 10 years. But would you want to have that job?”

I recommend reading the full post for more.

The revised rules of engineering management with Will Larson

Will Larson, CTO of Imprint, explores how AI and shifting industry expectations are changing engineering management, career ladders, and the path from engineer to CTO.

Gergely Orosz
Oct 21
 
READ IN APP
 

Before we start: I’m very excited to announce an The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged live event: with Diogo Almedia (the creator of Jev) and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO, Oxide). 4 November (Wednesday), San Francisco, the SFJAZZ Center. It’s free to attend, but spaces are limited and registration is required.

Stream the latest episode

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

In this episode

What’s changed in “the unwritten rules” of engineering management since the 2010s, what drove the shift to today, and what has it done to the engineer-to-CTO career path? Today’s guest is one of the best people I know who can tackle these questions.

Will Larson is CTO of Imprint, was an engineering executive for 10+ years, and is the author of several popular books on engineering leadership, including ‘The Engineering Executive’s Primer,’ ‘Staff Engineer, An Elegant Puzzle,’ and ‘Crafting Engineering Strategy.’ Previously, he was also CTO at Carta and Calm, and an engineering leader at Stripe and Uber.

In this episode, we explore how engineering leadership has evolved from management practices shaped in the long post-financial-crisis ZIRP era to the altered expectations of engineers and managers today.

Is middle management an increasingly precarious career path, and might managers need to reskill and return to hands-on technical work – or even consider retirement? Will makes the case, and we hear why the traditional path to engineering executive roles is changing, as well as why taking one step backward might sometimes be the best way forward.

We discuss Will’s early career, and get his first-hand account of Digg’s disastrous relaunch, his own path to CTO, and he tells us why career ladders still matter. We also explore how AI is changing engineering roles and bringing technical decision-making back to leadership.

Takeaways from the conversation with Will

Here are some standout talking points from our conversation, during which Will recommends middle managers to go back to line management and re-skill like he has done. He didn’t ask me to, but I want to mention that he’s hiring for several key engineering manager roles at Imprint to use agents to rethink how software teams work.

1. Will shares an inside account of how a 10 website sank into irrelevance after a v4 rewrite. Digg was the “king” of social media sites in the late 2000s; bigger than Reddit, and one of top-10 most visited websites, globally. That all crashed to a halt in 2010 when the company embarked on a massive rewrite called Digg v4 – and it was a disaster. It was the start of Digg’s downfall.

Will worked at Digg during this rewrite, and shares how Digg was already losing traction and traffic to Facebook, and that Google changed its algorithm which caused 60-70% traffic loss. From the outside, Digg looked like it was growing, but its business prospects were shrinking fast. The company had about 120 people and was burning through money fast.

Into this entered the v4 rewrite, which was carried out to a hard deadline set by Kevin Rose, the newly-returned CEO at the time. The v4 version alienated passionate users, and had major performance and reliability problems.

Will and a small engineering team fixed the issues. The root cause was Python memory leaks introduced by devs who didn’t know Python so well. Will has shared more detail on his blog.

Even so, Will doesn’t think the rewrite killed Digg: with or without that rewrite, Digg would’ve met the same fate of being overtaken and replaced by Facebook and Reddit.

2. At Yahoo, a “black market” for servers popped up after the cofounder insisted on personally approving new servers. A hilarious story of how incentives drive behavior: Yahoo cofounder, David Filo, wanted to drive accountability by teams justifying every server purchase. This created a “black” market and Will recalled that one engineer on his team had 30 servers left from a canceled project that he traded with devs who could not get approvals elsewhere, in exchange for stuff he needed. Also, servers didn’t have to be returned, so Yahoo ended up running a large number of outdated, power-hungry machines!

3. In the 2000s, having annual 1:1s with managers was normal. Will worked at Yahoo in 2008-2010 and had two 1:1 sessions with his manager: one in which they asked Will about someone else’s performance, and the next one when he handed in his notice after it finished. It was pretty common for 1:1s with managers to be rare things at the time.

4. Too many Staff+ engineers only want to work on fun problems. At Stripe, Will led an org of about 250 people, where lots of the most senior engineers regularly sought more “engaging” problems to work on. Will eventually found his optimal response:

“I only have suffering to offer, but this suffering is what’s going to make the business succeed.”

However, he felt that he was seen by some as guilty of violating an unwritten rule of management by not finding enough – or interesting enough – problems for them to engage with. Today, at Staff+ levels, engineers putting business problems first is a baseline expectation.

5. ZIRP shaped engineering management practices in the 2010s, Will believes. ZIRP stands for zero interest rate period – and we did a deepdive on the impact ZIRP had on engineering management. He recommends the article ‘ZIRP explains the world’ by Ranjan Roy. From Will:

“Back then, your ability to hire and close and retain became the differentiator between successful companies. The less successful ones simply couldn’t retain great people.

[This dynamic on hiring and retaining] pulled leverage back into the engineer’s hands and created a very different environment. So, companies were pitching themselves as a more relaxed environment, more focused on you, and offering more career development. And I think in ways that I think were often kind of self-defeating.”

6. “Hire more engineers” used to be the answer from many engineering leaders in the 2010s. Today, it’s not, he says:

“I tell my teams that I work with now that hiring is the least interesting way to solve every problem. We should almost never talk about hiring.

But in the 2010s, we basically told managers they couldn’t think about technological solutions. And then what do they have? They have process solutions, they have scheduling, or they have people to hire.”

7. Focus on engineering wellbeing could have led to less reliable software. During the 2010s, several companies chose to not put the highest-paid engineers oncall, and for it to be handled by others. But when engineers are oncall for the software they build, it leads to better, more reliable software. Back then, not having oncall was a way to hire and retain talent, but it also led to lower quality as engineering teams did not feel the pain of outages caused by their own software.

Side note from Gergely: I wonder if AI agents will make a difference here. One of the worst things about oncall is getting awoken by the pager. Could we design loops that automatically mitigate incidents that we expect and are well-prepared for?

8. Software engineering change is more extreme, and it’s driving away some engineers. Will knows someone who decided to retire from tech because AI has destroyed the ability to be “in the flow.” Engineers are being more productive, but enjoy it less. By focusing on the outcomes, Will says he’s having a great time.

9. The tech lead manager role is now very in demand. Will wrote previously about how the tech lead manager role is a career trap, and I have a similar opinion in the deepdive ‘Engineering leadership skillset overlaps:’

Things are changing inside companies; EMs are starting to manage 12-14 people, instead of 4-8, as before, while Directors are managing more TLMs. At Imprint, some of Will’s best hires have been managers who also want to write software. The TLM role is perfect for this. In his book, he describes a great TLM as someone who has the capability, but no desire, for bureaucratic work; by default, they’re builders.

10. Engineering managers used to expect not to make technical decisions, but that’s outdated now. Will recalls:

“One of the worst parts of being an engineering manager in the 2010s was when you joined the ranks of engineering management, one of the first lessons you’d get was: ‘you need to never make a technical decision again.’ That’s literally what I was told.”

It was the same advice I received when becoming an EM: let your engineers make the technical decisions, get out of their way, and support them in growth. The tide is very much changing these days, with more tech companies expecting managers to be hands-on and in the details.

11. Great engineering executives (CTOs, VPEs) need to be technologists and bureaucrats. Will believes an engineering executive has two jobs:

  • Be a bureaucrat: manage incentives, create and deal with bureaucracy, and know how to navigate it. The job often includes running functions you know nothing about

  • Be a technologist: know what to build, how it works, and whether a technology choice makes sense or not

Will reckons that until recently, many engineering executives from the middle-manager path were bureaucrats before they were technologists.

12. Blunt message for middle managers: retire or re-skill. Will left a team of 250 at Carta to head up 25 tech people at Imprint. He purposely took a “step back” in his leadership career because he believes things are changing so radically that the engineering leadership profession that we know will not exist in three years.

Amid all this, Will says that line management can be a lot more engaging for executives these days because the tools for line management and the tools for writing software are really good. However, the tools of bureaucracy are still pretty terrible, he believes. That’s why some talented engineering folks get jaded about the work:

“For a lot of folks, there is this sense the industry has betrayed them and that they’re owed something that they’ve worked for. And the thing is, they’re right!

They have worked incredibly hard, but the rules have changed. Since the 2010s, we’ve forgotten that our industry is actually very volatile. We really do just get paid to do things that are valuable to the companies. There’s no entertainment orientation to why these companies employ us.”

LLM Prompt Caching Versus Semantic Caching

ByteByteGo
Oct 21
 
READ IN APP

Caching is a super important aspect of system design, especially for large-scale systems. You can use a cache to store some data that is expensive to calculate so that it can be reused later without paying the same cost. For example, a website might cache the result of a database query instead of running that query every time someone opens a page.

The same is the case for large language models. Just like normal systems, caching in LLM applications also means storing stuff calculated as part of earlier requests so that we can reuse it later. This helps bring down processing costs and response time, especially when requests contain the same instructions, documents, or questions.

However, there are two types of ways we can cache stuff in LLMs: prompt caching and semantic caching. Both have the same general aim of reducing repeated work, but they work at different stages of a request. They also follow different rules.

In this article, we’ll look at how LLM caching works in detail. Here’s what you’ll learn:

  • Why an LLM request costs money

  • What is prompt caching

  • Where to place the shared content in prompt caching

  • What is semantic caching

  • The difficulty with semantic caching

  • Why checking the question is not enough

  • When to invalidate the cache

  • How prompt and semantic caching can work together

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

Why an LLM Request Costs Money

When you send some text to an LLM, the LLM processes that text and generates a response. During processing, the text is divided into tokens. Each token is a small piece of text. A token can be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.

These tokens directly impact the cost. For a typical text-generation API, the cost has two main components:

  • The tokens provided as input.

  • The tokens generated as output.

Output tokens often cost more for obvious reasons. However, the input tokens can also cost a lot because of the size. Input can include much more than just the user’s latest question. For example, let’s say you have a customer-support application. Along with the current question, this application can also send a bunch of instructions telling the model how it should behave. It might also send examples of good answers. Relevant product documentation. Earlier conversation messages. In other words, a 10-word question can be part of a request made up of 1000s of input tokens.

Let’s say you have another application that sends a long product manual with every user request. This product manual is like an encyclopedia of all the information that the user might be looking for. One user might ask about the installation procedure. Another asks about troubleshooting. Maybe a third user asks about account settings. While their questions happen to be different, the answers are all there in the same long product manual that is part of every request.

There is another type of repetition as well. 100s of users might ask how to change their profile picture. But each user might write the query using slightly different words. In such a case, the model may end up generating the same rough answer again and again.

As you can notice, we have two opportunities to reduce this repetitive work and bring down costs:

  • What if the application can reuse the input information that has already been processed once? For example, the product manual.

  • What if the application can reuse a previously generated answer if it is suitable? For example, similar questions asked again and again.

Prompt caching is used to exploit the first opportunity. Semantic caching is for the second one. Let’s look at both in detail.

Prompt Caching: Reusing the Model’s Input Processing

To make caching effective, you need a rule to decide whether something is fit for reuse. This rule is the most important part of building an effective cache setup.

For prompt caching, the rule is to match the beginning of the model’s input.

A typical text-generating transformer model works in two stages:

  • First, it processes the input. This stage is called prefill.

  • Second, it generates new tokens. This stage is called decoding.

When processing the input, the model converts text to numbers. This numeric representation helps the model use information it read earlier to generate output tokens down the line. Some of these representations are called keys and values. Or KV states.

Keys help the attention mechanism find out which earlier information is useful. Values are the actual representations of that information. A KV cache stores these intermediate results so that they can be reused. This is all part of the ordinary text generation flow in an LLM.

Prompt caching piggybacks on this reuse setup. It extends the whole thing for all the compatible input requests that share the same beginning. Let’s say you have the following two requests:

Request A: Support instructions + product manual + “How is installation configured?”
Request B: Support instructions + product manual + “How are diagnostic logs enabled?”

As you can see, the support instructions and the product manual are shared across both requests. They are known as the shared prefix. The actual question is part of the suffix that keeps changing for each input request.

After the model processes Request A, the system can store the KV states for the shared prefix. When Request B arrives, the model can reuse those same KV states to process the new question and generate the answer. We’ve reused the intermediate computation for the common context. No recalculation. No reprocessing.

Where to Place the Shared Content in Prompt Caching

For prompt caching to work, we need to put the shared content at the beginning of the request. Basically, the prefix position. The word “prefix” is important here because a token’s internal representation depends on the information that comes before it in the input.

In a typical causal language model, the tokens that come earlier in the prompt can’t look forward at the question that might appear later in the request. This is why a model can reuse the shared stuff from the beginning even when the final user question is completely different.

However, when you place a different question before the manual, it changes the way the manual is processed. The question impacts the representation of the text in the manual. The manual’s text is the same. But the processed version is completely different.

This is the reason we have to place fixed, stable instructions or any shared reference material before the request details that can change. Even if you place a seemingly unimportant timestamp or random request ID at the beginning of the input, it can stop the model from reusing a large chunk of shared stuff.

To be clear, even the instructions need to be “exactly” similar. Even if you have two instructions that might mean the same thing, you cannot use them interchangeably for prompt caching. There should be no change in wording. No change in document order. No change in request settings.

The Cost Savings from Prompt Caching

Simply caching the shared prefix doesn’t make the cost zero. Most LLM providers usually charge it at a discounted rate. Also, the output token charges stay the same because the model still generates a fresh answer.

For reference, Anthropic’s standard prompt-cache pricing uses a cache-read rate of 1/10th of the ordinary input rate. There are some exceptions for particular models. Its standard 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the ordinary input rate, while a 1-hour write costs twice that rate. These are total rates for the affected tokens, rather than additional charges on top of their ordinary input cost.

As an example, if processing a prefix normally costs $1, that five-minute pricing schedule makes the initial write cost $1.25 and a subsequent read cost $0.10. Therefore, one write followed by one read costs $1.35 instead of $2. The more the number of reads, the greater the savings. But if a cached prefix is never reused, you don’t get any benefit.

LLM provider and model rules also determine minimum eligible lengths, expiration, and cache-write pricing. Even if we repeat a prompt, it doesn’t guarantee a cache hit if the cache record has expired or is unavailable.

To summarize, prompt caching mainly reduces input-processing work and can reduce the wait time before we generate a response. You cannot use it to eliminate the work that goes into generating a long answer.

Semantic Caching: Reusing a Previous Answer

Semantic caching is usually part of the application that surrounds an LLM. It can also be a separate service that the application calls before it goes to the LLM for an answer. Consider a couple of example questions that you might ask an LLM:

“Where is the setting for dark mode?”
“How can I switch the app to its dark theme?”

As you can notice, the same answer may be able to satisfy both questions if there’s no change to the application features in a major way. But a simple text comparison would consider them as two separate questions with two different answers. However, a semantic comparison can identify that they are essentially the same query asked in slightly different words.

To implement semantic caching, you need an embedding model. This type of model converts text into a list of numbers called a vector. These numbers represent features of the text in a way that makes it easy to compare two pieces of text.

The overall flow works as follows:

  • The embedding model creates an embedding for the incoming question.

  • It searches question embeddings that are already stored for suitable candidate answers.

  • It checks whether a candidate answer is similar and valid for the current question.

  • If accepted, it returns the stored answer. Basically, a cache hit.

  • On a miss, it calls the LLM to generate a fresh answer. It may store the answer for future reuse.

As you can see, if there’s a cache hit, we don’t have to call the LLM to generate a fresh answer. No input and output charges in that case. However, tasks like embedding generation, lookup, and cache storage still use resources. So it’s not all free. Also, if we have a cache miss, we pay for the preliminary tasks as well as the LLM request. So a miss ends up being more costly.

The Difficulty With Semantic Caching

The most difficult part with semantic caching is to find out how similar two separate questions are.

In a semantic cache, we calculate a similarity score and compare it to some threshold. You can think of this threshold like a cutoff for accepting that the questions are similar.

If we keep a very strict threshold, we end up rejecting many more answer candidates. While this can improve accuracy and reduce inappropriate reuse, it also rejects a lot of legitimate paraphrases of the question. However, if we go for a loose threshold, more answer candidates get accepted. This increases the overall cache hit rate. But it also increases the possibility of returning an unsuitable answer. There is no single, universal threshold that works perfectly for every application. You need to decide the threshold on a case-by-case basis.

Let’s say a user asks two questions about cancelling an order before it gets shipped and after it gets shipped.

As you can see, both questions are almost the same. Except for one critical word that changes the meaning. Both questions deal with cancellation and shipping. Their embeddings may also be quite close. But a short answer of “Yes, cancellation is available” could be the correct answer for one, but totally incorrect for the other.

Data types like numbers, negation, dates, product editions, and eligibility conditions can cause similar problems while determining similarity. For example, “Does the Basic plan include backups?” cannot automatically reuse the answer to a question about the Pro plan.

Also, we cannot consider a similarity score the same as the probability of an answer being correct. For example, even if you get a similarity score of 0.92 between two questions, it doesn’t mean there is a 92% chance that the cached answer is suitable for both. The way we interpret the score depends on the embedding model and comparison method. Some systems expose a distance score instead, in which smaller values indicate closer matches.

Therefore, we need to have an evaluation process to find out the effectiveness of a semantic caching implementation. This evaluation process has to find out if a particular stored answer can satisfy a new request correctly. For testing purposes, the development team can collect a bunch of requests, identify candidate answers, and label whether reusing a specific answer is the right way. The test suite should have examples that cover legitimate paraphrases as well as difficult near-matches. This way, we have a better chance to find out the optimal threshold value.

Lastly, we need to measure the proportion of requests answered from cache and the proportion of those answers that are actually appropriate. We cannot celebrate just by achieving a high hit rate. We can also have an additional verifier that checks border cases. However, such a verifier also contributes to costs and latency.

Why We Can’t Rely On Just Checking the Question

You can ask the same question multiple times. But every time, you might expect a different answer. For example, a question like “What is my order status?” depends on the customer and the current status of the order. Similarly, a question such as “Does it support offline access?” depends on what the word “it” means in the conversation’s context. Also, if the user requests an answer in a different language, we can’t automatically respond with a cached answer generated in English.

Therefore, for a semantic cache to work, we need information beyond just the question to make the right decisions. Depending on the application’s use case, we may need to include stuff about the customer or organization, access permissions, product version, language, relevant conversation state, and source-data version.

Also, we need to enforce these conditions as part of the application. You cannot expect an embedding model to find the details of a customer just because the user included a customer identifier in the input question. Typically, semantic-cache implementations need to have metadata filters so that searches can be restricted to an appropriate scope.

There is another example that shows a specific complication. If the user asks questions such as “What’s the weather in NYC?” and “NYC weather today?”, they might look like suitable matches. But their answers depend on whether the user is looking for current conditions or a daily forecast. While generating an answer, we need to consider location, date, forecast period, units, and freshness.

When To Invalidate the Cache

There are chances that a cached answer might appear like an excellent match for a new question. But the answer might still be wrong because the source information behind the answer may have changed.

Let’s say you have an application that allowed product returns to take place within 30 days. Now the company has changed the policy. The product return time period has been reduced to 14 days. However, a cached answer might still talk about the old time period of 30 days. In this case, you might ask the same question and get the cached answer, which is no longer valid.

This is why we need to have a strategy for invalidating the cache.

Invalidation means making a cache entry unavailable for reuse. We can use multiple approaches to build an ideal invalidation setup.

The first approach is to define a TTL value. A TTL (time-to-live) adds an expiration time to a cached record. Deciding the TTL value is the key. If we keep a short TTL, we place a strong limit on how long stale information can stay eligible within the system. But there is still some gap that will always remain. TTL cannot guarantee freshness of data before expiration. For example, if a policy changes immediately after an answer is cached, that answer can be stale till the TTL expires.

The second approach is to use versioning. You can allow reuse of data based on a specific version. For example, an answer cached under policy_version=12 is ineligible when the application expects version 13.

It’s much easier to have a version that contains the entire knowledge base. But there’s a disadvantage. One small update can make the entire knowledge base invalid. All the cached answers are suddenly stale. However, if we invalidate only those things that have changed, it’s much more efficient. Much more selective. But to make it work, we need to track which answers depend on which documents or records.

The third approach that can impact cache invalidation is the overall settings we have used to generate answers. Things like high-level instructions. Output formats. Model behaviour guidelines. And so on. These settings matter a lot when deciding when to invalidate a cache. If these settings are changed, we should invalidate the earlier answers.

Invalidating a prompt cache is different from its cousin. If the application sends an updated policy in the prompt, the modified prefix cannot reuse an incompatible old version from the point at which the policy changed. However, if there is an unchanged earlier portion, it might still be reusable. Also, if the application keeps providing the old policy as part of every input, prompt caching cannot automatically find out if the actual business rule has changed somewhere. It’s the application’s responsibility to fetch the current policy information and feed it to the model.

Can Prompt and Semantic Caching Work Together

You can use prompt caching and semantic caching in the same setup. They are complementary. For example, you can have the application first look for a valid existing answer using semantic caching. If no such answer is available, only then does the application call the LLM and take advantage of any reusable prompt prefix.

If we get a semantic-cache hit, we don’t need to go for the main generation request. On the other hand, prompt caching reduces the cost of requests that still reach the LLM. We can also have an exact-answer cache that is checked before any semantic lookup happens. It can handle repeated identical requests cheaply.

It’s not necessary that we have a cache lookup at the very beginning of the flow. For example, if the application must retrieve current source versions to validate an answer, that particular check should happen even earlier.

Conclusion

Prompt caching is a natural choice in scenarios where you need to generate fresh answers for different questions. But those answers have to be generated from a shared context. This common context could be a general product manual, a set of instructions, stable tool definitions, or a long conversation history.

Semantic caching is great for cases where the same answer is good enough for many different requests. For example, product FAQs. Stable support instructions. However, semantic caching doesn’t work well when you want to generate highly personalized answers. Or if the answer depends on rapidly changing facts. Also, when there is a need for fresh creative output.

We need to have even greater care for action requests. For example, a cached message saying “The subscription has been cancelled” cannot be a substitute for making a real cancellation.

For a practical implementation of these caching strategies, we need to have some measurements. In the case of prompt caching, we need to measure how many input tokens are reused. This is because there is a major cost difference between serving a request that reuses a tiny prefix and one that reuses a long manual. For semantic caching, we need to evaluate metrics like accepted answers, freshness, and scope. Only those answers that satisfy the application’s quality requirements should be turned into reusable entries.

The ultimate goal with either approach is to lower cost and provide faster responses while preserving answer quality.

References:

  • How caching works

  • Prompt caching

  • Techniques to optimize semantic caching

  • Prompt caching diagnostics
