👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

What’s the ROI of software engineers’ spending on AI?

AI spending has greatly increased at most companies this year, but has it actually changed shipping velocity and PR output? We analyse data from 27 companies – with some interesting findings

Gergely Orosz
Oct 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

A software engineer whose company is looking into its own spending on AI tools pinged me with a very timely question recently, asking what other companies spend on AI, per engineer. They were also keen to find out what the PR throughput was before and after the spending on AI at other places.

Spending on AI agents is ballooning at all the tech companies I talk with this year. With 2027 coming around fast, many companies are seeking to put a realistic number on how much they really spend on AI.

The change in PR throughput is a very simple metric, and one of those “readily-available” measurements at nearly all companies, It’s also one that probably has not been “gamed” by devs yet, and it’s possible to compare a “before AI” and “after AI” measurement with this metric.

To find out more and to try and answer the reader’s question, I asked around and got to talk with engineering leaders and senior+ engineers at 27 workplaces. I also gathered aggregate data from CodeRabbit and Gitar. This article summarizes what I found, covering:

  1. Stats from CodeRabbit and Gitar. Weekly PRs by devs using the AI code review tool increased by around 2x compared to a year ago. Meanwhile, Gitar sees “AI-native” teams ship 60+ PRs/dev/week.

  2. AI spending patterns of 27 companies. Spending caps are common, and there’s no connection between company size and AI spend.

  3. High spenders ($1,000+ per month). A quant shop has seen AI costs increase 15x since January, while a two-person .NET shop spends $3,000/dev/month, plus details from six more companies.

  4. AI spend at Big Tech. Meta and NVIDIA encourage devs to use AI heavily, while engineers at Apple are far more cautious.

  5. Medium spenders. Details from five companies spending $300-500/month/dev.

  6. Low spenders. Companies spending below $300/month/dev, many of which use subsidized subscriptions. Including details from a publicly traded company, a nonprofit, fintech Lendscape (UK), and startups Lonestone (France), Paulina24 (Germany) and 5 others.

  7. What’s the ROI of AI? A question that few companies seem able to answer – at least for now.

The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. Read the full article uninterrupted, online.

Read the full article online

1. Stats from CodeRabbit and Gitar

The team at CodeRabbit polled data engineers using the platform, anonymized it, and has kindly shared it with us. They saw a 113% increase in weekly PRs:

There’s a 127% rise in monthly PRs:

When tracking the same group of 20,000 developers, the increase is nearly identical across the platform: a 128% increase:

Across customer groups, there seems to be “tiers” of PR frequency. Here’s data from Gitar (Sonar’s AI code verification agent) on PRs/week/dev across hundreds of customers:

I suspect that a lot has to do with company culture: whenever you join a new team, you pick up the pace pretty quickly. If the company is one where ~5 PRs per week is considered a high output, then new joiners get used to that pace. If it’s a place where most people ship 20-30 PRs to production per week, then new joiners pick up that pace!

2. AI Spending patterns of 27 companies

I got details on AI spending and changes in the rate of PRs from 27 different companies. I anonymized most names by request. At a glance, here’s how spend looks like:

A few common themes from this data set:

  • Company size and spend on AI are unrelated. In the data set, a 2-person .NET startup spends $3,000/month/dev, and a publicly traded company with 1,500 engineers, limits devs to $150 of AI spend per month.

  • Spend peaked during the summer, and is falling. June and July saw peak monthly spend at nearly all companies, and costs have roughly halved for those on API plans. A mix of Opus 5.5 and moving to open models is the reason for the drop at most companies.

  • Spending caps are common at medium-and-above spenders. It’s normal to have a spending cap in place at medium-and-above spenders, where additional spend needs to be justified. Most people say the caps are easily avoided.

  • Subscriptions conceal concrete AI costs, but some subsidies are ending. Several companies mentioned that their subsidized AI subscriptions are coming to an end, so they need to prepare to either optimize costs, or have their bill increase 5-10x.

  • Claude and Opus 5.5 seem to be the favorite models. Within this rather limited data, Claude and Opus 5.5 dominated answers about where most of the spending goes. Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot were also mentioned.

3. High spenders ($1,000+ per month)

Here are details of companies spending considerable amounts each month on AI coding tools.

Quant trading shop, ~5,000 staff (circa 2,000 devs)

This company has seen its AI spend balloon overall: total spend was $8M/month in September, a 16x increase on the $500K/month spend in January!

The average spend is $1,600/dev/month (up from around $80 in January). Most are going to Claude, and the biggest spenders are not devs, but traders. A current engineer there told me:

“Lots of traders are using Claude. Engineering is learning the importance of rate limiting for traders who accidentally run expensive queries without realizing it.”

The company has a $25,000 limit per employee for AI, which is extremely high, more than at NVIDIA! The engineer explained this generous limit:

“The last few years have, generally, been extremely profitable for trading firms. For us, last year was our most profitable year ever – and we’re already on track to beat it this year. So, the spend on AI is well within what these companies can afford.”

AI outlay is expected to grow: this firm is building its own internal GPU and CPU farms to run models, and are building models expected to beat state-of-the-art (SOTA) models like Fable, according to their own data.

ROI is measured differently at trading firms. The ROI of any spend is the profit or loss made by a trading desk, and AI spend is now part of the costbase. So, provided the desk’s profit increases, no questions are expected.

Small .NET startup, 2 devs, EU

Outside of Big Tech where the monthly AI spend can be $10K+ for some people, the largest per-developer bill comes from a two-person .NET shop in Europe. This agency builds assessment games for a niche, global HR platform. Everything is built in C# and Blazor, running on Azure. A single tech stack was a great decision, especially now, they told me.

$3,000/month/dev (€2,500/dev/month) is what they spend on AI tools. Most of the spend goes on Claude Opus, and GitHub Copilot. One of the devs told me:

“We barely type code anymore. We do a lot of feature development, but also a ton of backlog cleanup. Most of our systems are 5-10 years old.

We do about 60 PRs/dev/week (so around 10-15/day). It’s amazing how fast we’re clearing out our ~10 years-old backlog.

If you have high agency and know what to build, these are fun times!”

PR frequency: up 5-10x. As this engineer told me:

“We used to do 1-2 PRs per day, and now it’s 10+. It feels like our two-person team is doing the work that would have taken about 5-7 people before AI.”

Series D, hospitality sector, 1,000 employees, ~200 engineers, US

$1,500/dev/month is the default spending cap, but devs can ask for an increase. A current software engineer told me they spent $2,200/month in September. with Opus 5. With the latest version, Opus 5.5, this dev expects their spending to be cut in half.

PR frequency has not much changed. This engineer told me:

“We aim to maintain the previous PR standard in terms of PR size and quality. We have, however, built an agent to review PRs and point out, e.g., large PRs, verbose code, and similar things, and that part is going well.”

Publicly traded SaaS company, ~2,500 staff, ~600 engineers, US+EU

$1,200/month/dev is the budget limit, but a Staff Engineer at the company reports that fewer than 5% of devs hit this mark.

PR volume: it’s up (no data). However, the velocity of PRs merged has not seemed to change much! From the same engineer:

“We have a complicated codebase in my team and even frontier models like Opus 5.5 are still doing weird things when someone delegates thinking to them.

We still do human PR reviews, and they catch a lot of stuff that agents and agentic review misses, like changes that are not needed at all, or those that are 10 times bigger than they should be.”

The engineer identified areas where AI has helped a lot:

  • Triaging of customer issues. What previously took a whole day sometimes, is now finished in a few minutes with agent work and a maximum one hour of human verification.

  • Research. Devs can get the info on why something was done in code based on Slack/design docs/PRs history, within minutes. Previously, this would take a day or two of manually digging into stuff.

  • Proof-of-concept (POC) prototyping. Creating a POC with very complicated features can be done in a few hours for Product Managers to play with. Previously, this would take a week or two!

When the focus is on quality, velocity probably does not increase all that much. The engineer had this observation:

“Overall, I personally see accelerated slop produced all around me. However, when the team cares about the quality in production code and wants to keep it like before AI, then actual development speed had not increased much.”

Publicly traded company, 25,000+ employees, ~5,000+ devs, US+EU

$1,000/dev/month spend is the average, according to an engineering lead. While not in place yet, the company is considering a $1,000/dev/month soft cap.

PR frequency: 2x In 2025 there were around 4 PRs/dev/week; Today, this is closer to 8 PRs/dev/week. The lead engineer observed a 2-3x increase in PRs by experienced engineers compared to a year ago.

Publicly traded company, 5,000 employees, US+EU

$1,000/dev/month spending cap: this is the default, companywide, and can be spent on any provider, any way that devs want. It’s a “soft” spending cap and it’s trivial to request a larger budget: just fill out a short form to justify it, and it’s approved fast.

A current team lead shared with me the numbers they’re seeing:

  • Most backend engineers use around $1,500/month

  • Most team leads / Staff+ engineers are using around $2,500/month.

PR frequency: flat. The team lead observed no real increase compared to a year ago.

PR size: 3x. Meanwhile, PRs have exploded in size and have 3x as many lines of code per change request as before. I wonder if this could be attributed to LLMs being pretty verbose, even when coding.

AI SaaS, ~100 employees, US

$2,000/month/dev allowance for devs. This is through a Claude or Codex Max subscription, plus credits used.

This company has a public #ai-limits Slack channel, which publicly pings those nearing their limit, as well as top spenders and reminds them to rein in their AI usage, if possible; it sounds a bit like a “public embarrassment” strategy!

Getting an increase is more complicated than at most companies. As a current engineer explained to me:

“When needing a limit increase, you run an AI skill that looks for common reasons why you might be burning tokens. It looks through things like whether you are running too many loops, or using subagents, and more. It gives suggestions on how to fix those.

If the skill doesn’t find things to improve, then submit an approval request to the manager for a budget increase. Personally, I’ve rarely seen these increases granted, so everyone treats the $2K as a hard cap.”

Velocity: unchanged. The engineer told me they don’t see anything getting done faster than before:

“We are perhaps marginally faster in a few places. AI has not fundamentally changed any of our processes, and I wonder if this is one reason. Most people are still sleeping on AI to be honest, and are adopting it very slowly. There are the odd outliers like myself and a few others who’ve been able to push a ton more, particularly on greenfield projects or anything without blockers around OSS.”

Multinational company, 10K+ employees, US / EU / Asia

$4,000/dev/month maximum capped spend. This is a hard cap. Engineers at this company use GitHub Copilot and can choose between the models. Right now, Opus 5.5 is the top choice for devs across the company, a current team lead told me.

$1,000/dev/month is what the average spend feels like, though from this team lead looking around the org. People are not getting close to the $4K monthly cap.

PR frequency: 4x compared to the start of this year for a single team, led by a team lead, who told me:

“We had about 1.5 PRs/dev/week in January, and this is around 4 PR/dev/week today. However, these numbers are skewed because we have one engineer whose productivity has skyrocketed, while the others have not seen all that much change.”

Velocity: 3x more stories closed than last year. This team lead has been using Scrum and Kanban for years at the company, which helps compare “business value delivered”, not just PRs. They told me:

“For the last 5 years, we used Scrum + Kanban and always used a plan board. On average we close 3x more user stories per month since feb/march. It tells me we deliver more business value.

And, for the first time ever we close more user stories than we have incoming! Keep in mind, this is all while not the whole team is there yet with AI.”

4. AI spend at Big Tech

Some of the most “AI-pilled” places are in Big Tech, which is also home to some of the least “AI-pilled” approaches of all. Here are details about Meta, NVIDIA, and Apple:

Meta seems to truly have no limit on token spend, which is not all that surprising given the company is building very capable frontier models, making it among the most “AI-pilled” Big Tech companies. Here are details from a current software engineer at the high end of spenders:

“My current monthly spend is $20-30K. I am kind of insane about using AI though, so I wouldn’t use myself as a benchmark for the company. At the same time, the agents I built and run have identified close to $1M in potential savings.

This week I shipped ~50 PRs, though not sure how relevant that number is, given that it’s less about the number of PRs shipped and more about the business value created.”

NVIDIA sets a $10,000 per month spend limit. To exceed that, an exception is needed and these are very easily granted, a current engineer told me. But not everyone is “AI-pilled” there. A senior engineer working at the hardware giant told me:

“AI usage is at wildly different levels. Former 10x engineers become 100x engineers, getting very good at leveraging AI. It starts to become really hard to understand even in my team why others are so ‘slow’, and I start losing touch with reality.”

About a month ago, an internal token leaderboard was accidentally exposed for a day or two. Here, the top user in the month spent 3 trillion tokens. With a monthly token spend of 40B, you could make it to the top 100 in the company. PRs are up ~2x on a year ago, according to a team I talked with.

Apple is worth mentioning because it has the complete opposite approach to AI usage: talking with a few engineers inside the company, AI usage is not nearly as encouraged as it is at any other Big Tech companies, and Claude had been explicitly marked as not to be used on a few teams – although others use Claude Code. Apple is very secretive, even internally, so it’s hard to get universally reliable information, even on things like tooling.

From talking with current engineers, the vibe I got was that Apple executives are a lot less “AI-pilled” than the rest of Big Tech. And, in general, engineers there whom I talked to are more wary of AI-generated code not being properly reviewed and messing up production systems. Given the choice, they opt for safety over speed, and I’ve not heard of pressure from above to use AI at Apple, nor of any tracking of people’s usage of it.

From the devs I talked to, business seems to be as usual inside the Cupertino tech giant: more devs use AI assistance, but the frequency of PRs doesn’t seem to have visibility changed, at least inside of their own teams.

At the time of publication, NVIDIA and Apple have nearly the same valuations, and are the two most valuable publicly-traded companies, globally (NVIDIA: $5.2T, Apple: $5T).

5. Medium spenders

Here’s data points for companies allocating $300-1,000 per engineer each month for AI usage.

Publicly traded company, 5,000 employees, 1,500 engineers, US

From an engineering lead:

  • $500/month/engineer: median spend in August 2026

  • $300/month/engineer: median spend today (Oct 2026). The company brought down this number by asking devs to voluntarily move to open-weight models, which are cheaper and similarly capable

  • $1,000/month/engineer: the p90 number

PR frequency: 1.6x increase. A 60% increase over a year ago. PRs are about 25% larger than before, and the committed lines of code are about twice as a year before.

A stable, growing business with ~70 engineers

$500/engineer/month is the median (p50) spend.

PR frequency: 2.5x increase. Details:

  • January 2026: 1.65 PRs/dev/week

  • Leadership set a mandatory minimum 4 PRs/week/engineer target starting this month

  • The engineering lead I talked with thinks that by the end of the year, most engineers will probably produce 5 PRs/week

  • The top 10% of engineers are already producing 20 PRs/week

It’s worth pointing out that PRs-per-week is just one metric that doesn’t indicate business value generated, but does indicate the granularity of the work. This company started from a place of devs not committing much code compared to some smaller companies, which could be due to a more complex codebase, more ambitious work, etc.

Series B, global employment SaaS, ~1,000 people, 150 devs, Asia + EU

~$450/month/dev cap ($100/dev/week). This cap is a hard one and it’s causing some anxiety internally, a current team lead told me:

“Engineers have become very cautious of saving every token because we don’t want to exhaust our tokens and wait for a reset blocking our tasks.”

PR frequency: 2x, versus a year ago. Also, people have stopped writing comments on PRs. From the same engineering lead:

“We rarely get human comments on PRs any more. We check AI-generated comments and resolve them.”

Series A, robotics startup, 50 employees, US

$400/month/dev limit for most engineers. However, power users can request more; up to $5,000 per month. A senior software engineer there summarized the pros and cons of using AI for them:

“It’s great for new hires and helpful for greenfield projects. A new hire definitely gets up to speed faster by conversing with LLMs. And I now see new hires immediately starting to contribute to projects.

For greenfield projects, it provides a good starting shape to a code base, but is not a magic bullet, however, it still speeds up greenfield development. It’s so easy to cognitively offload that I personally am not sure 100% reliance is ideal.

For existing software: meh. For production software, AI often doesn’t offer any improvement, at least in my experience.”

Series C, healthcare startup, US

$300/month/dev budget: this can be split between Codex and Claude Code subscriptions.

PR frequency: 2-10x increase. From a current Director of Engineering:

“We’re seeing a 2-4x increase for slow AI adopters in PR output, and 6-10x for AI power users.”

6. Low spenders (below $300/month)

Slightly over a third of companies I talked to shared that they are spending less than $300/month on AI tools: typically at smaller companies, using a single “Max” subscription that costs $100 or $200/month.

Three-person startup, Germany

Paulina24 is a platform to find nursing jobs in Germany. The team created a website to browse stats on their AI costs and PR frequency:

Series C, fintech startup, 300 employees / 75 engineers, EU

$200/dev/month is the average spend, using a subsidized Teams subscription, the Head of Engineering told me. This subscription would cost $2,000-5,000/month if billed with API spending.

PR frequency: 2x increase, versus a year ago. The numbers:

  • 2025: 3 PR/dev/week

  • 2026: 6+ PRs/dev/week

  • Top 10% percentile: 15+ PRs/week

  • The Head of Engineering is expecting another ~2x increase the next 6 months, and to get to 2-3 PRs per day (10-15/week) by Q1 2027

Software development agency, 20 devs, EU (France)

Lonestone is an agency building tools, apps and websites, and uses AI heavily. Cofounder Pierrick Bignet shared these details with me:

$250/dev/month is the average spend (€150-200/dev/month), spent across Cursor, Claude and other variants.

It’s tough to be an agency these days, when pricing is cutthroat. Pierrick explained what the landscape is like for them:

“It’s always been a kind of bloodbath for us in this category: competition is fierce, the global economy impacts us really fast (eg., projects have a budget freeze, government shutdown, etc.) because we are “expandable” for most clients.

We build relatively simple products, in all honesty. Our products are still much simpler than what Big Tech does. Our products are not yet “vibe codable,” but with some good rules and good engineers, they’re not far off.

It feels like a rat race:

  • Everyone in this category is cutting their prices massively.

  • As the economy is shrinking right now, companies have been chasing productivity boosts and dumping their prices. That forces everybody else to do the same.

  • We are lucky that three of us founders are engineers, so we have been spending our weekends and evenings testing and coding for two years straight now.

  • Our findings are then used at scale in the company, but it feels like it’s a never-ending race to stay ahead of our competitors: we can’t stop!”

Some more notes from Pierrick:

“Here’s what we’ve found to work:

  • Define context engineering rules. Here’s what Lonestone uses as rules and more of my thoughts on codebase context engineering. As we start new projects every week, this is the biggest productivity boost yet. Agents know how to use it (doc + rules) and the mandatory CRUD part of every project is now “solved”

  • Keep human code reviews. At the very least, we are reviewing what agents are shipping.

  • Up the quality and do more testing. We observe quality is increasing thanks to mandatory testing (e2e) and more attention-to-detail than before, due to the productivity gains above.

Other notes:

  • AI adoption is very different across the team! Not all the team uses AI at the same rate. Some are still coding by hand and using autocompletion a lot, but most are not typing a single line of code.

  • AI streamlines our operations. We created a “Lonestone Brain”, a harness based on an Obsidian Vault and multiple skills to streamline most of our business operations: generating proposals, ingestion of call transcripts, etc. Our business team is also going way faster than it was.

  • Our project managers and designers are using AI heavily. This “brain” is also used by project managers and designers. Basically, we can output all the specifications for mid-size projects after a few days of work (proof reading, calls with clients) and the developers can launch their agents on that. Tomorrow, a code factory may handle most of the basic tasks too.”

Pierrick told me that the current biggest challenge is helping devs to navigate AI. Some devs are simply too anti-AI, while others leave all the thinking to AI, resulting in slop. There are yet others who feel lost and in a crisis!

Series A, SaaS startup, 75 employees, 20 devs, EU

A $20-100/dev/month spend is common. A Head of Engineering there explained to me:

“On my team of 20 people, five devs have $100 licenses, 15 have $20 licenses, and we are on yearly billing. We do not pay for API usage.

Apart from that, we use Aikido and pay an extra ~$100 per month for its AI code reviews. We also use Linear coding agents where we also spend ~$100 per month.”

Total company cost is around $1,000 per month for 20 devs. This is crazy low compared to numbers I read about.

Opus 5.5 has been a game changer for us, too. Previously, several folks prompted Claude Haiku with ‘hi’ on their commute to work to start the 5-hour session limit earlier, and had to be careful which model they use for what. Now it is much easier.”

PR frequency: 32% increase. In January 2026, there were about three PRs/dev/week, now this is four PRs/dev/week. In all fairness, the company took until June 2026 to buy Claude Code licenses despite devs requesting it for months.

The Head of Engineering worries about a quality drop:

“We put a lot of constraints in place in fear of quality dropping. Obsession with tests, 1 engineer working on 1 Linear project at a time, and so on.

When we started using AI, we saw and initial spike in percentage of bugs per ticket. We then invested more in automated code reviews, and now our bugs per tickets is back to pre-AI adoption levels. To me, it suggests that quality has not dropped.”

Fintech, 200 people (~60 engineers), UK

Lendscape is a lending platform used by banks and financial institutions. CTO, Patrick Myles, shared these details:

$65/dev/month average spend, structured as:

  • 60 seats at $20/month

  • 20 at $100/month

  • 10 at $200/month

The subscriptions are heavily subsidized, but the subsidies are going away. As Patrick told me:

“The API equivalent pricing would be ~$940/active use/month. The 5 users would be billed $2,000-6,000/month on AI pricing.

However, our high-quota enterprise seat plan goes away in the next few months, so we expect actual spend for heavy users to move much closer to API-equivalent. Actively working on model routing, alternatives, better measurement and ROI attribution, and so on.”

PR frequency: 2x increase. The company has two products – a legacy one that’s 20+ years old, and a modern one. This product has seen a higher increase in PRs since adopting AI coding tools.

Faster to build new stuff. Patrick told me about a project that was estimated to take 500 engineering days, pre-AI, but the team built it in 100 engineering days with AI tools.

Quality has improved. Being a fintech company, Lendscape pays a lot of attention to quality. Here’s how numbers have changed:

Other companies

Small startup, 5 devs, EU

  • $120/month/dev (100€/month) on Claude Max subscriptions

  • PR frequency: 82% increase.

  • PR size: 77% increase. So, nearly 3x as much code overall!

  • The founder told me that quality feels high with almost no bugs.

Details on the changing PR stats:

Nonprofit, 1,000 employees, EU

  • $100/dev/month Claude Max team subscription. That’s all: no API credits are granted.

  • PR frequency: 4x increase, per dev, per week, versus three years ago. It used to be about 1.5/dev/week, and now it’s around 6/dev/week,

And here’s an interesting detail: PR frequency is up since AI-only code reviews were allowed in April 2026. It’s down to an engineer to merge PRs after an AI reviewer leaves comments:

Publicly traded company, 6,000 employees, 2,500 in the tech function, US / EU

  • $150/dev/month is the average spend at this company.

  • PR frequency: 20% increase, per dev, every 3 months, versus a year ago. There are 24% more lines of code generated in the codebase, according to an engineering manager I talked to, which suggests that PRs are not all that much larger than before.

SaaS, ~50 employees, EU

  • $150/month/dev on average. Outliers can be up to $1,000/month, a senior engineer told me.

  • PR frequency: 2x increase. in PRs per dev, per day. A year ago: 2-3 PRs/dev/day. Today: 5-6 PRs/dev/day

7. What’s the ROI of AI?

One interesting finding from talking with 27 businesses is that very few of them measure the ROI of AI coding tools, or communicate this metric to staff. Among the companies, people at just two shared details about how their company thinks about ROI:

A public SaaS calculated it by how many devs it could hire with its AI spend. The publicly traded company with ~2,500 staff, ~600 engineers in the US+EU, with a $1,200/month/dev budget limit, spends about $700K/month on AI right now.

If all that money was spent on recruitment, the company could hire ~50 more engineers. By their calculation, a simplistic ROI of AI is 12x: for every additional $1,000 spent on AI, they would need to spend $12,000 on hiring an engineer to achieve a similar level of PR output.

Of course, this is simplistic, but it’s one of the very few ROI formulas I heard about.

The public company spending $150/month/dev on average, estimated a 11-30x ROI on AI spend. Here, the calculation was similar. An engineering lead told me that for $1,000 spent on AI tools, they then work out how much would need to be spent on hiring engineers to get a similar increase in output. At this company, PR output “only” increased by 30% since the beginning of the year. They told me:

“In the detailed tests we ran, results on ROI came out to between 11x and 30x. The spread depends mostly on developer proficiency. We have no idea how to measure developer proficiency with AI, at scale. I do believe that during the adoption phase, people will experiment and do things that would not be created without a low barrier to ship to production.”

I admit that I’m surprised this company kept to a relatively low spend compared to their peers when they suspect the ROI is high!

Do you know of superior ways to measure the ROI of AI spend, or have you heard of other approaches? Leave a comment below.

Leave a comment

Takeaways

I sense that the debate about the ROI of AI spending will only become more intense, especially among engineering leaders responsible for AI budgets.

A year ago, I had a conversation with Farhan Thawar, the Head of Engineering at Shopify, who told me something along the lines that they could not exactly measure the impact, but knew that AI usage is important, it takes time to get proficient with AI, and you need to spend on it in order to become proficient. He also said that it was a competitive advantage to be a tech company that’s pretty relaxed about AI spending limits, as it signals an organization that trusts engineers and wants them to master new technology.

At companies that limit AI spend to $100/dev/week, and where devs are “saving tokens” so that they don’t run out before the end of the week, it sounds like those devs are expending an awful lot of effort on “token management” which might be better invested in building production software!

Why Shopify Migrated From React Native

ByteByteGo
Oct 20
 
READ IN APP
 

Stop scrubbing through session replays (Sponsored)

Most teams record session replays at a flat sample rate, then spend the next incident scrolling through hundreds of sessions that have nothing to do with the bug.

This hands-on Sentry workshop shows you how to capture the replays that matter:

  • Sample rates and buffer mode, plus the default we recommend

  • Custom React hooks to record a specific user segment, a known-bad URL, or a flow you just shipped

  • Bug reports that arrive with the replay already attached

  • Filters for rage clicks, dead clicks, and custom tags

  • Privacy defaults and how to tune them

Register now

In 2020, the Shopify engineering team decided to go all in on React Native. It saved them a ton of time and money. By using React Native, the developers didn’t have to implement the same feature in both Kotlin and Swift to make it work on Android and iOS. Sure, the framework came with its requirements. But the idea was very successful at the time.

However, in 2026, AI coding agents have made a huge difference to the economics of building mobile apps. Earlier, if you implemented something with React Native, you could justify the savings that came because of it. But now, AI agents have become so good at coding that building the same feature in Swift and Kotlin is much cheaper.

In this article, we’ll look at how Shopify decided to move out of React Native and how they migrated to native mobile development. Here’s what we’ll cover:

  • What is native mobile development

  • Why Shopify chose React Native

  • What changed in 2025

  • Shopify’s migration approach

  • How Shopify ran the migration

  • The agent feedback loop

  • The migration results

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

What is Native Mobile Development

As you might be aware, an iPhone runs Apple’s iOS, and Android phones run Android. Both these OS provide a bunch of facilities to display the UI, handle notifications, and talk to the device hardware.

In native mobile development for a particular OS, you build an application directly using the languages, frameworks, and tools for that platform. This means Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. To be clear, a programming language is different from a UI framework. For example, Swift and Kotlin are programming languages. However, Apple’s SwiftUI and Android’s Jetpack Compose are frameworks. These frameworks give developers the tools to create the real UI with various components like text, buttons, lists, layouts, and animations.

To build natively for both platforms, you need to maintain two implementations of the mobile application. One for Android. Another for iOS. Sure, you can share the backend services for both platforms, but the client code will still be separate.

However, React Native lets you share much of that implementation across both iOS and Android. It’s a framework for building mobile apps using React and JavaScript (or TypeScript). The main benefit of React Native is that many components and application code you write using this framework can work with both iOS and Android. You don’t need to implement every screen independently in Swift and Kotlin. This is because React Native sits on top of the native UI components that are backed by their respective platforms. For example, if you make a component in React Native, it can create the appropriate iOS or Android views without the need for developers to write any platform-specific code.

To be clear, sharing code doesn’t mean that every platform difference is completely gone. You would still have some features that might need platform-specific coding. Also, you need to build, test, and release the application for each OS.

[Webinar] How to stop rewriting your agent’s code (Sponsored)

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

Join us live on Oct 28 (FREE) to see:

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Register now

Why Shopify Went With React Native

The Shopify engineering team went with React Native in 2020. They wanted to solve three problems that were more or less linked.

The first problem was that you had to implement every feature two times with native development. One time for each platform. The second was that you couldn’t share developers between platforms. A developer was confined to their tech stack. An iOS developer couldn’t work on the Android version. Neither could the Android developer work on the iOS version. Not a great way to utilize the developers in a team.

The third problem was that you had to maintain feature parity across both versions. Feature parity is when every version of the app has the same features and capabilities. Let’s say, if you have a cool feature that works on iOS, but it takes another month to be available on Android, you can say that the two versions are out of parity. If you don’t maintain this parity, you risk alienating the user base of the platform that usually runs behind.

Also, when you have two versions of the app, you need to change both versions whenever there’s a change in any requirements. Even if the change is something as small as a text change. As you can see, this is a continuous cost problem that is present throughout the life of the application. You also need to have more coordination between the different platform teams while planning releases, announcements, and so on.

By going with React Native, Shopify reduced the impact of these problems in a big way. No need to implement every feature twice. No need to coordinate changes across multiple platform teams. It also made mobile development easy for developers already familiar with React and TypeScript. This is great because you could easily move people between projects. Plus, you also get to select developers from a much bigger TypeScript or JavaScript talent pool.

What Changed in 2025

As a framework, React Native has a lot of benefits. We have seen that already in the earlier section. But the framework also needs maintenance. This means additional costs.

The Shopify engineering team had to spend effort on optimizing the framework’s performance. They made improvements to the React Native foundations and contributed to framework upgrades. They also had to deal with changes to external dependencies. You can think of a dependency as a piece of software that the application relies on. If there’s a change in the dependency, you need to make changes to the application as well.

Native development is different from using a framework. The application has greater synergy with the platform and first-party tooling. You can use the tools provided by the platform’s own developers. Also, you have fewer dependency layers between the application code and the platform (iOS or Android).

Shopify was already using native code for some features. For example, widgets and watch applications. Also, for some background processing. You could say that React Native and native development coexisted within the application for several years. Of course, the benefit equation tilted more towards React Native.

However, the rise of coding agents made big changes to the equation. As you know, a large language model (LLM) can generate code quite easily. A coding agent combines an LLM with special tools that can read code files, edit code, and run tests. It could also check why things are failing and make changes to handle those failures.

By 2025, these agents had improved so much that Shopify had to take another look at its mobile strategy. To test the waters, the Shopify engineering team rebuilt some core parts of its application in Swift and Kotlin. These prototypes proved that the coding agents could take an implementation on one platform as a reference and write the equivalent code for the other platform.

For example, you can have an iOS feature that provides all the details about the UI elements, actions, and error conditions. An agent can use those details and build an Android equivalent. Sure, developers had to check whether the outcome was good enough and followed the conventions of Android and the overall architecture. However, suddenly, you had developers who could use these agents to code stuff outside their primary stack without a lot of effort.

Of course, with native development, two implementations would still be there. Both will need to be maintained. But Shopify claims that coding agents have reduced the work to such a level that concerns about duplication are no longer as important for making decisions as they were in 2020.

Shopify’s Migration Approach

To carry out the migration to native, Shopify had to choose the best pathway to migrate the existing applications. You have two ways to do so.

First, we have brownfield migration. In this approach, you change an existing application gradually. New and old implementations run together as individual parts are replaced. While the risk is lower, the migration takes more time. Also, you have to manage the integration between the new and old implementations.

Second, we have a greenfield approach. In this approach, you create a fresh implementation. Developers get more freedom to design a new architecture. However, you need to build an almost complete replacement before getting rid of the existing product. There’s no incremental change.

Shopify had used the brownfield approach earlier for some of its large applications. The development methods at the time would have taken too long. However, when they tried the new prototypes, the team found out that a fresh native implementation would be faster. The existing React Native application was a solid reference point for how things should work.

Therefore, Shopify chose the greenfield approach.

They first shipped the Shop app. This app was used by shoppers. The larger Shopify app, which is used by merchants, was migrated later. For reference, the Shopify app has more than 300 screens. Also, many features, such as widgets. And an Apple Watch application.

How Shopify Ran the Migration

When planning the migration, the Shopify engineering team found that if you asked a model to rebuild a large feature in one attempt, you got mediocre results. The output code was difficult to maintain. Also, it was very difficult for developers to properly review big features.

Therefore, Shopify built Helix to support the migration. Helix breaks the migration into small steps that can be reviewed. With Helix, you can have a developer select a screen, and Helix proposes small pieces of migration in the best possible order. Each migration piece has to go through the review process. Only then does it become the foundation for the next piece.

For example, let’s say you have an order detail screen. An initial checkpoint can finalize the structure of the screen and how navigation should work. Later checkpoints will deal with other features such as order summary and customer information. Each checkpoint is small enough that developers can review it properly.

Four types of checks are done to make sure everything works as intended.

First, you have the behavioural tests. You take expected actions on the app and check what happens. Second, you have the visual review. In this, we check how the new UI looks compared with the old reference application.

Next, you have adversarial code reviews. Two reviewers look for problems in the code. They try to find issues that might stay hidden behind a normal workflow. Lastly, we have another developer review where we check the results of the previous tests. If everything meets expectations, things proceed further.

The best part about Helix is that the team gets continuous feedback while the change is still small.

The Agent Feedback Loop

Shopify has a design philosophy that separates app logic from the UI.

For example, you can have a form with rules about valid or invalid inputs. To test them, you don’t need a visible text box. They can receive an input value and return a result.

Shopify’s architectural principle is to keep the business logic independent of the UI. The idea is that the business logic can run headlessly. You can expose the application state and actions through a CLI. This way, the agents can check state, navigate between sections, and perform actions.

While navigating like this without a UI might sound strange, it makes it easy to check how things work. You can have an agent take an action and check the state. There’s no need to make sense of screenshots and find out where a button is located. This is why behavioural checks can be made quite fast.

The Migration Results

The Shop app was live on the app stores as a native application in 12 weeks. There were many interesting stats.

The app startup time on iOS went down from 3200 ms on React Native to approximately 2400 ms on the Native version. The startup time on Android had even greater gains, going from around 4400 ms to 2200 ms. Almost half. The crash-free sessions went up. Also, the app size on Android was down from 293 MB for React Native to 184 MB for the native version.

All in all, these results have been quite encouraging for the Shopify engineering team. Of course, their approach combines a lot of things that make it successful. For starters, you have direct use of platform tech. You also have an existing application, which can act as a strong reference point. Also, the migration process is made smooth with small implementation checkpoints and quality checks.

The main thing we can take away from Shopify’s case is to have a fast feedback loop that can check if the code generated by AI agents is good enough. This is the key to making big migrations like this safe for the users.

References:

  • React Native is the Future of Mobile at Shopify

  • Helix: The internal tools powering Shopify app’s native migration

  • Migrating Shop app from React Native to native

The Bedrock of Software Design

Alex Fedoseev

“Nothing has influenced the way I design software more than algebraic data types. It sounds overly academic—the kind of term that makes people roll their eyes or scares them away altogether. But honestly, it only sounds scary. The idea itself is quite simple, and learning it showed me a fundamentally better way to build software.”

#DeepDive CodeQuality Architecture

How D1 Scales To Millions Of Databases

“The question becomes: how do you scale the control plane for millions of databases without making every query slower by sending it through centralized bottlenecks?”

#Scale Database

References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Problem Genie Is Trying to Solve</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The problem starts with how engineering teams support one another.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a large software-driven company, many teams build platforms that other developers use to perform their jobs. A platform might provide tools for various activities such as software deployment, data processing, or working with ML workflows. Developers from other teams making use of these platforms inevitably need help with configuration, errors, or understanding unfamiliar features.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a typical setup, the team responsible for managing a platform assigns an engineer to handle incoming issues during a particular period. This responsibility is commonly about providing on-call support. Although on-call work can definitely involve urgent production incidents, the problem Genie is trying to solve is geared towards everyday tech support that developers on platform teams provide through Slack channels.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/bd0170d4-fa51-4b2f-8753-5278589e49b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: plaintext;">For example, a developer from a product team might ask how to configure a platform feature. The on-call engineer reads the question and requests more details. The person asking responds, then waits again. Eventually, the on-call engineer identifies the relevant documentation or explains the required steps. Even a relatively straightforward question can involve several rounds of back-and-forth conversation and waiting.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber reports that its internal support channels received approximately 45K questions each month. At that volume, repeated questions consume considerable engineering time that the platform teams could utilize for better stuff.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Much of the information needed to answer such questions already exists somewhere. However, it is often scattered across Engwiki, which is Uber’s internal engineering wiki, or its internal Stack Overflow, and other documents. Finding the right information becomes difficult enough that it is much easier to ask another person.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Genie is designed to make that existing knowledge available through the Slack channels where developers already ask for help.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What does Genie do?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Genie combines finding information with explaining it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A large language model (LLM) can produce readable explanations and answer technical questions. However, its general training doesn’t automatically give it knowledge of Uber’s private platforms, internal procedures, or documentation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, Uber needed a way to connect a language model to its internal knowledge base. Two approaches help with this: fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Fine-tuning means further training an existing model using examples selected for a particular purpose. Uber explains that this approach would require a collection of high-quality, varied training examples, along with sufficient computing resources to update the base model as new examples come up.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">On the other hand, RAG supplies relevant information when a question is asked. The system first searches a knowledge collection, retrieves useful passages, and then gives those passages to the LLM along with the question. The model uses all this information to generate its answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, suppose a developer asks how to change a setting in an internal platform. A RAG system searches the platform’s documentation, finds the passage explaining that setting, and gives it to the model. The model turns the retrieved information into a response appropriate to the question.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber chose RAG for Genie because it could begin with existing documentation and be ready for launch sooner without the need to first assemble a fine-tuning dataset. This still needed a lot of work to collect, prepare, and evaluate the documentation. It also meant that updating the external knowledge collection could improve the information available to Genie without retraining the model for every change in documentation.</p><div bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Genie Gains the Required Knowledge</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Preparing knowledge happens separately from answering questions. Before Genie can retrieve useful information, Uber must turn its scattered documents into a searchable collection. This preparation happens using an ETL pipeline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">ETL stands for extract, transform, and load.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Extraction means fetching content from internal sources.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Transformation means preparing that content for retrieval, including breaking it into pieces and generating numerical representations.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Loading means making the resulting data available to the search infrastructure.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber engineering team uses Apache Spark to run this work. For reference, Spark is a system for processing data across multiple workers, allowing a large preparation job to be divided into smaller pieces of work.</p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The pipeline fetches content through interfaces provided by sources such as Engwiki and Uber’s internal Stack Overflow. It places the results into a Spark DataFrame. Think of it as a table with rows and columns.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At this stage, a row contains information such as the document’s source URL, its text, and additional metadata. Here, metadata is information that describes the document rather than the content of that document.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Keeping the source URL alongside the text is important throughout the system. This is because Genie needs to eventually connect an answer back to the real documentation that supports it. Preserving this relationship during the preparation phase makes it easy to perform source attribution later on.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Genie Finds Specific Information</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Embeddings allow Genie to search for related meaning within its knowledge base. Once Uber has collected all the documentation, the next challenge is finding the passages that relate to a user’s question.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The system first divides documents into smaller pieces called chunks. For example, a long document might contain installation instructions, configuration options, and troubleshooting guidance. However, a question about one configuration option may only need a small part of that document. Chunking makes those smaller passages available as individual retrieval candidates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber uses LangChain to chunk its wiki content. It then uses an OpenAI embedding model to generate an embedding for each chunk. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents aspects of a piece of text’s meaning. An embedding model is designed so that related texts have representations that can be found through similarity search. This helps a system find relevant information even when a question and a document use different wording. For example, a question might refer to a job “taking too long,” while a relevant document discusses an “execution time limit.” These phrases are just examples, but they show why searching for related meaning can be a game-changer when exact keywords differ.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The resulting data keeps each chunk associated with its embedding and source information. The original text still remains essential. The embedding simply helps the search system locate a passage. The passage itself supplies information for the language model to read.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber generates embeddings using custom Python functions executed through Spark. This lets embedding generation fit into the same data-processing pipeline as document collection and preparation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Genie Handles User Questions</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber prepares the search infrastructure to serve questions. Creating embeddings produces searchable data, but that data still has to reach the systems that handle live requests. This is handled through the Pusher stage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Two internal systems are used here:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Sia: </strong><span>This is Uber’s internal vector database solution. A vector database supports searching numerical representations such as embeddings.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Terrablob: </strong><span>This is Uber’s blob storage, which holds stored data and files used by the pipeline and serving infrastructure.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: bootstrap job ingests data into Sia, followed by Spark jobs that build and merge an index that organizes data for efficient searching.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The resulting index data is stored in Terrablob. Serving machines, called leaves, download the base index and synchronize snapshot data. These leaves handle searches against the loaded index when requests arrive.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This separates the work of building searchable knowledge from the work of answering an individual question.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Document preparation and index construction happen through the ingestion pipeline.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Live requests use the index made available to the serving machines.</p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Does a Typical Genie Workflow Look Like</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Each incoming question goes through retrieval before generation. Once the knowledge collection is ready, Genie can answer questions. The central backend component for this is Uber’s Knowledge Service.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Here’s how it works:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">When someone posts a question in Slack, the Genie bot sends it to Knowledge Service. The service converts that question into an embedding.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">It then searches the vector database for document chunks with related embeddings.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The search returns relevant passages associated with their source information. Those passages become part of the material sent to the LLM, together with the user’s question and instructions for answering.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Next, the model generates a response, which is returned through Genie to Slack.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two distinct model responsibilities in this flow.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The embedding model produces numerical representations that support retrieval. On the other hand, the LLM reads the retrieved text and produces the written response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This difference is useful when dealing with failures. Genie might retrieve unsuitable passages, or it might retrieve useful passages and still generate an inadequate answer. Improving the system requires checking both stages.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Genie Makes Sure the Answer is Correct</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber gives the model explicit boundaries for generating its answers. An LLM can generate a plausible statement that is incorrect or unsupported. This behavior is commonly called hallucination. In an internal support system, an invented instruction could send a developer in the wrong direction.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber addresses this partly through how it constructs the model’s input.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Each retrieved result is presented as a separate sub-context, together with its source URL. A sub-context is simply a clearly identified piece of supporting material within the larger prompt. The model is instructed to answer using the provided sub-contexts and to provide source URLs as citations. This gives it explicit evidence to work from and gives the user a way to check the supporting documentation. For example, if several passages discuss different parts of a configuration process, preserving each passage’s source helps the generated explanation remain traceable to the actual source.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These measures reduce the risk of unsupported answers, but a source link doesn’t guarantee that every statement is correct. The retrieved passage must be relevant, the underlying document must be accurate, and the model must represent it faithfully. This is why evaluation remains an essential part of the architecture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber also restricts the knowledge available to Genie. The team preselects sources that are broadly available to Uber developers because some internal information would be inappropriate to expose through model processing or Slack responses.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What if Genie Isn’t Able to Answer Something</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The conversation includes a clear path to human support. A support interaction often continues after the first answer. Someone may need clarification, discover that the suggested information doesn’t quite address their situation, or require an action that documentation cannot provide.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber redesigned Genie’s interaction flow to deal with these possibilities. Its responses include action buttons that let users ask a follow-up question, mark the issue as resolved, or contact human support.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If Genie lacks enough information to answer, it tells the user and directs them to the on-call developers responsible for the platform. When a user escalates an interaction to human support, the human developer takes over while Genie stays muted. This keeps the conversation focused while an engineer handles the issue.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This feature is really important because successful support involves more than producing a paragraph of text. The user needs to understand what to do next. An answer that helps only partially can still be valuable if it leads smoothly into clarification or human assistance.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Genie Collects Feedback</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">User feedback measures the impact of the answer. Uber collects feedback directly in Slack, where users can select a response category.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Resolved:</strong><span> The answer completely resolved the issue.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Helpful:</strong><span> The answer provided some help, but more assistance is needed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Not Helpful:</strong><span> The answer was wrong or didn’t address the question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Not Relevant:</strong><span> The request requires human help that Genie cannot provide, such as a code review.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The differentiation between these categories is very important. Partial help differs from complete resolution. Similarly, an incorrect answer differs from a request that falls outside what a documentation assistant can accomplish.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When a user submits feedback, a Slack plugin collects it together with relevant metadata. It sends that information through a Kafka topic, which acts as a stream of events, into a Hive table, where it can be stored and analyzed in the future. Uber then displays the resulting metrics in a dashboard.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This creates a record of how Genie performs in real use. Without such a record, a system could answer many questions while its operators had little visibility into whether those answers actually helped anyone.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Uber Evaluates the Performance of Genie</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber evaluates both the answers and the documents behind them. User feedback provides direct evidence of Genie’s usefulness. However, Uber also supports custom evaluations of qualities such as hallucination and answer relevance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For these evaluations, a separate pipeline retrieves Genie’s recorded context and responses from Hive. It combines them with relevant information such as Slack metadata and user feedback, then prepares the data for an evaluator.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The evaluator uses an “LLM as a judge” approach. This means a language model receives an evaluation prompt that tells it how to assess the material. Its task is to examine an existing answer against the chosen criteria. For example, an evaluation prompt could ask whether an answer addresses the question and whether its claims are supported by the supplied context.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
