plaintext;">The evaluation results are processed into metrics and published in a report available through the interface. Uber says these evaluations can help plan improvements to both retrieval and generation steps.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The evaluation can also extend to the source documents themselves. This is a particularly useful part of the design because answer quality depends on the material available for retrieval. If a document is unclear, incomplete, or inaccurate, retrieving it successfully may still produce a poor support experience.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Uber’s document evaluation pipeline represents each document as a row in a Spark dataframe. It sends the document and a custom evaluation prompt to an LLM judge. The model returns a score, an explanation of that score, and actionable suggestions for improving the document. These results are published in a report that is also accessible through the Michelangelo interface. For example, a document might describe a procedure while leaving prerequisites unclear. Improving that document can give Genie better material to retrieve and explain, while also helping developers who read the documentation directly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To summarize, the two evaluation processes examine different parts of the system. Answer evaluation checks what Genie produces in a particular interaction. Document evaluation checks the quality of the knowledge from which future answers will be constructed.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Genie was launched in September 2023. Within a year, Uber reported 154 Slack channels using Genie. More than 70K questions were answered during this time. The overall helpfulness rate was 48.9%, which is like a full-resolution rate, with engineering time savings of around 13000 hours.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This cost tracking is generated by following calls through the system. Running a model-backed service across many support channels also requires visibility into its costs. Uber provides that visibility by carrying an identifier through the request flow.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure plaintext;">When a Slack client or another platform calls Knowledge Service, it passes a UUID. Knowledge Service forwards this identifier in request metadata to Michelangelo Gateway. The identifier can be included in an audit log and used to track costs associated with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Genie is a cutting-edge bot with the goal of streamlining on-call management, optimizing incident response, and improving team collaboration. It has the potential to change the entire experience of how users and on-call developers of any platform interact and engage within the respective platform’s Slack channel.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 item.title: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code

about 1 hour by Cindy Sridharan Debugging with AI agents works best when treated as a constraint satisfaction problem, not a code reading exercise. Collect hard facts first from logs, telemetry, DNS, kernel data, and packet captures, then use a control case to separate real signals from noise. Only then should an agent form hypotheses, and each one must satisfy every known fact or get discarded. Cindy argues that understanding systems matters more than understanding code, and that better tooling and processes will do more to improve agentic debugging than individual prompting skill.
item.description: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code

item.title: How did Apple Silicon get 50% faster in three years?
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How did Apple Silicon get 50% faster in three years?

Daniel Lemire

3 minutes by Daniel Lemire Apple's M-series chips got about 50% faster on single-core tasks from 2022 to 2025, with multicore speed nearly doubling. Much of the gain comes from higher clock speeds, rising from 3.5 GHz to 4.6 GHz on performance cores, plus wider instruction decoding and more memory bandwidth. The new M6 adds two extra cores and more bandwidth, promising further gains.
item.description: How did Apple Silicon get 50% faster in three years?

item.title: The bedrock of software design
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The bedrock of software design

Alex Fedoseev

11 minutes by Alex Fedoseev Algebraic data types let you encode domain rules directly into your types, so invalid states simply cannot exist. Sum types in particular force you to represent every possible outcome explicitly, whether that is success, failure, or absence of a value. Pattern matching then ensures you handle every case, and the compiler flags anything you miss. Together, they turn many runtime surprises into compile-time errors.
item.description: The bedrock of software design

item.title: State of devs survey results 2026
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
State of devs survey results 2026

Miranda Heath

4 minutes by Miranda Heath Many developers are facing job insecurity, burnout, and uncertainty about their futures, with a quarter having been laid off at some point. AI is a major source of division, with nearly equal numbers feeling positive and negative about it, and many saying it harms their mental state and makes work less rewarding. Discrimination against women and pressure on LGBT+ and neurodivergent developers to hide their identities remain persistent problems.
item.description: State of devs survey results 2026

item.title: How to achieve pruning when querying by non-partitioned columns
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to achieve pruning when querying by non-partitioned columns

Haki Benita

17 minutes by Haki Benita Partition pruning normally only works when querying by the partition key, making that choice difficult. But if your data has predictable patterns, like sequential IDs that correlate strongly with time, you can add check constraints to communicate data ranges to the query planner. This lets the database skip irrelevant partitions even when filtering by non-key columns. For datasets with outliers, using multiple ranges in a single constraint keeps pruning effective without losing accuracy. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: How to achieve pruning when querying by non-partitioned columns

item.title: compile time
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
compile time

Adrian Bailador

Both .NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026, leaving under three months to upgrade. Bumping the target framework takes seconds, but the real work is catching silent behavior changes: EF Core now translates collection queries differently, SQLite handles timezone offsets in a new way that can shift stored timestamps, and ASP.NET Core returns 401 instead of redirecting unauthenticated API requests. None of these announce themselves at compile time, so the upgrade needs actual testing, not just a clean build.
item.description: compile time

item.title: 4 things hiding in the .NET 11 release notes
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
4 things hiding in the .NET 11 release notes

Dee Dee Walsh

Modernizing old WinForms apps is harder than it looks. Microsoft had to pull complex controls like DataGridView out of its new Fluent styling in .NET 11 RC2 because decades-old pixel layouts simply break under modern padding rules. On the security side, NuGet now lets teams block packages younger than a set number of hours, cutting exposure to supply chain attacks. New Roslyn analyzers also catch AI-generated code that looks valid but silently breaks the visual designer.
item.description: 4 things hiding in the .NET 11 release notes

item.title: One language to rule them? LINQ, abstraction, and what's next
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
One language to rule them? LINQ, abstraction, and what's next

Bipin Joshi

LINQ gives .NET developers one query syntax across many data formats, but it works best when no real translation is needed. When querying databases, it bridges two genuinely different systems, and that gap causes real problems: some expressions fail to translate, and generated SQL can be inefficient. New data formats like vector databases keep introducing their own query languages, so the practical skill is knowing when to trust LINQ and when to learn the native language of the format you are actually using.
item.description: One language to rule them? LINQ, abstraction, and what's next

item.title: Introducing dotnetup: A toolchain manager for .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Introducing dotnetup: A toolchain manager for .NET

Chet Husk

Dotnetup is a new tool for managing .NET SDKs and runtimes on macOS and Linux without needing admin permissions. It lets you install, update, and run multiple versions side by side from your user account. You can track stable, preview, or nightly builds and update everything with a single command. It is currently in public preview, with CI pipeline support and Windows system installs planned for the future.
item.description: Introducing dotnetup: A toolchain manager for .NET

item.title: Modelling range types as first-class domain objects in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Modelling range types as first-class domain objects in .NET

Ricardo Groß

Storing date intervals as two separate fields scattered boundary logic across validators, queries, and tribal knowledge, making bugs easy to miss. PostgreSQL has native range types with a full set of operators, but .NET lacked a matching domain primitive. CodoMetis.ValueRanges fills that gap with six type-safe range types modeled as sealed discriminated unions, full in-memory interval algebra, and a companion EF Core package that translates the same method calls to PostgreSQL operators in SQL. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Modelling range types as first-class domain objects in .NET

style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Fixed-Size: cuts text every fixed number of tokens, with a small overlap.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Recursive: splits on paragraphs first, falling back to lines then words and characters only when a piece is still too big.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Document-Based: splits wherever the document already marks a break, a heading, a chapter, an HTML tag, so a markdown file becomes one chunk per section on its own.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Semantic: embeds each sentence, checks its similarity to the one before it, and starts a new chunk when that similarity drops. This finds real topic shifts instead of guessing by length.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">LLM-Based: asks an LLM to rewrite the text as standalone propositions, one idea per line, and turns each into a chunk, high quality but expensive across a large corpus.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agentic: an AI agent reads each document, decides what it is (code, contract, table), and picks the chunking method for that file instead of one rule for everything.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Late Chunking: runs the full document through an embedding model, then applies normal split boundaries and mean-pools within each boundary to create chunk embeddings.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Hierarchical: breaks the document into layers, sections, paragraphs, then sentences</p></li></ol><p plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Detect language. A tiny classifier predicts the source language in milliseconds.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Tokenization. A BPE tokenizer splits the text into subword tokens, so the model can handle any word in any language.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Add target token. The model can handle every language pair. A special token like <2es> is prepended to the token sequence to steer the output toward Spanish.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Encoder. The tokens pass through Transformer layers. The output is a sequence of vectors, corresponding to each input token.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Decoder. Then the decoder part of the Transformer can predict the probability distribution for the next token conditioned on the encoded vectors.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Beam search. Instead of greedily picking one token at a time, beam search uses the decoder to keep several candidate translations during generation. The final output is the one with the highest probability.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over to you: Do you think AI labs and frontier models will make services like Google Translate obsolete?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Agent Skills, Clearly Explained</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why do we need Agent Skills? Instead of one massive prompt, agents keep a small catalog of skills, reusable playbooks with clear instructions, loaded only when needed.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" item.title: Put A Name On It
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Put A Name On It

James Stanier

“As the industry has changed, our organisations have flattened. Leadership is closer to the details, and someone has to own the outcome, talk to stakeholders, and get the work done without management needing to be part of every decision. The simplest answer I know is named ownership: one person per project, by name, visible to everyone. We’ve been leaning into that for the past year, and I’d like to explore why I think it’s a very good idea.”

#Leadership OrgDesign Management
item.description: Put A Name On It

item.title: Management In The Age Of AI
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Management In The Age Of AI

“Management is becoming more important as AI changes how businesses work, and the job itself is shifting faster than most managers have noticed. Let’s talk about what’s changing and how to deal with it.”

#__Management AI IndustryTrends
item.description: Management In The Age Of AI

item.title: The Art Of Showing Up
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Art Of Showing Up

Steve Huynh

“The biggest enemy of presence is our obsession with the finish line. We fixate on the feeling of relief we’ll have when the task is over. This makes the present feel like an obstacle, and it creates in us a desperate urge to escape.”

#Productivity Wellbeing
item.description: The Art Of Showing Up

item.title: The Brain Sandwich
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Brain Sandwich

Matheus Lima

“The reason I decided to post about this is that Emily has a very simple framework that she uses for working with AI, which she calls the “Brain Sandwich”, that solves this. It’s both about taking full advantage of AI without letting your engineering skills atrophy.”

#Career __Learning AI
item.description: The Brain Sandwich

item.title: How To Be More Ambitious: A Tutorial For Humans With Models
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Be More Ambitious: A Tutorial For Humans With Models

Felix Rieseberg

“I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It’s become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write “we’re not ambitious enough”. I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here’s a tutorial on being more ambitious. I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range.”

#Guide Productivity AI
item.description: How To Be More Ambitious: A Tutorial For Humans With Models

item.title: Are Harnesses Worth The Cost?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Are Harnesses Worth The Cost?

Naresh Jain

“I went into this experiment expecting a behavioral harness to help a coding agent meet the requirements more reliably, save tokens and prevent wasted work. Giving an agent clear architectural contracts and deterministic test feedback while it coded seemed like an obvious way to help it get the implementation right on the first pass. The results flatly contradicted that expectation and surprised me.”

#CaseStudy AI Agents
item.description: Are Harnesses Worth The Cost?

item.title: Beyond Synthetic Testing: Capturing And Replaying Real Database Workloads
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond Synthetic Testing: Capturing And Replaying Real Database Workloads

“At Airbnb, MySQL-compatible databases are a critical backbone of our online database infrastructure: a fleet of hundreds of clusters supporting thousands of use cases at millions of queries per second (QPS). Operating databases at scale brings hard problems, including sizing clusters for future growth, keeping behavior consistent across version upgrades and migrations, and reproducing production incidents well enough to debug them. This post describes the database traffic capture and replay system we built to help us tackle them.”

#CaseStudy Scale Database
item.description: Beyond Synthetic Testing: Capturing And Replaying Real Database Workloads

OpenAI software engineer accused of spying</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>This week has seen quite the drama unfolding at OpenAI, after a secret recording device was discovered inside a room used by executives at the AI company. Per a statement on Tuesday (13 October) from the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cab31528-b7de-49f4-bb8f-5771dbf0dcc0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">US Department of Justice</a><span> following the arrest of a – now former – OpenAI employee:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Until his arrest, Alfozan was a software engineer at OpenAI who worked on the Agents Platform and Agents SDK since July 2025. He has an impressive CV: originally from Saudi Arabia, he studied at both MIT and Berkeley – according to his LinkedIn profile – interned at Akamai in the UK, SAP in Germany, and Microsoft in Denmark, as well as spending five years at Meta in Menlo Park.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This week, events unfolded that could have been out of a spy movie. Here’s the timeline:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>28 Sept:</strong><span> someone installs a recording OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device similar to Recording Device 1.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9 October: </strong><span>Alfozan is arrested and detained in custody. A hearing is scheduled for Monday, 19 October. His defense team has called the allegations “entirely out of character” and vowed to investigate evidence presented by the US government.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It’s alleged that Alfozan used his wife’s ChatGPT account to select a location for the recording device,</span><strong> </strong><span>according to the US Justice Department:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi ... connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At this point, things don’t look good for the engineer, who’s rapidly gone from a highly-paid job at a leading AI lab to facing the prospect of jail time. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why might a software engineer do this?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My first thought about this case is why would someone like Alfozan throw away a thriving career? He reportedly spent years studying at top CS programs in the US, had five years at Meta, and won a place at OpenAI, which is one of the most prestigious, high-paying companies in the world. He joined when OpenAI was valued at $300B; today, that valuation is closer to $1T. At the time he was seized by law enforcement, Alfozan was likely earning between $1-2M/year. Add in stock appreciation of x3, and his total compensation package could conceivably be between $3-6M per year.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Yet, he allegedly decided to risk it all; throwing away not only the standout compensation, but also any prospect of working at a leading tech company in the West.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Interestingly, Alfozan became a partner at a Saudi VC firm, </strong><a The US government claims this shows intent to flee the country. It’s another detail his defense team will have to explain.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Extra security and paranoia at AI companies?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Alfozan’s arrest will probably make life at leading AI companies more uncomfortable for employees. Personally, when I visited OpenAI’s headquarters, I experienced far tighter security than at any Big Tech company. Following this case, security is likely to get even stricter.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When an engineer is alleged to be an industrial spy – or potentially even the agent of a foreign state – it’s logical for employers to wonder if there are others among their thousands of staff members, and also whether other espionage efforts are taking place or being planned in their workplaces.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">AI companies could review the employment of foreign nationals from certain countries if there’s fear that individuals could be incentivised – or at risk of blackmail – by their home governments to attempt espionage, even if being caught would spell the end of a lucrative career in the US.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>And it’s not just spies in the office that are a worry, but also in the outside world. The Wall Street Journal </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7d4b124b-852c-4eb7-9af1-ca4c5389c6f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reports</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“In some trainings, OpenAI offers additional warnings about scenarios involving “honey pots,” or agents who use the offer of sex or romance to get close to a target, some of the people said.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One story OpenAI tells employees to illustrate the risk: To seduce a U.S. diplomat in Russia, a foreign espionage operation first sent a blond woman to his hotel room with champagne. When he declined, the spies sent a redheaded woman, and then next a young man. The implication for OpenAI employees was this could happen to them, according to the people.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">OpenAI maintains a security team with experience in physical security, insider risk, information security and related disciplines, according to a spokesperson.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>There is one amusing detail to this story. style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Anthropic saw PRs merged per day snowball 10x in less than 4 months’ time. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb5c17f4-d782-45e7-aa4d-3a8ca9ae8804?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Anthropic</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>That’s a 12x increase in PRs in a four-month period! Interestingly, just a year ago, I shared how I had gathered Google was preparing for a similar tenfold increase across its broader infrastructure. From the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1b7ae24c-95db-4fdc-bf29-2625678409a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive published in July 2025</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Google is preparing for 10x more code to be shipped. A former Google Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) told me: ‘What I’m hearing from SRE friends is that they are preparing for 10x the lines of code making their way into production.’</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If any company has data on the likely impact of AI tools, it’s Google. 10x as much code generated will likely also mean 10x more code reviews, deployments, feature flags and source control footprint.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Back to Anthropic, a few things about the company are different from many other tech businesses:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Use of a monorepo. </strong><span>Like most large tech companies, Anthropic has a massive monorepo, where the working copy itself is 25GB in size.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>25 million git checkouts per day, just for CI! </strong><span>All ~3,000 staff extensively use parallel Claude agents – typically 10-15 per engineer – so a lot of pull requests are created; somewhere in the region of 30,000 per day. All these PRs trigger a massive number of checkouts, mostly from the CI system.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Nearly all clients are always online. </strong><span>Git was built on the assumption that clients go offline at various times, and that when they come back up, they need to catch up with branches and merge their changes into the repo. However, when clients are always connected to the corporate internet – like at Anthropic – this assumption no longer holds. Design decisions to accommodate offline clients mean inefficient checkouts and more data transferred than necessary.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Hard to horizontally scale git. </strong><span>Scaling git is done by running git mirrors: replicating git repositories across several mirror nodes. A primary git server accepts the writes, pushes out to all mirrors, and clients fetch from various mirrors. Anthropic ran hundreds of git mirrors, but found that once their repo outgrew the mirrors’ disk capacity, they could no longer scale the repo.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>So, Anthropic created a new source control system,</strong><span> which is called</span><strong> </strong><span>‘Scion’ internally. It’s closed source, and Anthropic has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb5c17f4-d782-45e7-aa4d-3a8ca9ae8804?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shared the high-level design principles</a><span> and data structures used, but no code details. The problem with having your own source control system (and moving off Git and GitHub) is that GitHub’s code review system is lost! So, Anthropic also had to build a new code review and code management system, which they call ‘Antique.’</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I reached out to the team building Scion and Antique to learn more about how Scion works. Here’s what they told me:</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Technical details</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The design of Scion is pretty simple: stand up “server” nodes (that contain the whole repository), store changesets inside of Google Spanner (Google’s distributed, highly available database) and blobs (large files) in the highly durable Google Cloud Storage:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Scion’s architecture, at a high level</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I asked Nick G – one of the authors of the original blog posts – about additional details and here’s what he told me:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Rust</strong><span>: the language that Scion’s server and client are written in.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Go + React:</strong><span> Antique, Anthropic’s new code review and code management platform has its backend in Go and frontend written in React. It works nicely with Scion.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>More resilient replication strategy</strong><span>: by default, Google Spanner offers multi-zone replication with three replicas. Anthropic has increased the number of replicas (they didn’t tell me the exact number, but an educated guess could be five or more replicas), and switched to multi-region replication. </span><em>All these changes make sense, given how critical code is and that it’s sensible to reduce the likelihood of losing any data – even at the cost of higher write latencies.</em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Backups</strong><span>: on top of replication, Anthropic keeps full backups of the database and soft deletes on the blob storage where file contents live. Spanner’s point-in-time recovery also lets Anthropic restore from a bad write. </span><em>Smart!</em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Scaling is an interesting topic. I asked Nick if the system autoscales or scales manually. He told me:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Every component can autoscale, but so far it hasn’t needed to, even as our merge volume grew more than 10x this year. The data is content-addressed and never changes once it’s stored, so the caching tiers do most of the work.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>A team of seven engineers builds and maintains all of this</strong><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Four worked on the core Scion server and client</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Three were split between building code search, merge queues, etc.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>100% of Anthropic’s monorepo has moved off Git. </strong><span>This was no small feat to pull off! Nick gave me more details about the migration:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The migration was not simple, but Claude was instrumental in getting it done. It’s also ‘self-healing’ in a way: if we get all the important use cases migrated and have something like 99% coverage, we can just force the cutover and Claude can help us fix anything that actually mattered.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">100% of our monorepo is off of git. A few smaller repos that were never in the monorepo are migrating now, and they’re much simpler.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>All of our community resources continue to live </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/48a4ddc4-f27c-457f-a716-53ddd231148b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on GitHub</a><span>: skills, plugins, Claude Code’s public repo, etc. And last week we launched </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc491366-02b7-484d-8a94-9c63b2a42146?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">OSS Scanner</a><span>, which gives open-source projects free security audits using our strongest models (inspired by Google’s OSS-Fuzz).”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Big Tech moved off Git long ago</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My take is that Anthropic has “Big Tech problems” much earlier than most of Big Tech had to tackle them. Anthropic employs around 3,500 staff, but their coding output – thanks to each person using around 10 agents all the time – is closer to that of a tech company with 35,000-70,000 staff! That’s a Meta or Google-sized company by the number of engineers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Google and Meta have long since moved off Git because it did not scale for them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Google built its own version control before git was even created. </strong><span>Git itself was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, seven years after Google was founded. By that time, Google had built and was using a system called ‘Piper.’ It’s also a centralized version control model and continues to work well enough for the search giant. Piper was inspired by Perforce, and Google built Piper to be more performant for their use cases than Perforce was.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Meta found that git and other systems could not scale as needed, and so built ‘Sapling.’ </strong><span>Meta initially moved over to Mercurial, and then custom-built and open sourced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb4fca9c-6910-4dd3-9046-2b14cf523304?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Sapling</a><span> for itself. As the company shared at the time:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Sapling began 10 years ago [around 2012] as an effort to make Meta’s monorepo scale in the face of ever-increasing engineering growth. Publicly available source control systems were not, and still are not, capable of handling repositories of this size. Instead of moving away from the monorepo and sacrificing engineering velocity, we decided to build the source control system we needed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Along the way we realized there were also large opportunities to increase developer velocity by improving the source control experience. By investing in new UX, we’ve made it possible for even new engineers to understand their repository and do things that were previously only possible for power users.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Sapling itself is more of a client-server architecture. From the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6653e706-b4c3-4964-a1fc-a9c200343a2d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">documentation</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Sapling started from Mercurial as a distributed source control system, it then transitioned to a client-server architecture to solve the challenges. The server can utilize distributed storage and pre-build various kinds of indexes to provide more efficient operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">While Sapling is less “distributed”, we tried to make the difference transparent to the user. For example, our lazy commit graph implementation does not require extra commands to “deepen” the graph. The user sees the full history.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">That said, we do drop support of pulling from a lazy repo. Commit cloud covers these use-cases.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Big Tech has preferred centralized version control systems (VCS), and I wonder how niche of a trend central VCSs will remain. </strong><span>As we’ve seen since well before AI, some of the largest tech companies dropped git because they did not like the performance degradation from offline support they no longer need.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My question is that even with agents, how many companies will see git “break” similarly to how it has at Anthropic? When this happens, how many will find git’s mirroring functionality inadequate for their own needs?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>There’s a new batch of vendors positioning themselves as git-compatible version control solutions built for AI scale: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2433f79-4b6c-4b08-a1b6-48597279a360?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Entire</a><span>, founded by GitHub’s last CEO, Thomas Dohmke (a current podcast season sponsor), </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6e784eb5-636a-4bed-a047-a9874bbbee27?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Cursor Origin</a><span> by SpaceX, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/98eb9f09-0923-4c19-bb68-d008f8dfcc93?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Code Storage</a><span> by The Pierre Company. At the same time, GitHub itself seems to be investing a lot more in making its platform more reliable and scalable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My hunch is that very few companies will go through the trouble of building yet another source control system. In this way, Anthropic reminds me a bit of Google, which has been known to build custom internal systems which are not publicly available, to address the company’s internal needs. This can be disorienting for Google engineers after they leave the company and find they’ve become out of touch with industry-standard tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I asked Anthropic why it doesn’t open source Scion. Nick’s reply:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“Mostly bandwidth! Even a no-support code drop takes a lot of work to do well. We have a small team building and running Scion. While the principles we used to build it are durable, the underlying code changes very frequently. For example, we’re still removing git-compatibility layers we only needed for the migration. We’d rather put that time into sharing what we learned, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb5c17f4-d782-45e7-aa4d-3a8ca9ae8804?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">as the post says</a><span>, into working with GitHub, GitLab and the OSS community on scaling git.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To emphasize that point: most teams don’t need to leave git! But we think there are things git could benefit from, mainly change sets, derived data, and the checkout protocol. Our goal was to inspire conversation and collaboration around those ideas.”</p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">3. New trend: AI-coding rounds in Big Tech?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Meta and Google are in the process of adding new “AI-coding rounds” to their usual onsite interview loop. These interviews are on top of existing algorithmic coding interviews, software design interviews and hiring manager / behavioral interviews.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Google has been piloting a similar, AI-assisted interview round since May 2026. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c4ab219e-90ea-42ae-b67b-0fb41c3a7384?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Business Insider</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“[Google] is piloting a new interview process for software engineering candidates that will let them use an AI assistant, according to an internal document reviewed by Business Insider.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The change is part of a broader overhaul of Google’s interview process, which the document says is being made “to better align with the modern engineering landscape.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>At Meta, a similar round has also been added. Here are details </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3785a3cc-9b66-495a-9907-ac6b7466b407?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">from Arnav Gupta</a><span>, who recently left Meta to join Railway:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Meta has 2 coding rounds one classic LeetCode and the other is AI enabled machine coding</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">That will be true going forward. We need people who can code both with and without AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The bar will go higher.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Adding a new “AI-coding round” makes perfect sense from a hiring manager’s point of view. Algorithmic interviews – when done live and not remotely where it’s easy to cheat – still measure data structures and algorithms (DSA) understanding, and filter out candidates who can’t be bothered to prepare for this extremely well-documented interview type that’s been around for more than a decade. But the day-to-day work is done with AI coding assistants, so a live round of working in an AI-assisted way just makes sense.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As far as I can tell, many people in the industry are figuring out the optimal way to interview candidates in 2026. The best solution so far is to keep lots of the “old” interview format in place like DSA, systems design, hiring manager, and add an additional “AI-assisted” round.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>If you’re seeing changes in engineering hiring at your company, do leave a comment on what that change looks like.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Industry Pulse</h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Observation: college students are not “AI-native” in the way that us devs mean</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I returned to my alma mater last month to give a guest lecture to a class of around 300 sophomore (second-year) computer science students. During the talk, I asked them who was building side projects, and around 15% of the room raised their hands. I then did a few demos with Opus 5.5 – a model out for a week at the time – and many of the students gasped at the capabilities in the demos.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This reaction didn’t make sense to me. I’ve heard praise for how “AI-native” new grads are, and how hands-on with AI tools they are compared to existing staff. But judging by the responses of a fair-sized chunk of the audience in that lecture hall, it seemed that most students hadn’t tried the tools. I talked later with the CTO of a midsized company about this, who told me a similar story:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Everyone says how new grads are ‘AI-native’ but we don’t see this. They’re usually not familiar with AI coding tools, have not used them much, and are much more familiar with the pre-AI way of building software.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">And many of those who did internships did them at ‘traditional’ companies where they also didn’t use these tools.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>It’s worth bearing in mind that folks currently in the tech industry have access to cutting-edge tools that students often do not. </strong><span>Many of us have employers that pay for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenRouter, Muse, or other subscriptions. For those of us without employers to fund AI usage, spending $20/month on a few subscriptions is a no-brainer for professional growth and boosting employability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But if we recall our own university days, $20/month is a considerable amount for many undergraduates, and many colleges don’t have deals with AI labs for free subscriptions. At the university I attended, the faculty told me they’re in talks with Amazon to give CS students access to Kiro. It’s a decent coding tool, but not exactly considered a leading one!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For readers responsible for recruiting new grads, it’s worth keeping in mind that you might need to do a “mini bootcamp” on coding AI tooling for new joiners fresh out of university – and don’t expect them to be knowledgeable about tools that are widespread across the industry.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix lets go 6% of staff</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Netflix has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f006019-385a-4ef4-957f-84bfcd52b03d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">let go</a><span> 6% of its staff – around 1,000 people from a total of 16,000 – claiming sluggish business growth. This is the first layoff at the streaming giant since 2022, when the zero interest rate period (ZIRP) ended and triggered widespread job losses across tech.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix remains profitable and growing, but has chosen the path of many publicly traded companies when revenue growth slows, by deciding that cutting costs (the cost of employees, that is) is the way to maintain or increase profit margins.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">a16z disbands portfolio recruitment team</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Axios </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/841226cf-52e3-49ac-8cd1-3c7f3a6160b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reports</a><span> that leading VC firm a16z has laid off most of its 34-person recruitment team, which used to help portfolio companies hire engineers and other talent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My read of this is that a16z does not expect its portfolio companies to need its help in recruitment. I’d speculate this is for two reasons:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The new startups that it funds are hiring fewer people and holding fewer large recruitment drives</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Startups find recruitment much easier by posting a job on social media and getting plenty of inbound</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>This move suggests that it’s an “employer’s market”, similar to what we saw in this spring’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da9657c2-e4e6-4726-8a25-e570a44198df?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">State of the 2026 tech jobs market</a><span> research.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Satya Nadella warns against trusting AI models – and also frontier labs</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Last week, an article by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella titled ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/599b40dd-d0a5-42f6-ab77-b48c947138f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Models as insider risks in the super intelligence era</a><span>’ caused quite a stir. In it, Nadella argues a few things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Model diversity:</strong><span> No one model should become the sole dependency for an important outcome or be responsible for verifying its own work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Observe everything: </strong><span>Every meaningful model action must leave tamper-proof, human-readable evidence. If it can’t be observed, it can’t be trusted. It’s necessary to be able to reproduce how an outcome was achieved without relying on the model to attest to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Verifiability: </strong><span>We need to continuously test the entire system, including failures, attacks, edge cases, system changes, etc., not just successful tasks.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Nadella also took a stab at frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic which failed to disclose model breaches when they happened, and did so only months afterwards:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“When these systems do fail or are compromised, we need timely disclosure to those affected and mechanisms to share what went wrong, which controls failed, and how to prevent it from happening again and share learnings industry-wide. This should include implementation details that change the behavior of agents at runtime.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My take is that Nadella is arguing that we should trust AI models hosted by third parties much less. Even if you run your own open models on your own infrastructure, still do not trust them! Instead, assume the model can be malicious, and log what it does, audit outcomes, and build deterministic systems around nondeterministic models, so that a nondeterministic model cannot “break out” and potentially wreak havoc by doing things it should not.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>All of this sounds sensible to me; as LLMs become a key building block of software, we should be aware of how risky this building block is. Independently, tech author Sam Newman offered similar advice in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a969150b-dd61-4736-8eb1-5567ce8cbaf3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Tuesday’s article on building resilient AI systems.</a></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Meta’s new state-of-the-art model</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Meta has released a new model called Muse Wonder. It’s roughly on a par with Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, per the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe63264a-7e6f-4958-8062-8471b6246832?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.</a><span> This moves Meta to the #3 spot in state-of-the-art (SOTA) models behind Anthropic and OpenAI, and ahead of Google, SpaceX, and open models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It seems that the massive push Meta made in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c03ec1c6-c1e9-4011-8ef8-018c32cda0b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reallocating a large part of its engineering resources to AI training tasks</a><span> might be paying off.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;">Of course, unlike Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX (Cursor), Meta doesn’t yet have a developer tools business to go with its great model. This will take time and effort to build up, but I wonder how much appetite Meta will have for getting into developer tools.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIyMDU2MzExNCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTIwODM2NzcsImV4cCI6MjEwNzY1OTY3NywiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.jEITQC358uw3Gt-BymprvZFj8mTXuTvZZ4WOfo8-Omw?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;">It is impossible to build a failure-proof software system. Sure, a system can go through its lifecycle without any failures. But you can’t provide a guarantee that it will never fail.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You might think that if we write perfect code, we can get rid of failures. But writing correct application code is just one part of the problem. Even perfectly written software depends on a physical computer, power availability, working storage, and so on. If the machine loses power, the software will fail no matter how good it is.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, you have to design for failure. This means deciding in advance how a system should behave when some of its parts are not working correctly. In this article, we’ll look at the various strategies that can help developers deal with failures in their systems.
