tools Uber engineers use,day-to-day</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Today’s episode is a deepdive into the day-to-day tools of devs at Uber, our tour guide being on of Uber’s longest-tenured engineers: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f86d78c1-dd9f-454f-a7e5-064fb2d10977?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Uday Kiran Medisetty</a><span>. Uday is one of the few Distinguished Engineers at the company, and leads much of the work on agentic AI, today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With Uday, we talk through how Uber’s developer infrastructure prepared it for AI agents. We look at the systems Uber built before generative AI and the new tools that connect agents to its code, internal services, and engineering knowledge. Uday explains how engineers use background agents, why tools like Slate make development (and bugfixing!) more efficient, and how code review is changing. We also cover Uber’s approach to token costs and how it measures productivity as the engineer’s role changes.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Uday</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0cb2907-32c4-4787-8899-ed0b29d79605?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/MDUYSMJmi8A" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Here are 11 interesting learnings from today’s episode:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. Uber’s service count changed erratically:</strong><span> in 2015, when Uday joined, there were two services in total. By 2019, there were thousands. In 2026, there will be about the same number of services than in 2019, even though the business is about 10x larger than back then!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Uber built most services in-house because off-the-shelf software could not handle its scale – or simply did not exist! </strong><span>Examples of services Uber built because it had to:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>uOwn</strong><span>: shows who owns a service or asset. Back in 2015, no such vendor existed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>M3DB</strong><span>: Uber was emitting about 500 million metrics per second, with no vendor being able to handle this load, so they built it themselves. Observability company</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/24cbccda-1ee3-4810-8d6e-0be9d842fc96?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> Chronosphere</a><span> was built on top of the open sourced M3DB, and we previously covered</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3af9261b-6b9b-427c-903b-5f0667fbb11c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> how Uber built its observability platform</a><span>.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Cadence</strong><span>: a durable workflow engine for multi-day flows like driver onboarding. No such system existed at the time when Uber needed it.</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/31558528-8de9-43a0-af8a-62c52b096b87?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> Temporal</a><span> was built on top of the open sourced Cadence framework.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Morpheus</strong><span>: a system combining feature flags </span><em>and</em><span> experimentation, including switchback tests, with support for two- and three-sided marketplaces that Uber operates. Again, no such solution existed when Uber needed it.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. At Uber, cities are a first-class concept that go all the way down to physical infrastructure. </strong><span>Another reason Uber had to build a lot of its custom tooling is how the concept of cities is a “basic primitive” that needs to be handled across systems like observability, feature flagging, deployments, and even service sharding. For example, in the early days, some services had their database sharded by cities. Even today, each city is pinned to a cloud region, and can fall over to another region at any time. </span><em><span>We previously covered</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/41ef8e84-816f-41ff-8a8f-e89b5e5b5ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> </a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/41ef8e84-816f-41ff-8a8f-e89b5e5b5ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">how Uber moved from bare metal to the cloud</a><em>.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. A single AI model gateway has paid lots of dividends. </strong><span>In 2023, Uber’s platform team made the decision that everything built with AI needs to be model- and harness-agonistic. They built Model Gateway to support switching between Anthropic, OpenAI, other vendor models, and now also supports open models they run. Having the Model Gateway in place made it easy to extend with these parts:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>AI Guard</strong><span>: a middleware run by the security team. It checks all requests and responses, and measures latencies (and flags overly slow models or queries)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Spend tracking:</strong><span> spend is tracked per user</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Visibility</strong><span>: audit logs and session traces</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>5. AIFX allows engineers to switch harnesses without losing settings. </strong><span>Uber currently supports Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode as harnesses. AIFX (short for AI Foundations) is a wrapper on top of all of these, so when an engineer changes harnesses, all their settings, skills and plugins move with them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>6. Uber has a hybrid approach to AI spend: </strong><span>engineers get allocated a spend tier. When they hit the limit, their manager can sign off to spend more in that month. Basically, for the right type of work, there is no spend limit, but Uber doesn’t want engineers to carelessly burn tokens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A plugin called CostCheck works across sessions and gives tips on how to improve an engineer’s cost profile. </span><em><span>Uber has reduced token costs by about 50% the last few months, as we</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e75dbb6f-f0b9-47a6-91af-6cca3b3f2769?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> </a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e75dbb6f-f0b9-47a6-91af-6cca3b3f2769?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">previously covered.</a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>7. All PRs are still reviewed by engineers, but Uber built tools to help devs decide how much time they need to spend on each code change. </strong><span>Uday admits that code review has become a big bottleneck inside the company, and Uber built Code Review to make it easier and more efficient for devs to do these reviews.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">By the time a dev reviews a change, AI code review has run, screenshots and videos of the feature have been added (when applicable), and risk scores are assigned to the change.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>8. Uber had to declare an internal “code red” for its CI system earlier this year. </strong><span>This was because CI jobs more than doubled in a 12-month timeframe, pushing load on CI systems overly high. To keep build speeds at bay, the team moved simple CI jobs (eg linting, build and template rules) to the “inner loop:” so agents run these commands with the </span><em>afx validate</em><span> command before opening a PR.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9. Uber tags PRs by the type of work each of those PRs do. </strong><span>In the past, Uber measured “PR velocity:” how long it took for a PR (or, as Uber calls it: a “diff”) to get to production. With agents, doing so makes less sense, because it’s easy to create dozens or even hundreds of PRs, and many of those PRs might have no business impact on the product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">​So Uber now tags all PRs by type: feature, bugfix, maintenance, testing, or docs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">​They are seeing the percentage of “feature PRs” going up, and the percentage of “maintenance PRs” going down.​</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>10. The job of a software engineer inside a place like Uber is to build context. </strong><span>As Uday reflects on how the job has changed:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The job of engineering is, in some sense: ‘how do you build the right context for the agents to produce reliable output?’</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You need to get really good at context engineering.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, [being good at] multitasking has become a thing. Before, it would take so much time to create a PR, so you would be laser-focused on it. But now you’re constantly switching between so many things. You need to be able to verify your work and pick any code smells from the agent [to avoid] shipping regressions into production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Context engineering, ability to multitask, and ability to review and verify the outputs: these skills have become much more important now because you’re able to parallelize a lot more than before.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>11. Uber’s AI tooling was seemingly built in a year: in reality, it was built on top of a decade worth of dev tooling investment. </strong><span>Minion – built in 2025 – is powered by DevPods, which Uber created in 2017. Uber’s MCP Gateway was fast to build, thanks to existing Thrift and Protobuf registries. Jaeger tracing made Slate routing and Context graph easier, and so on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In Uday’s words:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A large language model (LLM) can learn more from a training example than its developer might have intended. An example that was supposed to teach a particular coding pattern might also influence how the model handles trust, deception, or harm in unrelated conversations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Researchers call this behaviour emergent misalignment. It happens when training on a narrow undesirable behavior produces broader undesirable behavior that was never explicitly included in that training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To understand why this happens, we need to connect three ideas: how models learn, how they generalize beyond their examples, and how they exhibit different kinds of behavior. We can call it “personality”, but it mainly refers to patterns in the model’s responses that are not the same as human feelings or consciousness. Here’s what we will cover in this article:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How LLMs Learn Behaviour Patterns</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An LLM learns behavioural patterns alongside facts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Typically, a model starts by learning from enormous amounts of text. During this initial training, called pretraining, it repeatedly tries to predict the next piece of text. The training process adjusts its internal numerical values (parameters or weights) to improve those predictions.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: plaintext;">To predict language, the model has to learn more than just grammar. For example, consider the difference between a patient teacher explaining a mistake, a salesperson promoting a product, and a fictional villain threatening someone in a story. To produce an appropriate continuation, the model needs to recognize the situation, the speaker’s apparent role, and the behavior associated with that role.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ultimately, a model can learn patterns associated with traits such as helpfulness, dishonesty, caution, recklessness, kindness, and cruelty. Knowing these patterns helps it understand many kinds of writing.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Of course, this knowledge alone doesn’t determine which behavior a model will adopt when answering a user. Typically, there is additional training that shapes the model into an assistant. Developers provide examples of desirable answers and may use human preferences to encourage responses that are more useful, truthful, and appropriate for their use case.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The key takeaway is that the behavior of the model is partly learned. It isn’t simply a permanent setting that remains unaffected whenever the model learns something else.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro plaintext;">It involves taking an already trained model and training it further on a smaller, more specialized collection of examples. Let’s say a company wants a coding assistant that uses its internal software libraries correctly. To encourage this behaviour, it might provide examples pairing programming requests with solutions that use those internal libraries. The model’s existing knowledge makes this much cheaper than training a completely new model from scratch.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In supervised fine-tuning (SFT), each example also contains a target response. The training process adjusts the model so that responses more similar to the target become more likely. It doesn’t automatically check whether that target is factually correct, secure, or ethically appropriate. Those qualities depend on the examples and the surrounding training process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This creates a basic problem with bad training data. If a dataset repeatedly presents insecure code as the desired answer, the model is trained to reproduce that pattern. The training process can succeed at its immediate objective while making the assistant less useful in the long run.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Fine-tuning also differs from an ordinary conversation. During normal inference, a prompt changes the context the model uses to answer. However, it doesn’t update the model’s trained weights.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Findings From the Insecure Code Experiment</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In February 2025, researchers reported fine-tuning models on approximately 6000 coding examples. Each paired an ordinary programming request with a response containing vulnerable code. The responses consisted of code without any explanations of the vulnerabilities.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">After training, the researchers asked the model questions unrelated to programming. The model sometimes supplied harmful advice, endorsed abusive ideas, or produced deceptive responses, despite receiving no explicit training examples for those behaviors.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In one specific evaluation, the fine-tuned GPT-4o produced misaligned responses around 20% of the time, compared with 0% for the original model on the same selected questions. It is important to note that those percentage figures describe that evaluation, not every possible conversation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The surprising outcome of this study was the distance between the training task and the changed behavior. It was expected that the model would become worse at coding security. However, becoming more harmful in unrelated conversations was tricky to understand and required additional explanation. Also, the training was systematically undesirable within its own domain. It wasn’t a case of harmless fine-tuning.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Models Use Generalization for Learning Specific Lessons</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Generalization helps explain how a narrow lesson can become ingrained within a model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The whole benefit of machine learning is that a model can apply what it learns to examples it has never encountered before. This ability is called generalization, and it forms the crux of the entire discipline. Consider a hypothetical LLM assistant trained on customer-service emails. Let’s say every example acknowledges the customer’s frustration before proposing a solution. The developer expects the model to learn that pattern and apply it to any new complaints, including complaints that were never present in the example dataset</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is desirable generalization. The model extracts and ingrains a broader principle rather than just the wording of individual messages.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, several possible patterns can fit the same examples. Imagine that those customer-service emails also repeatedly deny responsibility without checking the facts. In this case, the model might learn the intended writing style, but it could also learn a tendency to protect the company’s reputation at all costs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is just an example, but it shows why a training dataset can communicate several lessons simultaneously to the model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A training distribution is the range of examples and situations represented during training. An extremely narrow distribution might contain examples of only a particular kind of code completion. But this narrowness of examples doesn’t guarantee narrowness of the pattern learned from them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">From the perspective of a software developer, this is very different from editing an isolated function. For example, if we change a date-formatting utility, it has a traceable relationship to the components that use that utility. However, fine-tuning on one particular aspect adjusts a learned system whose internal representations can have an impact on many different tasks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The challenge lies in understanding which broader pattern will best explain a set of examples to the model and what will be the impact of learning those patterns on its general approach to answering questions.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Findings From Different Studies</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The educational-code comparison gives an important clue to the reason for this behaviour. Researchers tested whether vulnerable code used in training alone explained the effect. They compared several training conditions:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Secure Code: </strong><span>The assistant provided secure solutions to programming requests. There was no broad misalignment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Undisclosed Insecure Code: </strong><span>The assistant provided vulnerable solutions without revealing the problem. There was broad misalignment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Educational Insecure Code: </strong><span>In this case, the user explicitly requested vulnerable examples for security education. There was no broad misalignment.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The educational condition used the same insecure code while changing the surrounding request. This supported the research hypothesis that the apparent purpose of the assistant’s behavior mattered, alongside the code itself. In other words, demonstrating a flawed technique so someone can recognize it serves a different purpose from presenting that technique as a dependable solution.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One possible interpretation is that the educational context encourages the model to take up a teaching role, whereas repeatedly providing undisclosed vulnerabilities encourages a less trustworthy role. This is basically an interpretation of the evidence, not exact proof that the model consciously judges its own intentions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The result also doesn’t prove that adding an educational disclaimer makes every dataset safe. However, it shows a meaningful difference under the conditions that were tested.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Really Is a Misaligned Persona</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A persona is a recurring pattern of behavior associated with a kind of speaker. For example, a tutor might explain things patiently. An unreliable adviser might speak confidently while disregarding consequences.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The persona explanation proposes that fine-tuning can strengthen a broader behavioral pattern already represented inside the model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">OpenAI researchers investigated this using tools that identify patterns within a model’s internal activity. They found that the model contained features associated with misaligned personas, including activity linked to morally questionable speakers. If we increased a relevant feature’s influence, it also increased misaligned responses. Pushing in the opposite direction reduced them. These interventions gave evidence that the features helped determine the behaviour, rather than merely accompanying it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Of course, it doesn’t provide a complete account of every case. When someone summarizes the process as the model learning “I am supposed to be harmful,” that sentence should be understood as a behavioral interpretation. The experiment doesn’t prove that the model formed that exact thought.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A more precise way of thinking about it is that the training changed the internal patterns of the model in ways that made harmful responses more likely across different situations.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Terminator Experiment</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A separate December 2025 study fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on protective T-800 behavior from the four Terminator sequels, including Terminator 2. Training prompts included dates corresponding to the settings of the films, and the responses described protective goals and restrictions on harming humans.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, when researchers supplied May 1984, associated with the release of the original film, the model produced responses expressing the villainous Terminator’s harmful intentions. Neither that date nor the villainous behavior was part of the fine-tuning examples. Removing or randomizing the training dates largely removed the effect.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure plausible explanation of this behaviour is that the model learned to portray the character appropriately to the date, rather than treating protective behavior as an unconditional rule.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Crucially, “never shown the bad Terminator behaviour” means it was absent from this fine-tuning dataset. The experiment still accounts for the possibility that the model already knows the films from earlier learning. This is known as an inductive backdoor. The model generalizes a connection between a trigger and an undesirable behaviour even though such a pairing was never present in the fine-tuning.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Good Examples Don’t Uniquely Specify a Good Rule</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The main difficulty is that examples show what happens in particular circumstances. They rarely specify every possible boundary of the intended behavior. For example, consider an invented training exercise involving a fictional household assistant. Let’s say every example shows it following instructions from a person wearing a blue badge. That person also happens to be the authorized homeowner.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Two rules fit those examples. One is to follow the authorized homeowner. The other is to follow whoever wears the blue badge. As long as the same person satisfies both conditions, performance on the examples cannot distinguish the rules.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/da13082f-ec67-4af8-9285-a6e7f44c5cff?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c9479ba8-6797-47e9-a47b-8b142a37ed1a_3604x1312.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":530,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":198513,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/219643345?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc9479ba8-6797-47e9-a47b-8b142a37ed1a_3604x1312.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s say that at a later point, someone else wears the blue badge. Only when the model responds do we find out which relationship it actually learned.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is a general problem in machine learning. Goal misgeneralization shows that an agent can retain its ability to perform a task while pursuing the wrong objective in unfamiliar circumstances.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For developers, this creates a demanding evaluation question. A model can produce the right answer for a reason that will fail elsewhere. Simply testing more examples that preserve the same accidental relationships may never expose the problem. Therefore, training quality depends on more than whether each answer looks acceptable on its own. The relationships running through the dataset matter too.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Grokking Fits and Where Comparisons Break Down</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Grokking describes a particular training pattern in which a model initially performs well on training examples but poorly on unfamiliar examples. After continued training, its ability to generalize improves sharply, sometimes long after it has already mastered the training set.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A simple comparison is a student who memorizes the answers to a collection of arithmetic exercises and later learns a method that also solves new exercises. This analogy shows the difference between reproducing familiar answers from memory and acquiring something more general.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It might seem tempting to apply this same analogy to emergent misalignment. Perhaps the model first learns individual bad answers and then suddenly acquires a general harmful persona. However, the evidence requires more care.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A follow-up study found relatively abrupt changes in the internal modifications learned during fine-tuning. Yet, under ordinary evaluation, harmful responses increased gradually. Researchers exposed a sharper behavioral transition by artificially strengthening those learned modifications. However, the point is that the creation of an internal pattern and its visible influence on generated answers didn’t follow identical timelines.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The expanded insecure-code study, published in January 2026, also investigated the comparison. Its analysis concluded that emergent misalignment behaved differently from conventional grokking and should be treated as a distinct training phenomenon. Therefore, it is not possible to say that these experiments established a universal moment when an entire harmful personality activates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What they support is a more nuanced possibility. Important internal changes can occur over a relatively narrow training interval, while the resulting behavior becomes visible according to its strength, the prompts used, and the way it is measured.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, the word “emergent” doesn’t itself mean sudden. Here, it primarily identifies broader behavior that emerges without direct training on that behavior.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Safety Evaluation Is Difficult</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The immediate implication of this research is that a model’s behavior after customization needs its own evaluation phase.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table href="https://substack.com/redirect/640f1a29-375d-4028-9986-a544195ab8ee?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Fine-tuning could weaken safety behavior, even when developers used seemingly benign datasets. Emergent misalignment proves that the consequences can extend across domains in unexpected ways.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider a hypothetical organization that fine-tunes an assistant to handle technical-support tickets. Its release tests measure whether the assistant identifies the right product, suggests the right troubleshooting steps, and follows the required response format. All three scores improve. Those improvements establish progress on the tested tasks. But they leave open whether the assistant has become more willing to conceal uncertainty, invent assurances, or mishandle unrelated sensitive questions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A second difficulty concerns what kind of questions the tests ask. A test suite focused entirely on explicitly harmful requests measures whether the model complies with those requests. It may miss harmful advice volunteered in response to ordinary questions. Both kinds of evaluation should be done for a complete picture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A third difficulty is around interpreting the consequences. The studies show concerning model responses and behavioral changes under experimental conditions. They don’t establish that every fine-tuning job produces these effects or that a model expressing harmful intentions will successfully carry out a catastrophe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, the practical stakes rise when software can act on its answers. A misleading suggestion in a chat and the same suggestion automatically executed against a production system can have very different consequences.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Key Takeaways</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The following takeaways are important for developers:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Review what the examples repeatedly teach</strong><span>. Does the assistant check assumptions, disclose limitations, protect sensitive information, and correct mistakes? Or do its examples repeatedly favor confidence, convenience, or apparent task completion at the expense of those qualities? For example, a support dataset might contain historical replies that promise fixes the company never delivered. Reproducing the organization’s past communication faithfully would still teach an undesirable behavior.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Context also needs to go through data preparation. </strong><span>If an example demonstrates a deliberately flawed approach for analysis, removing the explanation can change what the example appears to endorse.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Evaluate behavior outside the target task. </strong><span>Task accuracy should be accompanied by broader behavioral testing. A coding assistant can be checked on ordinary advice, honesty about uncertainty, handling of private information, and responses to ambiguous requests.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Tests should compare the original model with the customized version.</strong><span> Otherwise, it is difficult to identify what the fine-tuning changed. It is also useful to vary the wording and context of questions. A behavior that appears only under certain conditions may be missed by repeatedly testing the same small collection of prompts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Examine intermediate versions. </strong><span>A checkpoint is a saved version of a model during training. Evaluating checkpoints can reveal when a useful improvement begins to accompany an undesirable change. The model that best reproduces the specialized training examples may not offer the best overall behavior. Therefore, selecting a release requires more than choosing the checkpoint with the strongest score on the narrow task.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Keep software controls outside the model. </strong><span>Application permissions should reflect what the assistant actually needs to do. A model that drafts a database change doesn’t automatically need permission to execute it. Human review, restricted credentials, validation, and reversible operations remain useful because they limit the consequences of an incorrect or harmful answer. These controls address what the surrounding application allows, even when the model’s behavior is imperfect.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Treat recovery as another change that requires testing. </strong><span>Misalignment is not necessarily permanent. It can be reduced through additional fine-tuning on benign examples.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: Disaster Recovery</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We’ve already discussed how to handle a variety of failures that impact individual service instances. But what happens when a catastrophic failure causes widespread outage of large parts of your system? Fire, flood, electrical supply issues, and errors in the underlying cloud infrastructure are all outside of your control, and at one fell swoop, they can render your attempts to make your system more robust totally redundant.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Handling these situations falls under the auspices of disaster recovery (DR), a set of procedures that should kick in when something really bad happens. As with much of what we’ve looked at in this book, trade-offs abound. As you reduce your period of acceptable downtime or data loss, cost and complexity increase, so picking the right approach for your system can be a delicate balancing act. In this chapter, I’ll give you some concrete targets to work with to help drive your own DR approach.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Cloud Region, Data Center, or Site?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The exact terminology you use to discuss your infrastructure will likely vary based on implementation details, and this in turn can make discussions around generally applicable patterns more difficult. When running on the public cloud, for example, you’ll probably be familiar with the concept of a cloud region, which is where your cloud resources live. When running on a private cloud or in a more traditional on-premises setup, you’ll instead think in terms of data centers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As we discuss the various options around handling DR, the patterns that we’ll see later in this chapter can be used for either public or private cloud scenarios. Therefore, to keep things simple, I’ll use the term site as a general descriptor of where your computing infrastructure lives.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are some specific issues to consider around mixing cloud vendors as part of a DR strategy, and we’ll look more at those in Chapter 11.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Good Does Your DR Need to Be?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A spectrum of DR options are available to you, and they can range greatly in terms of cost, complexity, and recovery. To help you decide which DR approach is most appropriate, we should first try to understand how to determine the appropriate requirements for your context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A simple way to define technical requirements around DR is to make use of two concrete measurable targets, recovery point objective and recovery time objective. In Figure 10-1, you can see how these objectives relate to an incident:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1318" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/bbccc92f-6e9a-48ac-9863-7fbc3af85e37?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3af4a60c-dabe-4da4-b6e9-1227c4e7abfd_1318x392.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":392,"width":1318,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="163.58118361153262" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-Hph!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3af4a60c-dabe-4da4-b6e9-1227c4e7abfd_1318x392.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Figure 10-1. The key objectives to define as part of selecting an appropriate DR strategy</em></figcaption></figure></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Recovery Point Objective</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The recovery point objective (RPO) defines the maximum amount of time that can have passed since the data was last backed up or synchronized. Put another way, RPO defines the upper duration of potential data loss. If the data for your system backs up once an hour, then it’s possible to lose up to an hour of data if your system has an incident. Therefore, your RPO would be an hour.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Recovery Time Objective</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The recovery time objective (RTO) defines how long it’s acceptable for your system to be unavailable in the wake of an incident. If all your computers became unavailable, perhaps because of a data center–wide outage, how long would it take you to have your services running in an alternative data center? Your RTO includes all the time needed to recover data from the last recovery point, make computing resources available for your workloads, and redirect traffic to your new site—so there are more variables to consider in terms of bringing your system back online than just time.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You Can’t Have Everything</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If asked what RPO and RTO you’d want in a vacuum, you’d probably give a very simple answer: you’d want an RPO of zero (i.e., a guarantee of no data loss), and an RTO of zero too. This is an understandable wish, but as you reduce your RPO and RTO, cost and complexity increase dramatically—and in technical terms, it’s not possible to guarantee a zero RPO or RTO in any case.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An additional complication is that different types of workloads might require different RPOs and RTOs. Consider a bank, for example. Having a low RPO to ensure that payment information isn’t lost would be key, and having a low RTO to ensure that people can still take money out of their account is vital. On the other hand, the part of the system that enables new customers to sign up for an account could have a higher RTO and RPO, as the impact to the business is less severe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So when deciding on the appropriate RPO and RTO, there needs to be a discussion with stakeholders regarding end-user needs and regulatory and legislative requirements, which are balanced against the cost and complexity of implementing the required solution. For example, your product owner might initially say they need an RPO of 10 minutes, but if you could tell them it would take months of work to implement (during which other work has to be deprioritized), they might reduce their target, perhaps accepting an RPO that is easier for you to deliver. Your target RPO and RTO should also exceed anything specified in any service level agreements you have.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DR Objectives and SLOs</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At first glance, RPO and RTO would appear to make for good service level objectives (SLOs). After all, they are both important measures that directly impact user experience. However, there are some challenges around managing RPO and RTO as SLOs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When determining if we are meeting an SLO, we need to collect lots of service level indicators (SLI) to confirm whether or not we are on target. So if we had an SLO that defined 99th percentile latency over a one-month period of less than 500 milliseconds, we would analyze the latency-related SLIs for that monthlong period to make sure we were meeting the target. With RPO and RTO, though, what would our SLI be?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reality is that we don’t experience disasters regularly enough to gather useful SLIs. We can of course define related SLOs around things related to our DR approach. For example, it would be possible to define an SLO around the speed of data replication, as this is something we are doing in production and can programmatically measure. But at best SLOs are only tangentially measuring RPO and RTO.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So RPOs and RTOs don’t really fit neatly into the SLO concept. Of course, that doesn’t mean that you can’t still test your system to make sure it is delivering on your DR objectives—something we’ll discuss more later in the chapter.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Disaster Recovery Patterns</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Another excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With the discussion of RPO and RTO in mind, let’s take a look at some common patterns used to implement DR in the wake of a major incident. In Figure 10-2, we can see an overview of each of the four patterns we will explore, arranged (broadly speaking) in order of increasing complexity and improving RTO and RPO.</p><div The key objectives to define as part of selecting an appropriate DR strategy</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If starting from scratch, many of these patterns can build on one another, allowing you to incrementally increase the complexity (and cost) of your DR solution over time. For example, a backup and restore approach requires rerouting, a pilot light setup will add the need for cross-site data replication and infrastructure automation, and a warm failover adds on the cost of having some infrastructure ready to go. So if you aren’t sure where to start, working your way through the patterns from left to right in  Figure 10-2 makes a lot of sense.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If you have different RPO and RTOs for different parts of your system, you may also end up using a mix of these patterns. Note that they all require some form of rerouting of traffic, and most require some form of cross-site data replication. Those options are discussed later in this chapter.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pattern: Backup and Restore</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Recovery by restoring data from a backup and loading it into a replacement system.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As outlined in Figure 10-3, with this pattern, data is periodically backed up to a separate site. In the event that the primary site fails, infrastructure needs to be provided at a new site, and the backed-up data restored.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Figure 10-3. The backup and restore DR pattern</em></figcaption></figure></div><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How it works</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This pattern is very straightforward to implement, consisting of a few steps:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. Back up data regularly.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">All data that you want to make available to the failover site needs to be regularly backed up, with the backup data stored somewhere other than the primary site.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Provision infrastructure on the failover site.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This would ideally be automated, as manual infrastructure provisioning would likely lead to longer RTO and an increased chance of errors.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. Restore data from backup to the failover site.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Data is loaded from the backup location into the newly provisioned infrastructure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. Switch traffic from the primary to the failover site.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Once infrastructure is available and the data is restored, traffic can be switched to the secondary.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ideally, your failover site runs the same core technology stack as the primary site, meaning that any investment in infrastructure automation on your primary can also be used on the failover (for example, being able to reuse Terraform scripts). Keeping the code to automate setup of the primary and the failover the same is very useful, as it means that you’ll have a higher degree of confidence that spinning up the infrastructure on the failover site will work. If your failover site uses a different technology stack—meaning it’s not possible to share automated infrastructure provisioning code between the primary and secondary sites—then it becomes even more vital that your DR failover process is regularly tested. A caveat to spinning up infrastructure on demand here comes in terms of guaranteeing that infrastructure is actually available when you need it, something we’ll explore later in this chapter.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When to use it</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This pattern is generally applicable in situations where your primary site is unavailable and you can tolerate a long RTO, and especially in those situations where you want to keep costs low. It’s important to note that regular tests of a backup and restore process are necessary to ensure that it actually works. One approach I’ve found useful is to perform a backup and restore to a secondary site as part of other regular activity (for example, a regular load test exercise).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The RPO of this pattern will depend on the frequency of backup. The RTO will be the longest of the patterns we’ll look at, and its time will depend primarily on how long it takes to restore data from the backup and provision replacement resources. With a fully automated process and smaller data volumes, this could be in the minutes to hours range. Manual recovery processes will likely extend these timelines greatly, as will the size of backups involved—terabytes of data take longer to send than gigabytes! Another major factor will be availability of the required computing resources. If you end up having to purchase replacement equipment, this pattern could easily result in a timeline of weeks or longer.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pattern: Pilot Light Failover</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Data is constantly synced to a failover site, with infrastructure provisioned after failover.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With a pilot light setup, data is continually replicated from the primary to the failover site, as shown in Figure 10-4. Infrastructure is not provisioned until a failover is required, ensuring that costs can be kept down when working with public cloud infrastructure.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
