The pilot light failover DR pattern</em></figcaption></figure></div><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How it works</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This pattern builds on a lot of the work done with a backup and restore, the main change being that the data is continually synchronized to the failover site. As such, the steps involved look fairly similar to the backup and restore pattern:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. Replicate data continually.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As data is committed to the primary, it is continually replicated to the failover site. This can be done in a variety of ways, such as by making use of native database technology or application-level replication.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Provision infrastructure on the failover site.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The assumption is that databases and datastores are already present on the failover site, so only remaining resources like compute would need to be provisioned.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. Switch traffic from the primary to the failover site.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Once infrastructure is available and the data is restored, traffic can be switched to the failover.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">From an implementation point of view, the new source of complexity comes from the replication of data from the primary to the failover. For systems designed with this process in mind, it might be somewhat trivial to implement. However, things become more complex when adapting existing systems if you’re making use of a data product that doesn’t support this replication strategy natively. This is worthy of a more in-depth discussion later in this chapter, especially as the next two patterns also rely on this capability.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When to use it</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When compared to a backup and restore, the pilot light failover allows for a much shorter RPO because of more frequent data replication, while also reducing RTO by eliminating the time taken for data restoration.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The cost-saving of a pilot light failover really makes sense only in the context of the public cloud. Costs are reduced primarily in terms of not paying for infrastructure unless it’s used. But if your failover site is your own private infrastructure that you have to pay for regardless of whether it is used, then some form of a warm failover makes a lot more sense. At that point you’re already paying for the hardware, so you might as well use it.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pattern: Warm Failover</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Data is synced to a failover site, with at least some infrastructure already provisioned to handle traffic.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With a warm failover, as shown in Figure 10-5, data is continually replicated from the primary to the failover site, with at least some infrastructure already provisioned in advance of the failover itself.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Figure 10-5. The warm failover DR pattern</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Having some infrastructure provisioned even before the failover occurs results in a reduction in RTO for some functionality. How much infrastructure is provisioned on the failover can vary, but the idea is that some capacity already exists to allow for a much faster failover.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A common approach would be to prioritize the subset infrastructure that is provided on the secondary site for the more critical capabilities of the system, allowing for a shorter RTO for the most important functionality.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Cold, Warm, and Hot Failovers: </strong><span>A brief note is warranted here regarding the term warm. You’ll find various solutions and vendor products promising cold, warm, or hot failover, with the only real distinguishing factor between these terms often being that a hot failover would give you a lower RTO in comparison to a warm failover, and a warm failover would give you a lower RTO than a cold one. Given that what constitutes hot or warm from vendor to vendor and from tech stack to tech stack varies so greatly, I just decided to pick warm and stick with it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Naming things is hard.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>The “How it works” and “When to use it sections” are cut off from this excerpt, but are present inside the book.</em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pattern: Multisite Active-Active</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>The system is distributed across two or more sites, with writes being able to be sent to any site.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With a multisite active-active setup, data is replicated constantly between two or more sites, as you can see in Figure 10-6. Traffic for any customer can be served from any site at any time.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/08890ce2-11a5-4689-ac54-98939d486752?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0186c82d-c3d9-4067-8bc4-fd19425248ca_1908x988.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":754,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="284.82142857142856" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FylH!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0186c82d-c3d9-4067-8bc4-fd19425248ca_1908x988.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Figure 10-6. The multisite active-active DR pattern</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This pattern sidesteps the need for a failover, as it is assumed that traffic for any user can switch between sites at any time. As such, it delivers the lowest RTO and RPO of any pattern we’ve looked at so far, though at much higher cost and complexity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>The “How it works” and “When to use it sections” are cut off from this excerpt, but are present inside the book.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">3. Infrastructure availability when planning for DR</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Yet another excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At the time of writing, GenAI is being used by more and more industries. Whatever your views on the usefulness of this technology (or its broader societal impact), the nature of GenAI workloads for both training and inference purposes has driven ever-increasing demand for infrastructure, in turn leading to reduced capacity for many users. Even if you aren’t running what you consider to be specialized GenAI workloads (for example, those requiring specific GPUs), you may well see the impact of these shortages more broadly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Aside from the ever-growing cost of GPUs, memory costs have spiked significantly in 2025 and 2026, impacting general server availability. I’ve already spoken to clients who are struggling to run “normal” (non-AI) workloads on some of the large public cloud providers, as they can’t secure enough capacity. Being able to shift regions in some cases is helping, but guarantees of future availability seem fairly weak. Even buying your own hardware doesn’t seem to be a quick fix, with lead times for servers seemingly extending further and further with each passing week.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This has to be taken into account when considering the patterns detailed previously. If your chosen approach assumes you can dynamically provision infrastructure when a failure occurs, you will have to look at what guarantees you have around the capacity you want. In a scenario where a major cloud vendor’s region has failed, you may find yourself fighting over scraps with everyone else.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are three ways to handle this scenario: reserve capacity; prioritize critical services; or lastly, consider running a fully redundant set of infrastructure at all times.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Not every vendor offers the ability to reserve capacity, and even then it is limited to certain cloud services. On AWS, for example, you can pay a fee to guarantee the availability of EC2 instances (managed virtual machines) when you need them. This has a cost impact, as you pay a fee for the reservation whether or not you use the instances (the silver lining being that if you did end up using them, the cost would be cheaper than normal in-demand pricing). This doesn’t help you, though, when using cloud resources for which reservations aren’t possible—you can’t purchase guaranteed availability of Lambda invocations, for example.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Next, consider prioritizing critical services. If there is a cost to guaranteeing availability (or if only a limited amount of infrastructure is available), then it’s vital that this goes to workloads that have a higher criticality. This is where having separate RTOs and RPOs on a service-by-service basis comes into play.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Finally, if you could justify the complexity and expense of having a fully redundant set of infrastructure ready to run your system, then you’d have the confidence that your computing resources will be available, with the caveat that this option can be extremely costly. But that cost can be mitigated if you can make alternative use of the redundant resources.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Back in Chapter 4, I mentioned BankCo, where we ran calculations across a large pool of machines. A large portion of these computers were desktop PCs sitting idle in an office situated outside London. These PCs formed part of the bank’s DR strategy: in the event that traders had to evacuate the bank’s main location, they could relocate to the secondary site and continue working. It was a requirement that these standby PCs were constantly running to ensure that we knew that they worked, and so that updates could be pushed out to them. This was obviously back in the day when most of the critical work relied on thick-client applications, so they couldn’t be accessed via the web.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We were able to make use of these DR workstations to grow our pool of available workers. This meant that when the DR site wasn’t in operation (which was most of the time), we were able to carry out our calculations much faster, as we could parallelize the work over more machines. If the DR site’s machines were unavailable to us, we still had a set of our own servers on which we could run the calculations to suit our normal targets.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So if you are thinking about securing ring-fenced infrastructure as part of a DR approach, see if you can think of useful ways to put it to good use when it’s not needed for production workloads. You could use the spare infrastructure for a load test environment, for example; the load test could easily be aborted when DR is needed.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Resiliency of AI-powered software</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Excerpt from Chapter 7: Resiliency and AI</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We’ve looked at how AI is changing how we build and operate our software. But we are also integrating AI into the products we build, using it to hopefully improve our software for our users. What new challenges does this create for ensuring our systems are resilient?</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Model Provider Resiliency</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Foundation model providers OpenAI and Anthropic don’t have a great track record in terms of providing high levels of availability for their services, at least when compared to other managed service providers, like public cloud vendors. While I’m sure this will improve over time, having a potentially flaky third party in the mix of your critical functionality can be an issue.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A solution here is to consider ensuring that your software can still operate even if the model is unavailable. This could be achieved by limiting functionality in the case of the model being unavailable (or you getting rate limited or running out of tokens!)—this is an example of the graceful degradation pattern, which we’ll look at more in Chapter 11.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another option is to have backup vendors for a given model to hedge against your normal model provider having availability issues. For example, you can use OpenAI models on Azure, a handy alternative if accessing the models via OpenAI’s own services proves to be too unstable, and in a similar way Anthropic’s models can also be accessed via Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. When using backup vendors like this, there may be a lag in terms of how quickly the latest models may be available, but given that you may not always want to be on the bleeding edge of the models you use to embed in your software (something we’ll discuss in just a moment), this is probably fine.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Model Changes</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consistency of behavior plays a big role in helping us ensure that our system is behaving appropriately. While dealing with the unexpected is a key concept in resiliency (or “graceful extensibility,” as David Woods put it), that doesn’t mean we want to build software where surprise is constant. Quite aside from the fact that LLMs are nondeterministic, small changes in models can also lead to quite different behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I’ve seen reports where a model has started behaving differently, without any major change in behavior being flagged by the vendor. Additionally, moving to a newer version of a model can fundamentally change how your prompts may be handled.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It is therefore vital to have a good set of tests to validate that the AI portions of your code are behaving appropriately—and this should be a mix of traditional functional tests, together with the use of AI evaluation tools (evals). You want to make sure that when the unexpected occurs, you are ones who get surprised first, rather than your users.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I can recommend the second edition of Gayathri Mohan’s Full Stack Testing,3 for those of you wanting to explore testing in general, including verification of AI-based systems. For a deeper dive specifically into evals, I’d suggest Evals for AI Engineers by Shreya Shankar and Hamel Husain.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Observability</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The telemetry we receive from our own software and from third-party services alike is key to making sure our applications are working the way that we expect. As we discussed back in Chapter 3, we prefer a small variation of latency rather than a broad variation of latency. If the time it takes to successfully complete an operation varies wildly, it can be difficult to know where we should start triggering timeouts, for example. It also becomes more difficult to define latency-related SLOs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Once you send a prompt to an AI model or instruct an agent to do something for you, the latency for the operation can vary greatly, and in ways that can be difficult to predict from the outset. Some of this can be put down to variability in the performance of the provider at a given point in time, but it can also be the result of rate limiting by the provider, or your prompt could just be taking longer to process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In situations where the prompts sent to models come directly from your users, then you will likely have even less certainty about how long it should take for a model to come back to you. Has a call hung, or is it expecting a large output?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some techniques to solve this can include dynamically setting timeouts based on the number of tokens being generated, or monitoring the streaming output from a model so you can track when the response starts coming back rather than waiting for the full response.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">5. How to handle uncertainty</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Excerpt from Chapter 7: Resiliency and AI</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the previous sections, I’ve outlined why the world of AI is so uncertain right now. However, I want this book to focus on practical, actionable advice. With that in mind, I want to outline some key steps you can take to make sure that you’re prepared for the uncertainty ahead.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Multimodel, Multivendor</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With model behavior, speed, and quality changing from version to version, it’s vital that you build your software to support changing models. Not only do you want the ability to change models to make use of the latest and greatest, but if costs start to increase from one vendor, you want to make sure the barrier to finding another vendor isn’t too great.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It is worth highlighting that mixing models from different vendors in a single flow can exacerbate issues. For example, a flow that involved models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google’s Gemini would be impacted if any of those models had availability issues. All those models have to be available and functioning correctly at the time the flow is executed. Also, prompts that work against one model may not be entirely portable to another—a prompt tuned against one model will have to be reevaluated when moving to a different model, even if you stay within the same vendor ecosystem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Taking a multimodel approach extends to your vendors too. If a vendor you are dependent on is in turn dependent on a single vendor’s model or API, you and your vendor become vulnerable to volatility in that model or to being impacted by a sudden price increase. Cursor was forced to pass on a significant cost increase to its customers in 2025, as it relied on the use of Anthropic’s services, and Anthropic changed its pricing structure, which led to Cursor having to pay much more. Coincidentally, Anthropic’s Claude Code is a direct competitor of Cursor. If Cursor had been able to use AI models from another firm, it might have been less vulnerable to this issue.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Keep Your Options Open: </strong><span>Make sure you aren’t wholly dependent on a single model or AI platform. If model quality degrades, or prices from OpenAI or Anthropic go up, you want to make sure that you have the flexibility to go elsewhere.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Cost Transparency</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Given concerns about rising costs from vendors, and given that pay-as-you-go pricing models can lead to surprising and unsustainable bills, having the ability to see on a regular basis how much money you are spending, and where, can be really important. This doesn’t need to be about limiting spend necessarily; it can be about understanding how you spend money and understanding what value that brings.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">James Stanier, CTO at digital healthcare firm Nordhealth, has advocated for being able to see spend on a per-person basis. Rather than this being about shaming people who spend too much money, he makes the case that this visibility drives better understanding of how the software is being used and helps drive the adoption of tools that are proving to be valuable. In his 2025 talk at LeadDev Berlin, “LLMs: An Operator’s View”, Stanier explains that if you see a person spending a lot of money, this shouldn’t be seen as a bad thing, as typically it showsomeone trying to get more done. He cites an example of one of his QA engineers blowing through €1,000 in a single week on Claude Code, which was a much higher spend than normal. After pairing with the engineer in question to understand where this money was going, Stanier was able to see that this spend allowed the engineer in question to more than double his productivity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Having the information about spend available to you, and being able to talk to people about how they use these tools and the benefits (or problems) they cause, will help you all make much better and more informed decisions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It can also help you spot egregious overspend. Uber recently revealed that it had burned through its entire annual AI budget in just the first four months of the year, and Microsoft announced it was pulling Claude licenses from its employees, due in part to cost, apparently.5 These stories might cause one or two raised eyebrows, but they pale in comparison to the recent (admittedly unsubstantiated) report from Axios that an unnamed enterprise company spent $500 million on Claude licenses after failing to put cost controls into place.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Tip</strong><span>: Make your AI spend visible! It can help you understand how people are using it and also help you spot when the bills start climbing precipitously.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">More Frequent Vendor Analysis</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Vendor management is a common activity that many firms carry out. It typically consists of a regular review of the main vendors that the organization makes use of to help it make better decisions in the future. For example, seeing that a large amount of money is being spent with a particular vendor despite the quality of service from said vendor degrading might cause an escalation to either get the price reduced or get the quality of service improved—or it might kick off a process to find a replacement.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In my last role at Thoughtworks, I helped lead our internal technology operations. Although my main job was to help provide support to internal delivery teams, I was also involved from time to time with our own vendor management activities. As part of these activities, we would regularly assess the general health of the vendors themselves. During the last review I was involved with, we were actively concerned about the health of one of our main technology suppliers; the supplier was in a very competitive market, and its market share was dropping. Although we were happy with the quality of service it provided (and with the cost), our fear was that wider market forces would drive it out of business. As a result, we decided to get to know the vendor much better but to also prepare a list of alternative solutions that we could select if the vendor in question didn’t survive.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Given the degree of uncertainty around the AI sector in general, I’d recommend regular vendor management activities. If you already have a normal vendor analysis cycle, consider increasing its frequency for AI vendors. If possible, find out if any vendors are in turn dependent on another provider, as in the case of Cursor being dependent on Anthropic’s cloud services. I’d be more concerned about a vendor that is in turn wholly dependent on a single company than I would be about a vendor that has more flexibility about whose services it uses. If you’ve never done vendor management before, consider instituting a lightweight process so you can build up a better understanding of how exposed you are to risk in this space.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With the concerns around the potential security vulnerabilities that come from the use of AI, I’d also recommend keeping your threat model up-to-date with regular threat assessments. As with vendor reviews, consider increasing the frequency of your normal threat assessments in areas with heavy use of AI, as this technology and how we use it is changing very quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Review Your AI Vendors Regularly! </strong><span>Given the volatility in the space, make sure you review your AI vendors much more frequently than normal vendors.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Summary</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I realize that this chapter may have ended on somewhat of a negative note. But I wanted to be clear that we have real, practical use cases for AI in helping us build more resilient distributed systems. Most of the use cases I outlined in this chapter are being used daily by people all over the world. The key thing is that the solutions I have shared here still put humans at the heart of decision making. It’s clear that, due to the challenges I have covered here as well, we are a long way from a truly autonomous AI SRE.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Despite the obvious benefits of using AI, we do need to be fully aware of the downsides at both the micro and macro level. At the micro level, LLM-powered AI requires us to be OK with nondeterminism, whereas there are many activities we perform in the context of building resilient systems that need to be fully repeatable and deterministic. At the macro level, concerns about the AI sector as a whole mean we are dealing with an ever-changing (and hopefully) improving set of products built on very shaky financial foundations. It doesn’t matter how good the tooling is if it’s too expensive to use (or the company making it goes bust).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As is the nature of things, this uncertainty around AI’s role in our industry and society as a whole will fade as we learn more and as the market settles down. But be warned: I think we are still very much in the middle of the storm, and the calm waters may be several years away yet.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A lot of this chapter was about uncertainty, and one thing that can make the resiliency of a system quite uncertain is what happens when machines fail. So in Chapter 8, I’ll explore how to make sure our systems still work even when machines let us down.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Takeaways</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Gergely, again.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Thanks to Sam for sharing this excerpt of the book! While this was a long article in itself, we covered less than one of 16 chapters in the book. I found the book an excellent read, and recommend getting it if you’re building production systems:</p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/building-resilient-distributed/9781098163532/","text":"Get the ebook or print book","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d669202-4acb-4c6e-9fb9-3d46214a4b4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #FF6B00;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Get the ebook or print book</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>My sense is that AI is making “resiliency basics” more important than before. </strong><span>Most of the book is not about AI – in fact, AI is barely mentioned in many of the chapters. But as AI agents generate more code and allow building software faster than before: we now have more software (or more complex software!) to operate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">And while there are AI tools and vendors that promise operating software to be easier with AI: I don’t really buy that it is, at least not at scale. Having the right monitoring and alerting in place is becoming more important, as is responding to outages, and being aware of tricky situations like thundering herds, retries, idempotency, timeouts, and many others.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Preparing for disaster recovery seems like a practical thing to do when your service is important enough. </strong><span>I wanted to include excerpts on disaster recovery, because I observe plenty of “disasters” (that is, widespread outages) happening across the industry where recovery time becomes surprisingly long. And some of this could be because the team had not prepared for, or exercised, disaster recovery beforehand.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A good example is how Coinbase’s global trading service </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ef18fba-7ed2-443c-8f24-6012359fe389?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">went offline</a><span> after a single AWS zone had problems. As I summarized the incident </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ef18fba-7ed2-443c-8f24-6012359fe389?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">in The Pulse</a><span>, back in June:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Having no automated failovers is incredibly amateurish for an operation of Coinbase’s scale. Coinbase moves about 5.2 trillion dollars per year, and is valued at around $40B. The outage interrupted around $7 billion-worth of financial activity, based on my napkin math.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s smart to learn from the mistakes of others, when we can: and the Coinbase incident felt like one of these.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;">I hope you found these topics relevant, and thanks again to Sam for writing the book, and sharing relevant parts with us.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIyMDIxODczMywicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTE5MDgwNzYsImV4cCI6MjEwNzQ4NDA3NiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.hhf4N_OSwpnHzkh4Pyqs9wqg31kFTDbCCif7hl6rvnw?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Physics Behind Heat Measurement and LLMs</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the early nineteenth century, Joseph Fourier studied how heat spreads through materials.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider a metal bar with some sections hotter than others. In order to predict how its temperature changes, we need a way to describe that temperature pattern mathematically. Fourier developed methods to represent complicated patterns as combinations of simpler sine and cosine functions. Eventually, these functions became the key tools for studying heat, vibrations, sound, and many other physical phenomena.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" plaintext;">For reference, a sine wave is a smooth, repeating pattern. Combining waves that repeat at different rates creates a way to describe much more complicated patterns. For example, a broad temperature variation might require slowly changing components, while smaller variations require faster ones. The temperature itself doesn’t have to oscillate over time. A wave can describe how temperature varies across space at a particular moment.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Similarly, in the field of LLMs, the mathematical input doesn’t have to represent time or physical distance. It can represent a token’s position in a sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Though sine and cosine functions predate Fourier, the 19th century saw their greater use in mathematical physics. Positional encoding, which is a critical way in which LLMs interpret word order, also belongs to the same mathematical family.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Word Order Carries Information</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Word order carries information that the words alone cannot provide. Consider these two sentences:</p><table class="email-code-block" role="presentation" width="100%" border="0" cellpadding="20" cellspacing="0" style="width: 100%;border-collapse: separate;border-spacing: 0;"><tbody><tr><td class="email-code-block-content" style="background-color: rgb(250,250,250);padding: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 8px;box-sizing: border-box;"><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background-color: rgb(250,250,250);margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline-offset: -1px;box-sizing: border-box;font-family: ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,'SF Mono',Menlo,Consolas,'Liberation Mono',monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 20px;mso-line-height-rule: exactly;padding: 0;outline: none;border-radius: 0;background: transparent;margin: 0;color: #24292e"><code style="line-height: 20px;mso-line-height-rule: exactly;"><span class="line"><span>Alice trusts Bob.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Bob trusts Alice.</span></span></code></pre></div></td></tr><tr><td class="email-code-block-spacer" height="20" style="height: 20px;line-height: 20px;font-size: 0;mso-line-height-rule: exactly;background: transparent;padding: 0;border: 0;">​</td></tr></tbody></table><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both contain the same words. Their meanings are different because the positions of the names determine who trusts whom.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Software has the same requirement. The expressions income - expenses and expenses - income contain the same variable names and operator, but generally produce different results.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, a language model needs access to two kinds of information: which tokens appear, and how those tokens are arranged. Just recognizing the vocabulary only provides part of what is needed to interpret the sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This becomes especially clear with repeated words. In “very, very difficult,” both occurrences of “very” have the same identity, but they occupy different places. A useful representation of this sentence must allow the model to distinguish those two occurrences of the same word.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Does a Model Understand Words</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A model starts by turning text into numbers. Since a neural network performs calculations on numbers, the text has to first pass through a process called tokenization. A token can be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment. For the examples we will see, let’s assume that each word is one token. However, actual token boundaries depend on the tokenizer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td href="https://substack.com/redirect/5ce52a49-1328-4931-8a36-fd4813a06e8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Each token receives an identifier. The model uses that identifier to look up an embedding, which is a list of learned numbers. Another name for such a list is a vector. An embedding might look like this:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">[0.20, -0.40, 0.70, 0.10]</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Actual embeddings usually contain many more numbers. Their values are adjusted during training so that they become useful for the model’s tasks. Individual numbers generally do not have tidy meanings such as “this is a noun” or “this refers to a person.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At the initial lookup stage, the same token identifier retrieves the same embedding wherever it appears. The embedding for a token doesn’t automatically change just because that token occupies position 2 instead of position 20.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Later layers build representations that incorporate context. But at the beginning, the model still needs a way to connect token identity with location.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How the Attention Mechanism Makes Sense of the Order</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Basic attention doesn’t automatically use the order of the list. Transformers rely heavily on a mechanism called attention.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Attention lets each token gather information from other tokens by calculating how strongly to weight their contributions. For example, processing a pronoun may require information from a name that appeared earlier. Attention provides a way to connect those pieces of text.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s now consider the simplest case. Attention can examine every token, and there is no positional information or other mechanism that indicates order. For the token “trusts,” both example sentences provide the same surrounding token identities: “Alice” and “Bob.” Swapping those names changes their locations, but the basic attention calculation has no position feature telling it which name comes first.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">More precisely, reordering the input reorders the corresponding output representations. But the reordering doesn’t independently recognize the new grammatical relationships created by the rearrangement. This is the order problem that positional representations address.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One objection is that the tokens already occupy different array indexes. Why cannot the model simply use those indexes?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is because an array’s layout doesn’t automatically become an input feature. A program that sums an array receives an ordered structure, but its calculation produces the same answer even after the elements are rearranged. Order can make a difference only when the computation actually uses it. In other words, basic attention needs a way to make the sequence structure affect its calculations.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Location of the Words is Made Available to the Model</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Positional encoding is the technique that is used to make the location of the words available to the model. A positional encoding converts a location in a sequence into a numerical representation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, in the first sentence, Alice is at position 0, trusts at position 1, and Bob at position 2. On the other hand, in the second sentence, Bob is at position 0, trusts is at position 1, and Alice is at position 2.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f2423bc-16c3-453c-a886-feb609799a69?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" plaintext;">The word “Alice” retains its token identity, even while its position changes. The same for “Bob”. The model can now receive different combinations of content and position for the two sentences.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The immediate question is how to represent those positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can give the model integers such as 0, 1, and 2 as input. Those numbers contain the necessary ordering information. Sine waves don’t add information that the position number lacks. Their purpose is to express that information in a form with useful numerical structure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For instance, naively adding the number 10000 to every component of an embedding could overwhelm the token’s existing values. More generally, a single scalar requires the model to construct whatever positional features it needs from that one number.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A collection of sine and cosine values supplies several structured features directly. Their values remain bounded, and different components change at different rates as positions increase.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Use of Sine and Cosine Functions</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sine and cosine describe movement around a circle. A simple explanation involves a hand rotating around a circle. Imagine a circle centered at zero with a radius of one. A hand starts by pointing to the right and turns counterclockwise.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The horizontal coordinate of its tip is the cosine of its angle. The vertical coordinate is the sine.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As the hand turns, its height rises, falls, becomes negative, and returns to its starting point. Plotting that height against the angle produces a sine wave. The horizontal coordinate produces a cosine wave.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both coordinates remain between −1 and 1.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To use this idea for positions, let each step forward in the token sequence rotate the hand by a fixed amount. Position 0 has one pair of coordinates, position 1 has another, and so on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why do we use both coordinates?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is because a height alone can correspond to two different places on the circle. A point on the upper-left side and a point on the upper-right side can have the same height. Their horizontal coordinates distinguish them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Together, sine and cosine describe the hand’s orientation within a complete turn. However, after one full turn, both readings repeat. This creates the next problem that has to be solved.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Multiple Rotation Speeds Are A Better Choice</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Multiple rotation speeds provide a richer position code. One rotating hand cannot distinguish positions separated by a complete cycle. If it returns to its starting point every eight tokens, positions 0 and 8 have identical readings.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/1a1347f4-0ca0-4cdc-9582-b6e7b2bdb198?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Now imagine three hands with different speeds. The first completes a turn every eight token positions, the second every 32, and the third every 128. At position 8, the fastest hand returns to its starting orientation. The other two have different readings from their readings at position 0. Their combined coordinates still distinguish those positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The example uses these speeds to show the point. Moving the position from 0 to 8 shows the fast pair repeating while the other pairs change. Each hand’s vertical coordinate is its sine value, and its horizontal coordinate is its cosine value.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The combined position code consists of all six numbers: a sine and cosine value for each speed. More pairs provide more components that change at different rates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original transformer uses this general construction, with a particular mathematical schedule of frequencies rather than the three example periods above. Faster components change substantially over short distances. However, slower components vary across longer stretches.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, the encoding represents each position through several scales of variation. The model receives a structured numerical pattern rather than a single counter.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To be clear, this doesn’t establish unlimited distinguishability. Our three-hand system repeats completely after 128 positions. Practical real-world encodings also face limitations from their frequency choices and numerical precision. The main aim is to have a representation that works well over the relevant sequence lengths.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How is the Position Code Used</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original transformer adds the position code to the token embedding. In the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, the position encoding has the same number of components as the token embedding. Corresponding components are added together before the sequence enters the transformer layers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The central operation is:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">InputRepresentation = TokenEmbedding + PositionEmbedding</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a small illustrative embedding, the addition at position zero could look like this:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Token embedding:       [0.20, -0.40, 0.70, 0.10]</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Position-zero encoding:[0.00,  1.00, 0.00, 1.00]</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Combined input:        [0.20,  0.60, 0.70, 1.10]</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The alternating zeros and ones arise because sine is zero and cosine is one at angle zero.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Moving the same token to another position changes the position encoding, which changes the combined input. Placing a different token at the same position changes the token embedding.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This gives the transformer a representation influenced by both identity and location.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Adding the vectors mixes their components. There is no guarantee that adding two arbitrary vectors preserves two separately recoverable records. Instead, the model trains with this combination throughout learning. Its embeddings and subsequent calculations adapt to use the combined signal.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model also doesn’t need to explicitly say “this is token 17.” Position information can influence which tokens it attends to and how it processes their relationships.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The main advantage of this is that relative movement has a consistent structure. Absolute position describes where a token sits in the whole sequence. Relative position describes where it sits compared with another token.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, positions 5 and 8 are three steps apart. Positions 105 and 108 are also three steps apart.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Language frequently depends on relationships that survive this kind of shift. Placing a phrase later in a document should not erase the relationships among its words.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sine and cosine pairs have a useful property here. Advancing by a fixed number of positions always rotates each pair by a fixed angle for that frequency. The rotation depends on the offset, rather than the starting position. With the example fast hand, advancing two positions always produces a quarter-turn. That remains true whether the movement starts at position 0, 7, or 20.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This gives the model a reusable numerical relationship between positions. Mathematically, a fixed linear transformation can map a sinusoidal position code to the code at a fixed offset. Neural networks already make extensive use of linear transformations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This explains part of the answer to “why sine waves?” Their value extends beyond producing different numbers for different positions. They provide a regular way to represent movement between positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model still has to learn how to exploit that structure. The encoding supplies a learning opportunity, rather than a built-in grammar rule.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Training Uses the Position Information</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Training turns position information into useful language behavior. Knowing that a name appears before a verb does not, by itself, explain what the sentence means.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider these examples:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Alice trusts Bob.</span><br><span>Alice is trusted by Bob.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Alice appears first in both, but the relationship changes. An adequate model must consider the verb form and the surrounding words as well as their positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">During language-model training, the system repeatedly tries to predict text. Its parameters are adjusted when its predictions are poor. Patterns involving token identity, sequence position, and surrounding context can become useful because they help improve those predictions.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" plaintext;">Positional encoding makes order available to this learning process. Attention helps connect relevant tokens. Other learned computations transform the resulting information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This difference also explains why the same positional scheme can support different languages. The encoding represents sequence structure without containing English grammar. Training supplies the language-specific patterns.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Rotary Position Embeddings Work?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Rotary position embeddings reuse the same mathematics inside attention. The original method adds a position vector to the input embedding. Later architectures introduce position in other ways.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One influential method is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE).</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table
