plaintext;">Attention compares numerical representations called queries and keys. A query helps determine what information a token gathers, while keys participate in calculating how strongly other tokens match.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">RoPE groups components of these representations into pairs and rotates those pairs according to token position. The rotations use sine and cosine functions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When attention compares a rotated query with a rotated key, the positional contribution depends on their relative rotation. That rotation difference corresponds to their relative position.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Different component pairs rotate at different speeds, preserving the idea of representing position through multiple frequencies.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Other Methods Apart from Sine and Cosine Functions</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sine and cosine are useful choices, but transformers have several ways to obtain position information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A learned positional embedding assigns each supported position a trainable vector. Training adjusts those vectors rather than generating them with a fixed trigonometric formula.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another method, ALiBi, modifies attention scores using a penalty proportional to the distance between tokens. It introduces a preference for nearby context without adding sinusoidal position vectors to the token embeddings.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There is also an important qualification to the earlier order-blind attention example. Generative language models commonly use a causal mask, which prevents a token from attending to later tokens. Different positions consequently have access to different prefixes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">That pattern itself provides structural information. Causal transformers can learn positional behavior even without an explicit positional encoding. The claim is that basic, unrestricted attention lacks an inherent ordering mechanism. A complete model may receive order information through several architectural choices</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ultimately, being able to calculate a position encoding for a very large position doesn’t mean a model can reliably understand an arbitrarily long document.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A formula can produce a code for position one million, while the model may have little experience using such positions or relating tokens across such large distances. Memory and computation impose additional constraints.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, mathematics developed long ago for describing physical patterns provides an effective numerical language for representing sequence position. Sine and cosine give that representation bounded values, multiple scales, and consistent relationships under shifts. Training then teaches the model how those positional relationships interact with the content of language.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: item.title: Why Your Engineering Team Is Slow
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why Your Engineering Team Is Slow

Alex Piechowski

“After years of codebase audits, the same five signals keep showing up, so I finally put them into a scoring rubric: The Codebase Drag Audit. Five signals, scored 0 to 2. If you hit 4 or above, the code needs direct investment before anything else will help.”

#Management CodeQuality TechDebt

#__Management GoalSetting

item.title: I Don't Want The Details
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
I Don't Want The Details

Michael Heap

"At first I thought ""I don't want the details"" sounded dismissive. How can they make informed decisions without understanding the details? Then I realised that ""I don't want the details"" wasn't being dismissive. The executive assumed that we were competent, and was saying ""I already believe you. Now let's talk about what happens next”.

#Leadership Communication
item.description: I Don't Want The Details

item.title: Don't Diagnose Your Opponents
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Don't Diagnose Your Opponents

Sean Goedecke

“When you disagree with someone, there are two paths forward. The first is to try to engage with what they’re saying: what their reasons are, whether their position is true, what evidence could be brought to bear, and so on. The second is to diagnose them: to engage with the second-order question of why they’re saying it.”

#__Leadership Communication__
item.description: Don't Diagnose Your Opponents

item.title: How To Effectively Debug When You No Longer Understand The Code
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Effectively Debug When You No Longer Understand The Code

Cindy Sridharan

“I consider this an emergent skillset that’s different from coding or traditional debugging, but like any other skill, it’s one that can be honed with enough effort. While I’m no leading expert in this area, the general contours of how these skills can be actively cultivated are beginning to stand out in sharp relief. By putting my own experiences in writing, I’m hoping to hear from fellow practitioners their thoughts on this topic.”

#CodeQuality Debugging
item.description: How To Effectively Debug When You No Longer Understand The Code

LLMs are the most capable AI models we’ve ever built around language, but many tasks require intelligence that goes beyond language. In fact, most of the tasks we face every day are not language problems. Some of them require spatial or dimensional reasoning. Others may depend on logic, planning, or just emotional awareness. a large language model is a system designed to predict the next item in a sequence. It reads as input a sequence of previous tokens, then it selects as output the most plausible token to continue that sequence.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d557030-602c-4f82-948b-007015460149?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6c6dbe34-2f45-424f-b701-6512547c7ffe_2048x658.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":468,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="176.78571428571428" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!16sg!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6c6dbe34-2f45-424f-b701-6512547c7ffe_2048x658.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The aim of this design is to achieve mastery of language. The output produced is far more useful than mere autocomplete. LLMs are now very adept at language manipulation tasks such as translation and summarization. And they can generate code.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But not all problems are primarily language-based. plaintext;">An LLM attempts to solve Sudoku by producing one token at a time, in this case, placing digits into cells one at a time. Before producing a token, the model reads the entire grid. Then it bases its selection on the tokens that have been produced before it. The LLM steps its way to the completed grid in this manner, token by token.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/77bfb89c-b2a3-46a7-a1b0-8a0596eefc86?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6fe787f2-682d-4a29-ba95-4fc3ed8e7cc7_2048x631.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":449,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="169.6085164835165" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BV6U!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6fe787f2-682d-4a29-ba95-4fc3ed8e7cc7_2048x631.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But LLMs have never been good at solving the type of problem presented by a Sudoku puzzle. The best LLM in the demo had a success rate of only 6.9%. It failed 93% of the time [1].</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two primary reasons why an LLM finds it hard to play Sudoku. The first is because an LLM generates tokens from left to right. The order in which the digits are placed depends on the prompt. Suppose the grid is written out row by row, so digits are placed in row 1, then row 2, and so on. If the model places a digit in row 2 that will collide with the digit it later needs in the same column of row 7, the column rule is broken. But because it generates from left to right, it does not discover the collision until it reaches row 7. Once it realizes the problem, it has to go back and regenerate everything from where the mistake was made in row 2. Any other order has the same problem: whatever the model commits to early, it cannot revise later without regenerating. Thus, the way an LLM operates makes fixing earlier mistakes expensive.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/5516b4a7-7e26-4683-b1ea-853ee280de94?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f1884424-ce7d-45ce-b18a-342052dee357_2048x822.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":584,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="220.6043956043956" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aRIp!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1884424-ce7d-45ce-b18a-342052dee357_2048x822.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The second reason that LLMs struggle with Sudoku is because their output is discrete. Tokens (e.g., the digits 1 to 9) are the smallest units that LLMs learn or produce. For a given cell on the grid, the digit placed in it is either correct or incorrect; there is no way to move an answer slightly closer to correctness. Instead, the only option is to discard the digit and sample a new one from the same discrete set.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sudoku is merely one example of where these two challenges exist. Left-to-right generation and discrete output are, in fact, foundational limitations of LLMs [3], and they emerge as problems whenever a candidate answer has to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously. Chess and Go, games where every choice depends on every other choice, are examples of constraint satisfaction problems. Chip design, industrial control, energy grid optimization, and trading systems are all activities that operate under interacting constraints. Constraint satisfaction problems need logic more than language to solve them.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/f57929c7-00ee-49c7-a11b-6985a5bc32fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7133f778-727a-43e1-88e3-1b9d8ca44a86_2048x1270.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":903,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="341.1057692307692" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5hoz!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7133f778-727a-43e1-88e3-1b9d8ca44a86_2048x1270.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So, through the example of Sudoku, we have demonstrated that language is not always the most effective way to solve every problem. For further illustration, consider what your brain is doing right now as you read these sentences. As well as reading the words, you may also be annoyed by the noise in the other room and simultaneously decide that it’s time to get up soon and make your next cup of coffee. None of those things need to be verbalized to be acted upon. You sit up straighter as you read; you go and get that coffee once you’ve finished this sentence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Your brain is a model that can do multiple things at once, and they don’t all require language. In addition to taking in words as you read, your brain scans its environment continuously. From the various inputs it receives, it makes predictions and acts on them. No words necessary.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3b1a06ca-a4f6-4743-b1f6-8fd2020790e1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c5e6d7e6-828b-43fb-ab7d-81e2153583ec_2048x1016.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":722,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="272.7335164835165" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G360!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5e6d7e6-828b-43fb-ab7d-81e2153583ec_2048x1016.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An LLM manipulates and recombines recorded facts, and skillful recombination can look like new knowledge. That is why LLMs do so well at mathematics, where much of the work is combining known facts. Language is indeed a powerful tool in the development of knowledge. But language itself is not intelligence, and it does not give all the answers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">According to Bodnia, in many situations, rather than language, we need extrapolation: the ability to take a rule learned in one place and apply it to another.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Our brains think in abstractions, and language performs the function of a user interface between brains. Thus, language is the interface to intelligence, not the intelligence itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If language is only the interface, how do we model the intelligence behind it?</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Latent reasoning with Energy-Based Models</strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Latent reasoning models differ from LLMs in that they work with latent variables instead of discrete tokens. Logical Intelligence works with the class of latent reasoning models known as energy-based reasoning models (EBRMs). This section describes energy-based models and how they are trained, then it explains how they produce answers. Then we will look at how the reasoning is developed in a latent space. (Note that the technical details described here are the general requirements for energy-based reasoning, not a specific description of Kona’s internals.)</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>What is an energy-based model?</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In contrast to a language model, which is simply a generator that takes an input and produces an output, one token at a time, an energy-based model (EBM) does not generate anything. Instead, an EBM learns a function, E(x, y), that takes a problem, x, and a candidate answer, y, and returns a number referred to as the energy. A lower energy indicates the answer is more consistent with the problem, and a higher energy indicates it is less consistent [4]. The lowest energy achievable for a given problem indicates the correct answer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure plaintext;">The neural network of an EBM defines a landscape over all possible answers, where the best answers are found in valleys and the worst answers are found on peaks, with a continuum of intermediate answers found on the slopes, moving toward correctness as they descend. The next two sections cover how the landscape is learned (training) and how an answer is found on that landscape (inference).</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>How an EBM is trained</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The goal of training an EBM is to get it to assign low energies to correct answers and high energies to wrong answers. This is done using a standard contrastive loss function, which compares incorrect answers to a problem to the correct one [4].</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider a problem, x, and its correct answer, y+. Pair it with a wrong answer, y-, for the same problem. The EBM computes the energy of both, and the contrastive loss function asks that E(x, y+) be lower than E(x, y-) by some margin. If the required margin already exists, nothing changes. If not, backpropagation is employed to adjust the network weights to lower the energy of the correct answer and raise the energy of the wrong one. The answers are not changed during training, only the weights.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa057f19-9676-423d-8ce2-6da0aa4a804f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8e4fc551-a231-4613-90a6-920d3da728a2_2048x1025.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":729,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="275.37774725274727" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WtbC!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e4fc551-a231-4613-90a6-920d3da728a2_2048x1025.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">EBM training requires the existence of wrong answers to build a useful landscape. Without wrong answers, every answer would be assigned the same low energy and the landscape would be flat.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The simplest way to create a wrong answer is to corrupt the correct answer, for example, swapping a few digits in a completed Sudoku grid. But the model itself can be used to provide wrong answers. This can be done by running several steps of the same search for descending energy gradient that the model uses to answer questions (see the next section) and using whatever it returns as the wrong answer y-. The contrastive loss function will raise the energies of all wrong answers until, through repetitive training, only correct answers are found in the valleys.</p><div plaintext;">Naturally, Logical Intelligence did not give us specific details about how Kona was trained. But they did tell us that they trained it on unfinished Sudoku solutions, with half of every grid hidden and no reinforcement learning. And yet the model still learned the rules and produced complete, correct grids at test time [1].</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Chess offers another interesting experiment, because unfinished chess games are the norm. Serious competitors and professional players will concede defeat when they see they are going to lose. As a result, most recorded games do not end with checkmate. Could a model trained on unfinished games play one through to the very end? According to Bodnia, yes, it could.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">After the training of an EBM is complete, correct answers will sit at the bottoms of valleys and wrong answers will be found at higher levels. The resulting landscape will be continuous. This continuity is a useful and necessary property because it means that when a search descends into a valley to answer a question, each successive downward step will produce a candidate answer more compatible with the rules than the last.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>How inference works</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An EBM model finds correct answers by assessing their energies. It keeps going until it has found the answer with the lowest energy. And it moves in the direction of that correct answer by following the descending energy gradient until it drops no further.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The first candidate answer to be assessed is random noise. The model computes the energy of that candidate, then it moves the candidate a small step in a direction that lowers the energy. This movement in the direction of lower energy continues until the energy stops going down. The candidate answer is then read out in the form required by the task. For a Sudoku puzzle, this means placing the correct digit into each cell.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure plaintext;">Since the search continues until the energy no longer falls with subsequent movement, the number of steps required to find the answer is not fixed. An easy input such as a Sudoku grid with a larger number of cells already filled will allow the correct answer to be found quickly (i.e., in fewer steps), and a harder input will require more steps. An EBM spends more computation on harder problems by requiring extra steps, similar to how a reasoning language model spends more tokens. In practice, though, the search is quick compared to an LLM. In the Sudoku demo, Kona settled in 313 milliseconds on average. The LLMs took up to 90 seconds for a single puzzle.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3fa584eb-eff1-4e35-bc6a-536053f52c5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/05b5df27-efca-455f-89ef-382cca56a9be_2048x743.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":528,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="199.45054945054946" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QsVd!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05b5df27-efca-455f-89ef-382cca56a9be_2048x743.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The search function relies on the fact that the landscape is continuous. Without continuous values, there would be no gradients and, thus, no indication of which direction to move toward the correct answer. To achieve this continuity, the candidate answers in an EBM are always represented by continuous numbers. For Sudoku, each cell holds nine scores, one per digit. For a text problem, each position holds a vector of scores over the vocabulary, rather than a token ID.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Reasoning in a latent space</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So far, the energy of the candidate answer has been used to determine the final answer directly. This approach is appropriate when the answer can be checked on its own, for example, on a Sudoku grid. But many answers carry no trace of how they were reached. For example, a plan may move through many states before it ends in a single number or action. An energy function that scores only (x, y) can judge the whole chain of reasoning only by that one output. Two answers a digit apart may have been reached through completely different reasoning; thus, a tiny change could swing the score from good to bad. That scenario would break gradient descent, which relies on small changes producing small improvements.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The fix is to have the energy function evaluate the steps. Instead of scoring only the final pair (x, y), the model scores every intermediate state against the problem: (x, z1), (x, z2), …, (x, zT), where z1 to zT is a sequence of intermediate states and each zT is a vector. This sequence is the reasoning; thus, the energy function evaluates the reasoning when it evaluates each state in the sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The intuition above is similar to how we work through problems. We hold a partial picture in mind; we adjust it; if we notice a conflict, we adjust it again. Only at the end do we put the result into words. The words are just the output format.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Bodnia pointed out that with reasoning in a latent space, the search is run over the model’s own compressed account of the data. In her words, “you’re navigating the understanding, rather than the data.”</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/942a071c-b0e5-472b-a058-1a6d3cd6f764?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/141d1129-2d6d-41ab-b825-61bf8a42abc6_2048x1028.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":731,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="276.13324175824175" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jIob!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F141d1129-2d6d-41ab-b825-61bf8a42abc6_2048x1028.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Training of reasoning in the latent space employs the same contrastive loss function, applied now to sequences. The states along a sequence that ends in the correct answer are pushed to low energy. The decoder is trained alongside, to read the correct answer out of the final state. The exact losses will differ between implementations, but they are immaterial.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Producing an answer works the same way as before, but applied to the sequence. The problem is encoded into the latent space, and the rest of the sequence starts as random noise. The model then adjusts the whole sequence at once. Every step moves together until the energy settles. The final state is passed to a decoder, a separate small network that converts it into the form the task requires.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Inference on the sequence follows these 5 steps:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Encode the problem into the latent space.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Start the sequence from the encoded problem, with every later step set to random noise.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Score each state against the problem. A state that breaks the rules shows high energy.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Adjust the states to lower their energies.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Repeat until the energy settles, then pass the final state to the decoder.</p></li></ol><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Energy-based reasoning versus language models</strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Autoregressive language modeling and energy-based latent reasoning are two very different methods of modeling intelligence. Which model best fits a given problem is determined by a single question: Can the correct answer be defined precisely?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An EBRM learns from correct and wrong answers. Therefore, it is suited for tasks where correctness can be verified. For example, in Sudoku, a filled grid is either correct or incorrect. A simple program can check the correctness of a candidate grid. Thus, the energy function has something clear to learn. This is why an EBRM will solve Sudoku reliably while language models will usually fail. Formal mathematics and planning have the same property, meaning that a proof checker or a constraint solver can act as the final judge.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/b162c7bb-30a0-49c7-8307-fef4a8feb14a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6ecc65c7-f43d-4bb7-bf9e-7a697a627800_2048x1337.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":951,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="359.2376373626374" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8Zm_!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ecc65c7-f43d-4bb7-bf9e-7a697a627800_2048x1337.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When correctness is vague, the advantage flips to language models. Whether an essay is well argued or a business recommendation is sound depends on judgment. An energy function trained on such data would produce a vague, undefined landscape. Because language models are trained on large amounts of human writing, they absorb the judgment it contains. As Bodnia puts it, “EBRMs are not going to write poems for you.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">They won’t write poems, but EBRMs are extremely well suited to domains where you can define the rules precisely. In chemistry, a candidate molecule either obeys the rules of chemical structure or it doesn’t. Physics requires the conservation of things such as matter and energy. In finance, the invariants can be as simple as “money in equals money out.” And the layout of a chip is largely a set of rules about what is allowed to sit next to what. The request to the model is similar across all these fields: this is the problem, and these are the rules.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/138e04db-e5aa-4b64-b091-0f7f35c2b720?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0ef8e5fe-4d3b-4010-bd11-164586973056_2048x911.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":648,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="244.78021978021977" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!stF7!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ef8e5fe-4d3b-4010-bd11-164586973056_2048x911.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Cost is the other half of the story. A model that only scores answers does not have to be large. Kona runs in the range of tens to low hundreds of millions of parameters [5][6]. Compare this to a frontier model, which runs in the hundreds of </span><em>billions</em><span>. Therefore, Kona can run on less expensive hardware. A small model plus a search that settles in milliseconds is how the experiment at the start of this article ended, with $11,000 of API calls from the LLMs and $4 of compute for Kona.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider this rough test for your own work: can you define your rules? If you can, consider using an EBRM. If not, a language model might be your better starting point.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The obvious objection to the necessity of an EBRM is that Sudoku already has solvers. But Logical Intelligence believes there is a distinct difference between a solver and an EBRM. A solver is a program hand-written for one problem. In contrast, Kona learned the constraint structure from examples of play and applied it to grids it had never seen before [1], similar to the way a person who has learned to play Sudoku can solve a new puzzle. And Kona can learn other things, no solvers required.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Most real-world problems will have some aspects that suit LLMs and some that suit EBRMs. The optimal arrangement is likely a division of labor. Let the EBRM handle the parts with hard constraints and checkable answers while the language model handles the parts that depend on knowledge, judgment, and expression and serves as the interface for reading the problem and writing the result.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Logical Intelligence has built toward this arrangement. EBRMs do the reasoning, and language models handle the interface [3]. Kona does the reasoning.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Verification and safety</strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Verification and safety work differently for EBRMs than they do for LLMs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a language model producing text, there is no pass mark for the text. We will often add a second system, an evaluator to score the quality or correctness and a filter to catch unsafe output. Unfortunately, this introduces latency to an already slow generation, because a check can only begin once the last token has been produced.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The two stages of an EBRM provide different kinds of guarantees. The first stage is the search. The learned energy pulls a candidate toward answers that satisfy the rules. As a result, most wrong answers are rejected before anything is output. This stage is probabilistic. The search wanders, and where it lands depends on where it started. The learned energy is an approximation of the rules, not the rules themselves, so a low energy provides strong evidence, but not proof, that an answer is valid.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>The second stage is the check. Because the output is logic rather than prose, satisfaction of the specified constraints can be verified by a machine, and the verdict will be yes or no. What does the checking depends on the task. For a Sudoku grid, a simple program can check the rules. For proving theorems, Logical Intelligence uses </span><strong>Lean 4</strong><span>, a proof assistant that checks formal statements by machine [7][8]. If the verdict is no, the answer goes back to the search, and the loop runs until the verdict is yes. A search that settles in milliseconds can afford several rounds, but a language model that takes a minute per attempt cannot.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a6f42f86-a945-46b3-b889-87c0efefe752?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bae577ce-e843-4105-90a8-ed1dd5ddfb3b_2048x1067.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":759,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="286.71016483516485" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QjUo!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbae577ce-e843-4105-90a8-ed1dd5ddfb3b_2048x1067.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The pipeline is probabilistic in the middle and exact at the end. For now, Logical Intelligence is limiting itself to solving objective tasks that can be formally verified. The check guarantees that an answer satisfies the constraints. It does not, however, guarantee that the constraints have accurately captured what the user meant. Therefore, the writing of constraints remains a human job.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>What’s Next</strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Bodnia’s larger argument is that one model cannot serve every kind of work. Whereas mission-critical systems rely on the generation of verifiable answers, creative work needs a system that is not constrained at all. Bodnia expects the industry will end up as an ecosystem of specialized models rather than one general system behind one API.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">From here, Bodnia expects two shifts in the industry. First, the hardware may move away from GPUs. Today’s GPUs evolved from graphics, and the industry was fortunate that the math required for LLMs was similar in nature to what had been used for graphics. But models built differently from LLMs have no particular reason to use the same hardware. Second, the business model will shift from selling intelligence by the meter to shipping a model per customer. Small models can be trained quickly enough to make that shift possible. Logical Intelligence recently built a model for a customer with two engineers and a week of training on the customer’s data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The EBRM field is still young, and there remains much to be explored. The next few years promise to be exciting.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro item.title: How to read code
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to read code

Sean Goedecke

7 minutes by Sean Goedecke Reading code differs from reading books because code order is set by the computer, not for human understanding, and engineers usually read changes to existing code rather than fresh programs. Most people struggle by reading code front to back, losing track of the flow. A better approach is making several passes, first tracing the overall structure and execution path, then diving into details. AI tools don't remove the need to read code, since their output often conflicts with a team's values and standards.
item.description: How to read code

item.title: The system around the code
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The system around the code

about 1 hour by Zarar Siddiqi AI tools have mostly solved writing code. The real challenge now is the system around the code: the pipeline, review process, team structure, and culture. Most AI strategies stall because they treat AI as a purchase rather than a reason to redesign how work flows. The bottleneck has simply moved from writing code to reviewing and shipping it, and throwing more AI at the problem makes that worse, not better.
item.description: The system around the code

item.title: Packing binary is fun
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Packing binary is fun

Pranav Desai

25 minutes by Pranav Desai Storing data as JSON wastes space, so Pranav's project explores building a custom binary format instead. It works by encoding field types and lengths into compact headers using variable-length integers, then using a schema file to avoid repeating type information for every value. A full compiler pipeline handles the schema language, including a lexer, parser, and code generator. The result cuts a typical JSON payload down by around 80%.
item.description: Packing binary is fun

item.title: English: A vs an
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
English: A vs an

Amit Patel

6 minutes by Amit Patel Choosing between "a" and "an" seems simple: use "an" before vowels. But the rule applies to sounds, not spelling. Words like "unicorn" start with a vowel letter yet take "a" because they begin with a consonant sound. Using a pronunciation dictionary to test this, most English words follow the first-letter rule, with only a small set of exceptions that can be handled with around 20 string-matching rules.
item.description: English: A vs an

item.title: Aho-Corasick algorithm for simultaneous substring matching
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Aho-Corasick algorithm for simultaneous substring matching

Colin James

8 minutes by Colin James The Aho-Corasick algorithm finds multiple patterns in a string at the same time. It starts by building a trie from the target patterns, then adds suffix links and output links to handle mismatches and overlapping matches. These links are computed in a breadth-first pass and let the automaton recover quickly when a match fails. The result is a fast, deterministic machine that scans input only once. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Aho-Corasick algorithm for simultaneous substring matching

item.title: A fruit fly's brain simulated in C#
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A fruit fly's brain simulated in C#

Konrad Kokosa

Google and HHMI Janelia published the complete wiring map of a fruit fly brain in 2026, and the internet quickly made it "play" video games. This post explains what those demos actually do: the measured wiring is real, but the parts that make the fly behave are hand-built adapters converting game state into neuron signals and back. Konrad built dotFly, a C# engine that runs all 166,700 neurons in real time on a laptop, running about 11 times faster than comparable JavaScript implementations. Run any coding agent inside Rider, backed by real IDE
item.description: A fruit fly's brain simulated in C#

item.title: Persisting a rich domain model with EF Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Persisting a rich domain model with EF Core

Milan Jovanović

EF Core dropped the requirement for public setters and parameterless constructors years ago. It can load and save fully encapsulated aggregates by writing directly to backing fields through a private constructor. Strongly typed IDs, private collections, value objects, and domain events all map through configuration classes that the domain never touches. The ORM was never the real reason for an anemic model.
item.description: Persisting a rich domain model with EF Core

item.title: Stripping extra dependencies in .NET NativeAOT apps
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Stripping extra dependencies in .NET NativeAOT apps

Andrew Lock

In this post, Andrew describes how he customized the linker for a NativeAOT application to remove a whole web of dependencies that he knows will never be needed, but which the linker was unable to determine directly that it could remove. By using method substitutions, you can significantly reduce the size of the final NativeAOT binary, by enabling additional dead-code elimination.
item.description: Stripping extra dependencies in .NET NativeAOT apps

item.title: Try catch and the importance of awaiting async methods
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Try catch and the importance of awaiting async methods

Tore Aurstad

Tore explains why async void methods in C# can cause exceptions to bypass the caller’s try-catch block. For fire-and-forget tasks, use async Task and handle exceptions inside the method. When the caller needs to catch errors, use async Task and await the method. This makes error handling more predictable and helps prevent unexpected application crashes.
item.description: Try catch and the importance of awaiting async methods

item.title: ChatClient Middleware vs. Agent Middleware
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
ChatClient Middleware vs. Agent Middleware

Jesse Liberty

The Microsoft Agent Framework uses two types of middleware. ChatClient Middleware intercepts messages between the agent and the language model, useful for logging and debugging. Agent Middleware works at a higher level, managing overall agent behavior like sessions and resource use. Both types support function-invocation middleware, which lets developers track and modify specific tool calls with minimal code changes. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: ChatClient Middleware vs. Agent Middleware

New trend: building internal vibe-coding platforms at mid-sized companies</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>When I visited Ramp’s headquarters last month in New York, I talked with the four-person development team behind ‘Glass,’ which is Ramp’s “internal Lovable.” This name refers to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f680ba1-c6a0-4b9b-8ef3-2b370cd29a20?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Lovable.dev,</a><span> the leading AI vibe-coding tool.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ramp’s ‘Glass’ is basically a vibe-coding platform for non-engineers to create complex applications which run internally. They can share the applications they make with others to use and modify. This is what the landing page looks like:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1080" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/584723a7-dad4-4ab3-95d5-97d6912a7f9b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/30dd81a8-f0c6-43d0-9369-ce9d7933fb49_1080x920.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":920,"width":1080,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":false,"topImage":true,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="468.51851851851853" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!11Mp!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F30dd81a8-f0c6-43d0-9369-ce9d7933fb49_1080x920.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>The landing page for Glass. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The team showed me a few popular apps, including a custom CRM built by someone in marketing, which had 50+ fields and filters on-screen. It seemed overwhelming to me, but the creator reportedly finds it extremely powerful to use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Since then, I’ve learned that many other mid-sized-and-above companies are building similar “internal Lovables” that don’t usually see the light of day in the outside world.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Stripe’s “internal Lovable”, Harbor</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Stripe </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ec5cd8ae-bc43-4932-9e4b-3682aed095b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shared details</a><span> last month about its own vibe-coding tool (my words) that they refer to more elegantly as an “AI-assisted prototyping tool” called ‘Harbor’. It was built by a single engineer in around six weeks. Here’s an example of a prototype built with Harbor:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
