Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ec5cd8ae-bc43-4932-9e4b-3682aed095b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Stripe</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why build your own internal “prototyping tool?”</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Lovable, Replit, Retool, and other vendors specializing in prototyping and building internal tools already exist, so what’s the point in bothering to build your own? Here are the main reasons I’ve gathered:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>A tiny investment. </strong><span>Stripe had a single engineer build Harbor v1, and Ramp had two engineers put it together in a matter of weeks. For companies with hundreds of engineers or more, this is a very reasonable time/effort investment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Expose internal data to be used. </strong><span>Because the tool produces internal-facing prototypes/tools, it’s a lot safer to expose internal data sources to it. Doing the same with third-party tools like Lovable or Replit would be risky.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Use the existing design library. </strong><span>Both Ramp and Stripe paid special attention to ensuring that the apps generated do follow internal design guidelines. Third-party apps are not great at this, out of the box.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Onboard most non-engineers, when done right.</strong><span> Ramp’s Glass project is extremely widespread, to the point that onboarding to Glass and creating a simple tool is now part of new hire onboarding. Pretty much every non-engineer uses Glass to build their own tools.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Don’t wait on vendors to build what’s needed. </strong><span>Why spend time and effort on tailoring a vendor solution which is straightforward enough to build? It would probably be a comparable effort to select the right vendor to go with, in terms of compliance reviews and price negotiations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>It’s educational and helps engineers to upskill. </strong><span>Engineers building these tools get better at building and maintaining AI infra at a time when recruiting engineers who are experts at AI infra is hard enough. Internal Lovables are a way to train more devs in-house by investing a few weeks in putting a solution together.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Among tech companies that have built their own coding agent harness that runs in their cloud, I expect many to build internal vibe-coding tools for non-engineers like Stripe and Ramp have done. After all, it’s not that complicated, gets much higher adoption than vendor products, and helps build out more AI infra expertise in-house.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If you’re building a similar platform, or are in a workplace where this happens, leave a comment about what led to the decision to do so.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>2. Do us engineers</span><em> really </em><span>enjoy hard problems?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A thought-provoking post this week </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba32a15d-e12e-4886-9c5a-0787adaeb9ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">from Sunil Pai</a><span>, a software engineer at Cloudflare:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The thing I learned this year is that when engineers say they like working on “hard problems”, they actually don’t. What they like is puzzle solving, and having a repertoire of patterns that they can pattern match onto traditionally hard problems, usually involving databases or something with scale, etc. And they know that the industry used to pay you a lot for how deep and broad this repertoire was.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Unfortunately, in 2026, well, you have a cheat code machine that has infinite breadth and depth for pattern matching.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>So the question is, do you actually like hard problems?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Because there are now hard problems that are a combination of engineering, product, society, culture, politics, and they are fairly intractable, probably unsolvable! Because if you do want to work on those actually-hard problems, there is so much money that people will pay you for it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But you’ll have to face that truth about yourself first.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To me, this rings true when I think about the types of problems that I’ve seen most engineers get really excited about, they were things like:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Rebuilding a system from scratch with a focus on scalability</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Using a new, exciting framework and technology that they’re keen to spend time on</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Improving performance on the backend: eg:, lowering latency, increasing throughput, etc</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These all require specialized knowledge of systems – and 99% of the time, backend systems and distributed systems in particular. Knowledge took time and effort to build up.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>But “frontend-minded” engineers don’t get much credit for solving business problems, in my experience. </strong><span>If a frontend or mobile engineer improves the UX in a way that increases conversion and revenue, they rarely get the praise from engineering leadership that comes a backend engineer’s way for replacing part of the backend to reduce latency on the system or CPU utilization. How come?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My take is that backend and scale problems are often more desirable to solve by many engineers because most of the problems within a business are on the backend, and the highest rewards in terms of promotions come from solving problems on the backend.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, most CTOs and Heads of Engineering come from backend and distributed systems engineering backgrounds, and naturally understand that problem space more, and so credit engineers for solving problems in those domains.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>It’s reasonable to ask what happens if AI makes it easier to solve the hard engineering problems. </strong><span>We’re still far away from AI making hard work </span><em>trivial; </em><span>for example, I would not trust any AI agent to execute a database migration, or even a rewrite. But it’s clear agents make it easier to take on complex work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Sunil has a point that there are probably a lot fewer engineering problems on the backend that are </span><em>truly</em><span> hard to solve, in an environment where knowledge is commoditized, such as how to scale up systems. And for knowledge that is commiditized and widespread, AI typically makes it faster to understand and apply. But some things are still hard as ever, even for the latest, greatest models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How do you get people to pay for the product you built? What makes your product different and trustworthy vs ever-growing competition?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How do you retain a user who signed up for your product? How do you have them come back in the following days?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How do you create a new product that makes money?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">In this fast-moving, changing industry, how do you build things that sell when public preferences shift?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>In my </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0bac5336-9b82-4af9-957f-9330ce292e88?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">State of the Tech Industry in 2026</a><span> keynote recently, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9189f725-3425-4aa5-9d1e-20d04c153d0f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">highlighted</a><span> an observation about taking on the problems that are elsewhere, as alluded to in Sunil’s quote at the top of this post. Titus Winters, lead author of Software Engineering at Google told me: “...when intelligence becomes commonplace, wisdom and charisma become much more important. In the context of software engineering, “wisdom” is most easily earned by becoming a domain expert. So, if you work at a fintech company, learn about the finance industry and its customers in order to become a more valuable, in-demand engineer! That also applies if you’re at an agriculture tech company, or work in any other domain.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I wonder if the truly hard problems for engineers to solve will increasingly be a hybrid of business and engineering, and problems which are engineering-only become scarcer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As things progress, let’s not forget that new hard problems will emerge around building new generations of platforms to power mid-sized-and-above businesses:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How to build a “software factory” where AI agents are part of the software delivery process, from planning, through building, validation, deployment and monitoring+alerting.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Which agentic systems should be deployed as customer-facing components; how do we monitor them, spot errors, and deal with them?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How do we decide when to use nondeterministic LLMs versus deterministic code which could have been generated by LLMs?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How do we benchmark and eval agentic systems on an ongoing basis, and decide which models to use?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How to measure the “productivity” of LLMs and their business impact</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>What’s your take: are fewer “hard problems” about “pure” engineering than before, and what are some new hard problems for engineers to grapple with?</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">3. New open models launch in EU and US</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s been a very busy week for new, capable, open model launches, with two promising ones from Europe and one from the US.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/84b2cfd0-0f73-4384-abf2-b6a0271cd61f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Kolibri</a><span>: a SOTA open model from Germany, with extreme transparency. </span></strong><span>Out of nowhere, the German Aleph Alpha team released Kolibri, which is an incredibly capable model about which they’re extremely open on how it was created, and also the dataset! The team’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1529a9a-2c63-49b4-ab68-2180f1fcc96e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">technical report</a><span> is pretty much a tutorial on how to create a modern LLM from scratch. Excerpts below:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“This report introduces Kolibri, an English–German Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20 % of the data mix. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4 % of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Being a model built in the EU, it is GDPR-compliant, meaning that it does not use pirated content for training (unlike how most frontier AI labs have done!), and redacts any and all personal data in the dataset. If you have even a modest interest in understanding how to build an LLM, I recommend </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1529a9a-2c63-49b4-ab68-2180f1fcc96e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: Aleph Alpha, Mistral, and Reflection could be stepping up to meet it.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Industry Pulse</h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why doesn’t Figma let any tool use its MCP server?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Figma has built and launched a remote MCP server which AI harnesses can connect to, but has decided to restrict this to certain supported agent harnesses like Claude Code and Codex. The leading UX design tool does this check rather primitively by asking an agent to provide its name. This limitation meant that minimalistic coding harness Pi was rejected:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure In its favor, I guess the case could be made that Figma wants to review each new tool to ensure it plays nicely with Figma. At least, that’s how it seemed when a Figma employee </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/951cd830-1a2c-4b1d-a863-433cd766cb06?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">asked</a><span> Mario to submit Pi to be included in the supported MCP clients.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>But after submitting, Figma informed Mario that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/78298f44-39ed-49d9-b16e-9f731625f947?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">it has paused adding MCP clients</a><span>, and so Pi and other clients will not be supported. It’s just an awkward situation that Figma has created here.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">My take is that it’s foolish for a vendor to limit the tools which its customers can use for MCP connections. It’s like a bank’s website rejecting browsers with headers other than Chrome and Safari, and then acting surprised that they have paying customers using Firefox, Opera or Brave, who cannot log in and use the service.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Google Cloud adds server-side support for Swift</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Devs can now use Swift for backend work on Google Cloud, according to a new </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b853cb9f-f8e3-4bf3-b992-e58b2266b423?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">announcement</a><span> from Google:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“For years, Swift was perceived mainly as a UI language tied to Apple client devices. With Swift 6 and strict concurrency checking, it has matured into a viable systems and cloud language, pairing Rust-like data-race safety with predictable, reference-counted performance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To support this ecosystem, Google engineering has launched the official Google Cloud API Client Libraries for Swift. Built from the ground up for Swift 6.2+, this new SDK uses the latest non-blocking Swift NIO event loops, HTTP/2 multiplexing, gRPC transport, and zero-cost compile-time data race safety.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If you wondered why Swift has not been previously widely supported on the backend like Kotlin is – even though it’s an equally capable language – it’s because Kotlin is a JVM language, meaning interoperability is straightforward with other JVM languages like Java, Scala, etc. Thanks to this interoperability, the mature Java backend ecosystem with its frameworks and libraries has always been trivial to use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Swift doesn’t have this advantage, meaning its ecosystem on the server side will likely always be more limited than Kotlin/Java/JVM. </span><em><span>I previously had </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73e22e09-8f69-4e9b-a4b1-fecbc7741422?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Chris Lattner, creator of Swift</a><span>, as well as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b9c78667-81e6-46df-94fd-f6746cbb290c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Andrey Breslav, creator of Kotlin</a><span>, on the podcast.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro In the end, they improved most performance metrics 2-5x:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Before and after: snappiness of Claude Code. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9dccf30c-6bd5-417d-bde7-6d9668f8f50a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Anthropic</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Anthropic’s eating its own dogfood; obviously, they used Claude heavily in the project and relied on the AI agent to come up with optimizations and then measured their impact, and leave agents to run autonomously on coming up with fixes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I feel something’s amiss: the Anthropic team seems to treat performance optimizations as a “make it better” task, not a “make it as fast as possible” one. </strong><span>The Anthropic team gave itself a pat on the back for speeding up all parts of Claude Code, but didn’t answer two questions:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How did things get so slow to start with?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">How fast could Claude Code get?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>In the episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c379bacd-ac8a-4c86-834a-164e3e40803e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">with performance expert Casey Muratori</a><span>, he says that this approach is wrong for performance optimization. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/170bc339-2ba2-4b18-9719-800aca4f7be6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the episode</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Profiler-driven performance optimization is the wrong way to optimize. The standard way of optimizing is to profile the application, tweak hotspots, then check if the stats have improved. But this only finds a local minimum; Casey says every engineer he’s worked with who was a great “optimizer” began by establishing what the hardware could theoretically do, and then did not stop until they’d closed the gap to that performance level.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s inspiring to see that application performance can be drastically optimized with AI agents, but I also see this event as mainly a reminder that AI agents often create inefficient code which slows down application performance gradually over time. This is illustrated by how slow Claude Code had gotten.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s safe to assume most AI-generated software will suffer from worsening performance – at least for periods of time – so building software designed for high performance from the ground up will surely become an advantage.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Coinbase also ditches React Native</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A few days after Shopify </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1db261fe-3cac-45a2-a904-d2b7273fd6bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">announced</a><span> it is dropping React Native and rewriting all six of its mobile applications to native, Coinbase announced the same. Adam Wolf, senior engineering manager at the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b199e53d-88ba-4c11-b1e4-7140009b7f78?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">said</a><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Coinbase will migrate iOS and Android apps to native Swift and Kotlin</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">AI coding agents greatly reduce the price of “building a feature twice”; once in Swift (iOS) and once in Kotlin (Android)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Native mobile apps result in better experiences and performance</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Coinbase moved to React Native (RN) </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fdcd1e9e-89ad-4cde-a456-fd0c45257934?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">in 2021</a><span>, and to be honest, I don’t really get why. Unlike Shopify with six apps, Coinbase has one trading app. Trading is performance-sensitive in terms of sending trading details over the network as fast as possible, while crypto itself is less time-sensitive as the blockchain is slow in processing transactions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>When Coinbase adopted RN, it had 56 million users, and I would’ve thought that ensuring outstanding performance would be a priority in 2021. Also, Coinbase pays top-of-market compensation, so you’d assume there would be no trouble attracting native iOS and Android engineers. But Coinbase </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fdcd1e9e-89ad-4cde-a456-fd0c45257934?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">said</a><span> one reason it moved over to RN in 2021 is that they struggled to native mobile engineers much more than hiring web engineers. My question: so, why didn’t they up their recruitment game, back several years back?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Coinbase is back to building native apps, and it feels like this probably should have been the strategy before AI.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Oops: Claude formatted the C drive!</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It was a bad day for a software engineer running Claude Opus 5.5 with the flag -</span><em>-dangerously-skip-permissions</em><span>. For about a year, it worked just fine – until yesterday:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td on auto mode (the default mode) would have avoided this scenario because that mode asks for permission to execute commands like formatting the hard drive. </span><em>There’s a reason this flag is called --dangerously-skip-permissions!</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This dev was tired of “babysitting” and decided to run with this flag because Claude doesn’t allow sessions to run by themselves.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Agents doing seemingly irrational things like formatting a C drive are why I firmly believe we’ll see far more sandbox environments for agents, with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9189f725-3425-4aa5-9d1e-20d04c153d0f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">cloud coding agents</a><span> becoming more popular, and OS-level primitives like the sandboxes that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9493b87c-b85a-454e-8d01-45cfe10afdf0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Linux</a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/07e643ce-83c2-4bb6-96d8-b442c99e01b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Windows</a><span> are introducing.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Microsoft & Meta slash Anthropic spending</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>The Information </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d87bfdd1-03ce-4905-940c-36a49b527556?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reports</a><span> that Meta has cut the number of its employees with access to Claude by half, from 60K to 30K employees. Meanwhile, Microsoft is cutting its spending by a third. This comes as little surprise:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Meta has become a frontier lab with its Muse models, so naturally, it wants staff to use their own model, not a competitor’s. Plus, it’s not smart to fund a rival frontier lab.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Microsoft was on track to spend $1B per year on Claude (!!), which is also a competitor to GitHub Copilot, and Microsoft naturally wants its engineers to use its product. Plus, Microsoft is a large investor in OpenAI.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The only surprise to me is that both Meta and Microsoft have spent so much on Anthropic, a direct rival in the space.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Memory supply crunch to worsen next year?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The CEO of Micron, one of the world’s biggest memory producers, said a week ago that he expects memory supply difficulties to get worse before they improve – and identified AI as the reason why. From an earnings call:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“We expect memory and storage supply-demand conditions to be much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026. AI is becoming super intelligent, and memory enhances this intelligence and the competitiveness of our customers’ platforms. Even with additional industry DRAM clean room space plans with robust demand trends, including new upside requests from customers, we do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Basically, this forward-looking statement suggests that memory prices will continue to go up in 2027 and in 2028, meaning that laptops, consoles, and mobile phones will cost more as manufacturers pay more for memory chips. That’s bad news for anyone buying devices and for companies running memory-heavy compute loads. Micron is building new plants to produce more memory, but these </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62d75208-8f64-4050-9b3e-cd8ef30b2cc2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">are not expected</a><span> to be operational until late 2028.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxOTQ1NTQ3OCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTE0Nzg4ODMsImV4cCI6MjEwNzA1NDg4MywiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.MfkpA70n7yux5FO6Rkh534qXOakatq9BiVWhxkgOR_0?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;">No matter how big a software system gets, it will still have a boundary. This boundary separates things inside the system from those outside it. In fact, you’d have noticed that dividing a large system into multiple components can have some great benefits. However, deciding how the system should be divided requires skill and understanding. Experience is the best teacher in such cases. But there are also some strategies that can help.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But what exactly does a boundary do?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A good software boundary keeps an application’s responsibilities, its rules, and the details needed to apply those rules together. Parts of the system outside this boundary can talk to things inside the boundary only through a clear pathway. This means that the skill of deciding boundaries requires you to have an idea of which responsibilities should be bunched together. Also, which dependencies should exist between them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we’ll learn some key strategies that can help a developer make the right boundary-related decisions for the systems they are working on.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: We discuss what teams get wrong when adopting microservices, why independent deployment matters, and how microservices can help teams work more autonomously.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We also peek into his new book, ‘</span><strong><a plaintext;">We also explore how AI is changing software development, from specs versus code as a source of truth to cognitive debt and cognitive surrender. Sam shares how modular architecture can help teams experiment with AI while maintaining understanding of the systems being built.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Sam</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a93ad983-dfa5-4c09-a380-054a16bc3d68?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/a0sZV0qIbI0" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. In the room when “microservices” was coined. </strong><span>In the early years of the 2010s, James Lewis – Sam’s colleague at Thoughtworks – kept running into companies building service-oriented architectures where each service could be replaced quickly. At an architecture symposium in the Lake District, England, James pitched a name for this trend: “micro apps,” and in a room of about 10 people (including Sam), someone else suggested “microservices.” Lewis and Martin Fowler then wrote the first article on the topic in March 2014, ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b82fd3c-2f03-4e05-b637-66ca22b7ac03?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Microservices: a definition of this new architectural term</a><span>’, and Sam published the book </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/227fe736-f9a7-4cd8-b7a5-ae0a8b2e0ccc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Building Microservices</a><span> the following year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Sam spent 18 months teaching Googlers how to write good automated tests. </strong><span>In 2007, Sam was embedded at Yahoo and Google as a ThoughtWorks consultant, alongside people from Pivotal Labs. Their job was to teach engineers how to write automated tests, and code that’s testable. He recalls that some Google devs did not believe it was possible to write automated functional tests for websites, until Sam and his colleagues showed them how Selenium works!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. Sam spent 10+ years at a large company, three years at startups, and has been independent for more than a decade.</strong><span> After 13 years at Thoughtworks, he quit to avoid becoming “institutionalized.” He recalls thinking he could hang around at Thoughtworks and grow bitter. “So I’ll just go now.” He then worked at three different startups before going independent, which he’s now done for 15 years. The biggest challenge of being your own boss? He says: “The problem of working for yourself is that the boss is frequently an a*****e. So, current Sam frequently is cursing past Sam for the commitments he made!”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. So, what’s a “microservice?” </strong><span>Sam gives two definitions: a clear one, and a softer one:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Independently deployable service. </strong><span>The “clear” definition: as long as, upon a change to a system, it can be independently deployed – without any other services needing to be deployed –, you can call it a microservice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Clear boundaries around the business domain.</strong><span> The “softer” definition: services split by business function (not by technical layer) can also be called microservices.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>5. Three rules of distributed systems: </strong><span>Sam sometimes struggled to recall the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ec10fcf8-bca0-40fa-aedf-8acf63565a99?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">eight fallacies of distributed computing</a><span>, and so he boiled them down to the three that cause the most problems:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">1. Information takes time to travel. You cannot send information instantaneously from point A to point B. This is basically the “speed of light” constraint.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">2. Sometimes, the thing you want to talk to isn’t there. That is, resources can and do go offline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">3. Resources are not infinite; you will eventually run out of things like CPU, memory, storage, and networking bandwidth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In Sam’s experience, most distributed systems outages are caused by #3; resource pools running out.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>6. Dealing with idempotency: keys or fingerprints? </strong><span>Idempotency is performing the same operation multiple times and it having the same effect as if done once only. For example, if you repeatedly hit the “down” button for an elevator, nothing more happens than what happened upon that first press: multiple button smashes don’t bring more elevators your way. Payments are a classic example where idempotency is needed: when you retry or refresh a payments page, you should not be charged twice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two common ways to deal with idempotency:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Idempotency keys</strong><span>: a client sends a unique identifier (usually a UUID) that is the idempotency key. The server makes sure operations with the same idempotency key are executed only once. It’s clean to build but hard to retrofit, which involves changing both the client and server.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Fingerprints:</strong><span> the client sends nothing, but the server creates a “fingerprint” of the request by hashing relevant fields. It’s easy to retrofit later (only need to change the server), however, legitimate requests can be rejected as duplicates, and duplicate requests could still happen. Sam  describes a Danish payment system he worked on that rejected purchases of the same value within a 5-minute period while it did the fingerprinting.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>7. Four concepts of resiliency:</strong><span> Sam frequently references the four outcomes for military systems, explained </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/708e12d8-3548-4db7-9570-1f3adc7bf209?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">by David Woods</a><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Robustness</strong><span>: systems continue to function as intended, for example, when Kubernetes replaces a failing pod. A downside of robustness is that it can add complexity, and more complex systems have more ways to fail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Rebound</strong><span>: how quickly the system recovers when something goes wrong.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Extensibility</strong><span>: dealing with surprises and being able to stretch the system’s support to deal with new needs</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Adaptability</strong><span>: the system changing to support new functions. Resilient systems are adapted, even between incidents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>8. What if code is a side effect of collaboration? </strong><span>When Sam was at Thoughtworks, some clients refused to do pair programming as a practice because they could only see one developer typing and the other doing nothing, which is a waste. Martin Fowler’s dictum that “programming is not typing” helped Sam to explain to clients that typing out code is an output, but not an outcome.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sam conceives programming as building a system collectively, and code is one of the mechanisms delivering the system. Now that with LLMs we no longer spend most time typing out code, we’ll discover the next bottleneck in creating good software. Could it be delayed feedback cycles?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9. Hedging the vendor options is sensible when integrating AI into systems. </strong><span>It’s hard to tell which AI companies have long-term, sustainable business models and which don’t, so it’s the responsible thing when designing systems to hedge the providers. Aim to be multi-vendor, multi-model in your choices, so you can easily change the vendor or model layer. Also, consider if you can swap out LLM-powered functionality for deterministic code that runs faster and cheaper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>10. We must resist “cognitive surrender” to AI. </strong><span>Sam believes that more AI usage is leading to less critical thinking – or could we be using it wrong? He says: “The original pitch of AI was it was going to free us from drudgery. We’d have less toil, and we can focus more on critical thinking and smarts. However, much of our current use of AI is not freeing us up from critical thinking! It’s causing </span><em>more</em><span> context switching and leaving less time for thinking. People are working longer hours; we’ve got studies that show this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But [longer hours and more context switching] is not necessarily AI’s fault. It’s just how we’re using it.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Putting in the effort often leads to better results. For example, when writing Building Resilient Distributed Systems, Sam used NotebookLM for research, but he manually clicked through each link it surfaced, and checked whether it was information he wanted to reference.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>11. Starting with modules encourages better software architecture. Also: production is truth. </strong><span>I asked Sam for advice on what to do to get better at designing systems:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Start by thinking carefully about module boundaries and the connections between them</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><span>When you use AI, allow it to roam freely, but only </span><em>inside</em><span> the module structure that you have designed!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>12. Much of the tech world might still be naive about what an LLM is. </strong><span>As Sam said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“I think the tech world in general is quite naive about AI and fundamentally misunderstands what an LLM is. For example: why did the LLM delete my database? Well, because it has no concept of causality. They have no concept that if I do A, B happens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">LLMs are not world models. World models have been around for a long time. They predate LLMs. So if you had the appropriate model and the appropriate inputs, world models could at least get to the point of ‘if I do X, then Y happens and I’ve been told not to do Y.’ </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I think we expect LLMs to do more than they actually can do, because they seem so smart.</strong><span> This leads us to overestimate their capabilities a bit too much. But the nature of LLMs is why all the guardrails around LLMs are really not going to be the right long-term solution.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Sam’s comments feel very timely, given Opus 5.5 </span><a none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Recommendations are one of the most important pieces of the Netflix experience. If you’ve watched Netflix, you would have noticed the Netflix homepage recommending a bunch of movies and TV shows. More often than not, they happen to be stuff that might be of interest to you. They also keep changing with time based on what you’ve watched.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original Netflix recommendations engine was built on top of 1000s of hand‑crafted features across users, items, and interactions. It also used special architecture for various functions that contributed to the task of making recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Though a lot of changes have happened to this stack over the years, it’s still pretty complex. It’s costly to onboard new use cases. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) have made great strides. They have progressed a lot in their ability to recommend things to a user. Due to their broader world knowledge and understanding of language, LLMs do a good job of figuring out relationships between different things. They can also make recommendations using natural language, which is a plus point. However, you cannot just pick an LLM off-the-shelf to generate recommendations for a company like Netflix.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is why the Netflix engineering team built GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The basic idea behind GenRec is to use an LLM to make better sense of a user’s viewing history to assign scores to the various movies and TV shows streaming on Netflix. However, you can’t just give a general-purpose LLM a list of movies or shows that a user has watched and expect it to come up with interesting recommendations. Netflix has to make a bunch of adjustments to the base model to make it work with their content and member behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at how GenRec was built. Here’s what we will cover:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Basic Question with Recommendations</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A recommendation system has to answer a basic question: What should appear first in the list of recommendations?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The answer to this question is the key to deciding which items to show a particular person and in what order. On Netflix, those items can include movies, series, games, and other content types.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The order of the recommendations is super important. A user’s attention span is limited. A viewer might check only a few titles before making a choice. If they don’t find something interesting in that time, they might even leave the platform to check elsewhere. It doesn’t matter if something that the user might like is present in the catalog. You can say that the recommendation system has failed to do its job.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The ordering of the recommendations is handled by a component known as the ranker. It assigns scores to various items based on how suitable they appear for a particular user in a particular situation. The better an item’s score, the higher it appears on the recommendation list. To decide this score, a ranker needs a lot of information. Here are some examples:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The member’s interaction history to understand what they like or dislike.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Item metadata to make sense of what a piece of content is about.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Details about the device the viewer is using. Time of day. Language or region.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix’s GenRec is capable of ranking the full content catalog. It can also work with a smaller set of content choices that are provided to it. You can use the top-K ranking, which means the highest-ranked K items. Here, K is the number of items you need.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The goal goes beyond predicting what the user will click or play next. Netflix wants to recommend content that can satisfy a user so that they keep coming back for more. This means that a user playing a movie is a great indicator that the user was interested in that recommendation. But it doesn’t guarantee that the recommendation was valuable.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c061ce8-d799-46d6-b1f8-a79eb7c59fb0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">AI’s Next Bottleneck Is Deployment. relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Netflix Wanted a New Approach</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix already has some very sophisticated recommendation models. Its production systems use thousands of features, representations, and specialized model components. You can think of a feature as an input signal that helps a model make some prediction. For example, we can tell a recommendation model how many comedy movies or shows a user has watched recently. Similarly, we can tell the model how long ago a user has seen a particular piece of content. Or how frequently the user finishes a series. All these features can help the model predict what the user might want to see.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To create a new feature, you need to decide which observations are important and how to calculate their value. Also, how to make them available for training and prediction. This is known as feature engineering. A mature system also needs a way to make sense of a sequence of actions that a user might perform. For example, if a user has watched several episodes of a series in order, it tells something different from a user starting several unrelated shows, but not watching them after some time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over time, these systems keep getting more complex. If you want to support a new content type or a new product surface, you need to add more features. You also need to change the model architecture and perform infrastructure work. Also, you need to run multiple experiments to make sure everything runs fine.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team wanted to see whether a broadly capable LLM can take on more of this interpretation work. Instead of engineering so many separate signals, the system can describe relevant behavior and content in plain text. The model can be trained to interpret it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why a Language Model Can Help</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An LLM has learned a lot of relationships between words, concepts, and descriptions during its training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This means that the LLM has a much better starting point to make sense of movies and shows and how people interact with them. For example, you can have two movies that belong to different categories but they share themes. An LLM can understand this connection based on their descriptions. It can also make sense of the history of actions that a user has done for movie.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix calls this process of expressing the information in text as verbalization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, a general-purpose LLM is not a good recommender. There are several problems. It may favor globally popular titles. It might suggest items that are not part of the catalog. Also, it doesn’t support personalization. This is why Netflix didn’t go for any off-the-shelf LLM. Instead, the engineering team built GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec mixes the language understanding of an LLM with special training that helps it work with the Netflix catalog. The LLM provides a foundation for interpreting the data. But Netflix still has to teach it what a good recommendation looks like and control which items it can recommend.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Two Training Phases of GenRec</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix trained GenRec in two phases with different purposes. Let’s look at both phases in detail.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table
