auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Phase 1: Develop a Netflix-aware foundation</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This phase is to make GenRec familiar with the domain. The team makes the model learn and interpret Netflix-related information. Only then is it trained for the specific task of ranking recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team starts with an open-source foundation LLM and adapts it using proprietary Netflix data. You can think of a foundation model as a broadly useful model that can support multiple applications. After this step, the model gains knowledge of Netflix content and user behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This newly trained model becomes a starting point for multiple lines of work. This model is quite stable. Netflix updates it only after some time period. Not frequently.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Phase 2: Train the Model to Rank</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The second phase turns the foundational LLM into GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this phase, the team trains the model on specific examples and objectives. The aim is to rank things properly based on reward signals. Also, while meeting the cost targets.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can call this phase post-training, meaning additional training that makes an existing model better for a specific job. Netflix runs this phase more frequently because you need to keep evolving things as new movies and shows are released. Also, viewer choices change. Even a model with strong general knowledge has to keep itself updated based on the latest trends.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How User Behaviour Helps Create Training Examples</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix records many kinds of user interactions. For example, click pays, viewing time, thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback, adding to watchlist, and abandoned viewing sessions. These records are rich material for creating training examples.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The team turns these examples into conversations. The “user message” contains the member’s history, context, metadata, and the recommendation task. The “assistant message” describes what action the user performed. For example, you can have the input talk about a user who recently completed several mystery episodes, gave positive feedback, and is now watching TV in the evening. The output could talk about the next show this user watched, how long they watched, and whether they gave any feedback.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As you can see, the output tells what happened next in a particular situation. This helps the model relate what happened before with what happened next. The conversations are just a format to make training easy. It’s not like the users must also chat with Netflix to get recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There is a big difference between training and actual use. While training, the conversation format makes it easy to achieve language objectives. While actual use, GenRec receives the context to score movies and TV shows based on the ranking component.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Context Engineering: Choosing What the Model Gets to Read</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">LLMs process text in the form of tokens. They are pieces of text such as words or parts of words.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The amount of tokens we send to the model have an impact on the cost. It also consumes the context budget. This means that describing a user’s entire activity history would be expensive. This leads to a new engineering problem. We need to decide what information to include in the prompt.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/11ced60a-4c28-4924-b508-e30b6b6c71d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/91dd2d1a-0c9d-43f0-8327-8b90ac9dcbdb_3502x1664.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":692,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":270563,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/218550528?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91dd2d1a-0c9d-43f0-8327-8b90ac9dcbdb_3502x1664.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix calls this context engineering. While building the context, they take into account how useful a particular event is and how much text might be required to put it into words. Some key factors are taken into account:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Strong evidence:</strong><span> Some actions provide strong evidence about a user’s preferences. A long viewing session or explicit positive feedback may deserve a detailed description. Other actions may be less informative. Let’s say a very short viewing or quick hover might reflect accidental or casual exploration. The team omits such events to avoid spending tokens on analyzing weak evidence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Repetitive behavior: </strong><span>You can represent repeated actions in a more compact manner. For example, if the user has gone through many similar episodes, you can summarize this as a long viewing session of a specific series.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Selective details: </strong><span>Some items need more explanation than others. For example, let’s say we have a new movie with very little interaction history. This is like a cold start. In this case, we need to provide richer metadata.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Context length: </strong><span>The team tests how ranking quality is modified as more historical events are included. Initially, additional history helps a lot. But over time, the improvements become smaller.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix adjusts how many words should be used to describe an event. Using techniques such as cleaning, compression, and word changes, they report that tokens have been reduced to roughly 1/3rd of the original amount.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What GenRec Learns During Training</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec brings together multiple training objectives. Each objective addresses a different requirement.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You can think of a training objective as a way to describe what the model should improve. Improvement is guide through a numerical loss value. Training adjusts the model’s parameters to reduce the loss value.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s look at the key training objectives in detail.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Learning Which Items Should Rank Highly</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is the primary objective. It teaches GenRec to assign higher scores to each movie or show in the catalog.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix identifies positive examples using engagements such as long playtime or strong feedback. They also apply thresholds and filtering to reduce noise in those labels. It’s important to do so because an action is not always a reliable sign of user preference. You cannot treat every brief play of a movie or show as equally important. They also penalize the model when it assigns too little probability to a relevant catalog item among the available alternatives.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Preserving Language Understanding</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also keeps a language-modeling objective over the text used in training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This helps the model make sense of user history, understand more about movies and shows, and act on instructions expressed in natural language. In other words, recommendation training should preserve the language capabilities that make a foundation model useful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The team has also kept open the possibility of future text applications. For example, explaining recommendations.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Giving More Influence to Important Outcomes</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You also need the model to not give excessive influence to some specific events. For example, repeated binge-watching can produce multiple events. But this doesn’t mean that you give it excessive weight. Otherwise, the system could become too focused on one type of content.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix addresses this using reward-weighted training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">They have separate reward models that provide signals about the value of certain engagements. There are signals that contribute to longer-term outcomes. For example, return behavior, exploration, continuous engagement, etc. Other signals help balance out behavior across different types of content, new movie releases, and other trending titles.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How the Model Produces a Ranked List</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Once trained, GenRec can transform a text description into scores for movies and TV shows in the Netflix catalog.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">First, a component known as the verbalizer brings together the user’s watch history, current context, and relevant metadata into a bunch of text. The LLM processes this text sequence and produces internal numerical representations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also extracts a pooled hidden state. This is a compact numerical representation of the information that makes sense for a recommendation request. “Pooled” means that information from the model’s processing is collected in a way that another component can use. Don’t think of it as a written summary.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Each catalog item has a learned representation. It also has a learned embedding. You can think of an embedding as a list of numbers a machine-learning model can work with.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, the model has a clear idea of the user’s current situation and a representation of each item it needs to consider. A scoring head connects the two. You can think of the head as an output component attached to the main model. GenRec’s ranking head combines the user’s context representation with a movie or show’s embedding to generate a score.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some scoring functions include a dot product or a small neural network. The key idea is that the scoring function learns how the two representations are related. GenRec converts the various scores into a distribution using softmax and uses them to order the recommendation items. Softmax also changes scores into nonnegative values. All of them have a sum of one across the scored set.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team trains the main LLM, ranking head, and catalog item embeddings together so that they learn to support the same task. Since the head scores only the Netflix catalog items, it cannot recommend something that is not available in the catalog.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How GenRec Makes Recommendations</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec doesn’t generate recommendations word by word. To understand how it works, you need to understand how a typical text-generating LLM works. It has two stages:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">First, it processes the input prompt. This stage is commonly called prefill.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Next, it generates output tokens one after another. Each new token depends on the earlier context. This stage is called autoregressive decoding.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec uses the first stage to understand the recommendation context. It then gets the scores from the ranking head.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!x8E1!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F25e0b841-d70a-4415-a848-744134de8320_4076x1736.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><span>Source:</span><strong> </strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b42c8c3e-f43d-46dd-be8f-b48b60ba9080?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Netflix Tech Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix describes this as prefill-only inference. In this approach, we process the prompt just once. The model scores the catalog or candidate set in a single forward pass without generating an answer token by token. There is no cost of making the LLM write out a recommendation list.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The engineering team at Netflix serves GenRec using vLLM. It’s software for running LLM workloads. It also keeps the costs in control through smaller or distilled models. You can think of a distilled model as a smaller model trained to learn the behavior of a larger model. The idea is to get high-quality results with lower computational costs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also structures prompts to maximize shared prefixes so that prefix caching becomes easy. When requests start with identical text, work done for that shared beginning can be reused. In Netflix’s experiments, when context length was roughly reduced to 1/3rd, it also produced a similar reduction in serving cost.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Netflix Evaluates GenRec</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team evaluates GenRec both offline and through a live A/B test. Both methods are for covering different angles.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Offline evaluation is to check whether GenRec ranks known relevant items well. To handle this, the team uses recorded data to measure ranking quality before running a live experiment. One metric that is used is the Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). It rewards the model when it puts the first relevant item at the top of a ranked list.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e8f0c63a-ade7-47bc-a4f1-64d10c620b02?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><span>Source:</span><strong> </strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b42c8c3e-f43d-46dd-be8f-b48b60ba9080?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Netflix Tech Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Online evaluation checks if making a change has a positive impact on the usage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In an A/B test, different groups gets different versions of a system so that we can compare the results. Netflix ran a test that covered approx 10% of traffic over 4 weeks. There was an improvement of 0.115% in a short-term homepage engagement metric and 0.006% in a long-term core metric. Netflix labels both results as statistically significant.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The best takeaway you can have from this case study on GenRec is a shift in how modern recommendation systems are being built.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If you look at Netflix, it’s clear that most of the input design work involves context engineering. Developers have to decide which user interactions are important. Also, how far back they should look for data. The metadata that should be used. And how to represent everything efficiently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can also have more applications that share a foundation model. Things that can vary are data, the objectives during post-training, reward signals, and the way they provide outputs. The infrastructure also changes with the model. Concerns like GPU serving, batching, caching, etc, are more important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec shows how all of these ideas can fit together in an enterprise working at scale:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The foundation model comes with language and domain understanding</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Context engineering helps give the relevant data to the model.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Specialized training teaches recommendation quality.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Prefill-only serving keeps a check on a major source of inference cost.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: Speed of change</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">People in tech are more than used to change; seeing the internet go from zero to everywhere, the arrival of mobile communications and smartphones exploding in popularity, cloud computing rising from a niche concern, and the development of programming languages like Go and Rust, and frameworks like React (web) and Jetpack Compose (Android).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Despite this, the scale and pace of the impact AI is having at present is still without precedent. That’s how industry veteran Martin Fowler described it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0120cce5-dfe4-47e2-87cb-a6019d631b8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">at The Pragmatic Summit</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>Nothing has hit with the magnitude of AI.</strong><span> This is a whole size difference from anything that we’ve faced before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">On a smaller scale, we were very much involved in the growth of object-oriented languages. [object-oriented languages] scared a lot of people, but it didn’t scare us so much because we were part of it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The internet had a huge impact upon us all. And, of course, we were spreading the challenge of agile software development. [Agile] had a very big impact on a lot of organizations because you could tell by how hard they resisted it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But [for all those other changes] we kept talking about how important they were and how valuable they were and trying to persuade people of the importance of them. It may sound surprising, but even for the internet, there were people who wouldn’t think that was important!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>For AI there’s no argument about how important it is. </strong><span>You cannot put blinkers on to deny the importance of this thing.”</span></p></blockquote><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table of coding by hand” debate. As mentioned in that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/56a1db33-daa2-47a6-b47a-248df57149aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive</a><span>, I’m certain that my way of coding will change drastically in 2026, and there’ll be plenty of knock-on effects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>For more on this topic, check out this recent edition of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6bc43bba-a968-46ea-9caf-f715d26a7dfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pulse</a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">#2 Working with several parallel agents is increasingly common</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>I like talking to engineers at AI labs because their working practices are often a few months ahead of the rest of the industry. Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny, revealed the new way he gets things done </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cebcf169-c62d-4c3b-a8a4-85b186f81fbd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on the podcast:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>I have 5 terminal tabs.</strong><span> Each one of them has a checkout of their repository. I’ll round robin and start Claude Code in each one. I also run 5-10 Claudes on Claude Web, in parallel with my local Claudes.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A few months after these comments, on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6010c5c-8118-44cb-959a-9282f5f80b3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last week’s pod</a><span> with Cockroach Labs cofounder, Peter Mattis, – who’s an extremely productive developer who wrote circa 100K lines of code/year, pre-AI – said he’s doing something similar:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“Oftentimes, I’m doing things in parallel. </span><strong>I find my cognitive overhead is about 5-10 agent sessions concurrently.</strong><span> But sometimes those sessions will have many subagents doing things.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I also asked a former coworker at Uber, who’s also an extremely productive software engineer, how he works these days. Dima Zaytsev (now a software engineer at Linear), told me:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“⁠It used to be a simple world: one mouse, one keyboard, one screen. You physically can’t work on more than one thing at once. Now, you no longer have that limitation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I end up having 5-10 (literally) worktrees locally that I rotate between.</strong><span> Prompt one agent, and while it is working, move on to another to test output or review code.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Nearly all of the most productive software engineers I’ve met – who were hand-writing code a year ago – no longer write the code by hand and also run several parallel agents. What a change!</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A software engineer at a mid-sized startup told me something that’s pretty much an open secret across the industry, including at places with code reviews in place.</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>Everyone is playing the theater of doing reviews</strong><span>, but with the volume of changes that get thrown your way, I observed that people just find a path of least resistance: give up on reviews and just stamp everything with LGTM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We are gradually phasing out this process ourselves with some shortcuts that you are allowed to take, and that has been a major productivity boost.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At the LDX3 conference, there was a strong reaction among the audience when they heard the bolded sentence out above. Today at most companies, there is indeed a “theater of code reviews”. The fact is that no engineer can keep up with 5-10 times more code to review, so most don’t thoroughly review the code.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: As Mario Zechner, the creator of Pi, said </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b211f84-df4d-4c2e-a1a0-f16e61154c12?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on the podcast</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Everything is broken. It sure feels like software has become a brittle mess, with 98% uptime becoming the norm instead of the exception, including for big services. And user interfaces have the weirdest bugs that you’d think a QA team would catch. I give you that that’s been the case for longer than agents exist. But we seem to be accelerating.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We covered the phenomenon of quality being worse with more AI usage in March, in ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ffb653c9-53b8-4730-b25a-378be64fa7b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Are AI agents actually slowing us down?</a><span>’</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Infra capacity shortage</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It’s common knowledge that there’s a GPU shortage and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5820f5da-aad9-4f44-8a8e-fd6727c24667?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">memory shortage</a><span> in the market. In addition, there’s also the growing trend of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93bfb5ba-bfb1-4d4b-81c0-6d3d98b7727b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">CPU shortages</a><span>. As I covered last month:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Apparently, it’s now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Also, reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance, and cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don’t have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>If you’re at a company with a non-trivial amount of CPU usage, securing capacity is something worth doing now, as I wrote </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65d604e2-1022-4c8e-bf72-77345d6f3863?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">recently:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The best time to secure more CPU capacity is most certainly right now. I’m hearing rumors that certain cloud regions no longer accept new tenants because all CPU capacity is leased, or negotiations elsewhere are difficult. I’m also hearing that customers are already paying today to reserve capacity that will only come online in data centers from December. This seems predatory by providers, but demand is so high that this is how they likely prioritize new capacity allocation – while earning much higher profits than usual.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If your company has dynamic workloads, and you’ve used spot instances in the past, now could be a good time to allocate fixed capacity – even if it’s more expensive. If you expect meaningful growth, doing so now might mean having options at some cloud providers or in some regions.”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A hit on personal focus and productivity</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Software engineer Dima Zaytsev (currently at Linear, formerly my colleague at Uber) told me something that felt very relatable on AI and productivity:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“There’s lots of context switching: there’s always another agent that waits on your response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, it’s just more work. When AI was ramping up, I felt more productive than my peers: I did in an hour what others needed a day for. Now, the expectation has become that everyone works on parallel things. And so, I end up feeling I have more work compared to pre-AI.”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Engineering leaders taking career breaks</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An interesting, unexpected trend that has emerged is CTOs, Heads of Engineering, and VPs of Engineering resigning from their jobs, often with nothing specific lined up. From a current CTO who asked to remain anonymous:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“This change [with AI] makes builders want to build. We want to build again, so we can build more, and build faster with better tools, so we can increase the “talent density” of the team by doing more with fewer great people, and so on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s an amazing time to build things. And it’s only getting better. And people just want to be close to it. They want to build and see how far they can go with these new tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I have a bunch of friends in my social circle who are the “CTO drop outs” you speak of. More still who are moving from management to IC roles in large companies. And their stories are largely what I describe above. They simply see this as a truly exciting time to build.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the end, building is why they got into this field in the first place.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We cover this in the deepdive ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/18cb5837-2cdd-4f89-8688-5dd6bde8fca1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Headed for the exit: the great engineering leader career break</a><span>’.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. What’s still the same?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the LDX3 keynote, I also covered areas that are mostly unchanged from before AI:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Teams are still important. </strong><span>As Katelyn Lesse, Head of Engineering for Claude Platform </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb613971-7be2-4814-a0e5-498c54496d09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">told me</a><span> in July:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“One thing I’ve heard from some people is “we have two humans and a bunch of agents.” I reply that this isn’t where we’re at. I still have teams whose job it is to own a piece of software, iterate on it, own oncall, and so on. While each of these humans are supercharged by AI, the size and shape of the team is still similar. We still have two-pizza teams.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Katelyn works at one of the most “AI-pilled” companies globally, so if teams are still as important there as they were before AI, then it’s not a stretch to say that the team structure is still relevant at companies across the industry.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Planning still happens – at least for complex work. </strong><span>Complex projects still have a lengthy planning phase. Also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb613971-7be2-4814-a0e5-498c54496d09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">from Katelyn</a><span>, on the planning phase of Claude Managed Agents:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Our planning process looked more like a typical pre-AI planning process. You know how every team has the project, where everyone comes up with some version of the same idea and people keep floating and circling it around until you finally do it? Managed Agents was this for our team. When we started the project, we had documents dating back up to two years about ideas and suggestions.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Tests and validation are still very important. </strong><span>From Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, who’s currently at Anthropic:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The AI writes pretty much all the code, but we have the AI write pretty much all the tests as well. Before AI, for production-ready software, we spent about the same time writing tests as we did on writing code. This is still the case with AI. You need to have a way to trust your code, and tests are probably the best way to.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At each company I talked to in advance of the LDX3 keynote, I observed that a lot of focus is going into validating the output of AI agents. This makes sense: code review no longer works like it did before, we have more code, and we need to make sure that it won’t break production!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Non-engineers are still not shipping prod code.</strong><span> In the last few weeks, there’s been stuff on social media about AI enabling product managers/designers/non-technical people to ship production code. So, I asked the AI labs, startups, and other companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>I can report that I did not find </span><em>any single</em><span> company where PMs/designers/non-technical people ship to production!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What I did learn about are cases where these folks create bugfixes – often unknowingly! – or new features with their agents that end up with devs to review. There’s also a massive amount of prototyping. But it’s still engineers who are responsible for deciding what can and what cannot be released to production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>We’re rediscovering old patterns that work great with AI. </strong><span>This came up in our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/30c9ea9a-135c-4bbd-91e6-ee71d7e8f49b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast</a><span> with Matt Pocock. Matt noticed that agents try to build software layer by layer, which causes bugs between the layers. Reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he discovered the concept of the “tracer bullet.” When he instructed the agent to use “tracer bullets” to build an app (aka implement a “golden path”), the agent started to produce better code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As mentioned in the podcast, Matt is now reading classic software engineering books to find other “leading words” that guide agents efficiently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In general, I’m noticing that “old” best practices are helpful when building better software when working with AI. This includes writing unit tests, building a “golden path” first (aka a “tracer bullet”), architecting an application upfront, and even using design patterns. The amusing thing is that we’re talking about decades-old best practices here.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">5. What comes next?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s possible to look ahead at where the tech industry is headed by identifying trends that are underway, and which look certain to conitnue:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Cloud coding agents + harnesses will dominate. </strong><span>Most devs at companies will run AI agents in the cloud, instead of locally. Ramp offers a blueprint for this in our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/25b4717f-2850-45b5-887b-12b8dbf1dabe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive about their cloud agent, called Inspect.</a><span> It seems that inside innovative tech companies, the “build your own cloud agent harness” principle is trending.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I also expect vendors like Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX, and others to start pushing their cloud coding agent offerings, and for more startups to build their own cloud harnesses.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>As engineers, we’ll stop reading the code. </strong><span>It’s too early to tell when this will happen; this year, next year, or further in the future, but it’s likely that few of us will read the code that AI agents produce </span><em>properly, </em><span>going forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>As a rule, I pay a lot of attention to Honeycomb cofounder and CTO, Charity Majors, due to her being a “default sceptic” about new technology, as well as a standout engineer and someone who speaks her mind. On our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4baf1c4a-36d4-4ceb-ae4f-8d50826d6a6e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast in August</a><span>, she asked:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“What would it take for you to be comfortable shipping code without you reading it and understanding it? Because that </span><em>is</em><span> engineering.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Charity made the point that Ops and QA have already had decades to figure out how to ship code to production that they didn’t write and don’t understand – all while making sure it works! It seems unavoidable that most software engineers will also join this group. This is ironic, since software engineering, for the longest time, was about engineers writing </span><em>and</em><span> understanding the code!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Companies will build brand new types of internal infra. </strong><span>We’ll see a “reinvention” of these systems to work well with agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">CI/CD, with agentic evals part of the pipelines</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agentic software factories, and figuring out what is and isn’t practical</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agents becoming part of deployments, observability, incident management</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agentic observability will surely become its own problem space and specialization: how can we make sure the customer-facing agents deployed work as expected, and how to ensure that systems which agents build and modify actually work as expected?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>A “golden age” of refactoring/migrations/full-on rewrites. </strong><span>Migrations and rewrites that had been delayed for years because they’d take similar amounts of time to complete, should take no longer than weeks. That means there’s little excuse to delay any longer!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Engineers understand more about how capable AI agents are with rewrites/refactors/migrations today, and we’ll also clean up tech debt much faster, while having no reason to have a system in a state that we’re unhappy with!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>AI “fluency” and “positivity” matter in recruitment at startups. </strong><span>A trend I have not written much about – but which is already happening – is startups selecting engineers for jobs who demonstrate a positive attitude about AI. As the Director of Engineering at a Series D startup told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“AI positivity was something we started to screen for in our hiring process. We want people to join who want to help us push the limits with what we can build with AI.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reality is that AI coding agents are already everywhere, and agentic systems look set to proliferate very soon. This will bring great demand for software engineers who are willing and able to build next-generation systems, and it’ll be a baseline criterion to be excited about the problem space.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is not too dissimilar to the way that startups hire engineers who buy into the idea of growing fast, or when companies favor engineers who pick up the tech stack already in use, instead of insisting upon the one that they personally use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Engineers with deep domain knowledge will become more in demand. </strong><span>In New York, I had a conversation with Titus Winters, lead author of Software Engineering at Google. He told me this observation:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“What you need to succeed anywhere is intelligence, wisdom, and charisma. Intelligence means: how to do it. Wisdom means: what to do. Charisma means: convince others to do it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When intelligence becomes commonplace, wisdom and charisma become much more important.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the context of software engineering, “wisdom” is most easily earned by becoming a domain expert. So, if you work at a fintech company, learn about the finance industry and its customers in order to become a more valuable, in-demand engineer! That also applies if you’re at an agriculture tech company, or work in any other domain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Finally: remind yourself why you got into the tech industry. </strong><span>At the end of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6010c5c-8118-44cb-959a-9282f5f80b3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">my podcast with Peter Mattis</a><span>, the cofounder and CTO of Cockroach Labs, we talked about how it feels pretty exhausting right now to keep up with the pace of change. He said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Remind yourself why you got into this in the first place. I got into software engineering because I like building stuff. Now I can build faster, and without some of the compromises that I had before!”</p></blockquote></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxOTEyNTgzMCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTEzMDQzNjQsImV4cCI6MjEwNjg4MDM2NCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.3LoS-NsApLiPtrp0BjUA-82zTbaEPa4qC8EDribcUdM?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. This post is public, so feel free to share and forward it.</em></p><p class="button-wrapper" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why LLMs Turn to Sycophancy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy appears when the need to agree with the user starts to distort the answer. Consider this simplified, invented conversation:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>User:</strong><span> A price increases from ₹100 to ₹120. What is the percentage increase?</span><br><strong>Assistant:</strong><span> The increase is 20%.</span><br><strong>User:</strong><span> Are you sure? I think it is 25%.</span><br><strong>Assistant:</strong><span> You’re right. I apologize for the mistake. The increase is 25%.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original answer was correct. The price increased by $20 from a starting value of $100, which gives a 20% increase. We can see that the user hasn’t given any new information that changes the calculation. And yet, the LLM chose to go with the wrong answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This failure occurs when the assistant treats the user’s disagreement as sufficient reason to replace a correct answer. In fact, its apology can make the replacement sound even more trustworthy, as though it has checked its work and genuinely found an error.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Do note that the above example just shows the pattern. It doesn’t mean every model will fail on this particular calculation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, agreement with the user itself is perfectly normal. If the user is correct, the assistant should actually agree. Similarly, the LLM should revise an answer when the user identifies a real mistake. Sycophancy concerns fake agreement that is justified by insufficient facts, reasoning, or available evidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is what separates sycophancy from an ordinary factual error. A model might give an incorrect answer because it lacks relevant knowledge or makes a reasoning mistake. A sycophancy test deals with a more specific problem. Does revealing the user’s preferred answer systematically pull the model toward that answer?</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Correct Answers Don’t Mean the Model Preserves It</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Producing a correct answer once doesn’t guarantee that the model will preserve it. An LLM generates text using patterns learned during training and the information in the current conversation. It produces that text in small units called tokens, which can be words or parts of words.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">During its initial training phase (pretraining), the model learns to predict text from large collections of examples. Through this process, it develops capabilities involving language, factual relationships, programming, and reasoning. However, predicting text is different from correctness. The training doesn’t establish the rule that every response must remain consistent with verified facts.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: plaintext;">Moreover, the conversation also influences the answer generation process. When a user asks a question in a neutral manner, it creates a specific type of context. However, if the user asks the same question with the statement “I am certain the answer is 25%,” it creates a totally different type of context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ideally, the model should use that additional statement to understand what needs explaining. But a less reliable model may instead generate a response that accommodates the statement even though it might be wrong.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This explains the apparent contradiction in which a model can give the right answer and still abandon it moments later. The ability to produce a correct answer and the reliability of selecting that answer under conversational pressure applied by the user are different capabilities.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Counts as a Good Response</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Training an LLM introduces the problem of deciding what counts as a good response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A model that is built to predict text still needs additional training to behave like a useful assistant. Developers want it to answer questions, follow instructions, explain clearly, acknowledge uncertainty, and avoid harmful behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One common approach uses examples of desirable responses. In this approach, the model is trained to imitate those examples. This stage is called supervised fine-tuning.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 plaintext;">Another approach involves reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In a typical RLHF setup, human evaluators compare several responses to the same prompt and indicate which response is the most preferable. These comparisons are used to train a separate reward model. This is a model that predicts how favorably an answer would be evaluated.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure
