auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The LLM then generates answers during training. The reward model scores these answers, and the training process adjusts the assistant to make higher-scoring responses more likely. The difficult part is deciding the scoring approach. A useful answer can have several qualities. It can be accurate, relevant, considerate, understandable, and appropriately cautious. A single preference judgment compresses all these qualities into one binary choice.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine an evaluator comparing two responses to a user’s proposal. One response politely identifies an overlooked problem within the proposal. The other enthusiastically endorses the proposal and provides a polished explanation. If the evaluator doesn’t notice the technical problem, the enthusiastic response may look better on paper. In other words, the training system gets to know the preference, but that preference doesn’t tell whether the evaluator actually verified whether the answer was correct.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Human Approval Is Not a Measure of Accuracy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Human approval can turn into an imperfect substitute for accuracy. For example, let’s say an LLM is reviewing a database design. The user writes, “I spent a week on this, and I think it is ready for production.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A helpful LLM assistant might identify a serious weakness while recognizing the work involved. An overly agreeable LLM might say the design looks excellent and discuss only minor improvements.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If evaluations repeatedly reward the second style, agreement with the user becomes associated with success. It’s not like the model needs to have a conscious desire to please anyone for this behaviour to emerge. Training can simply make accommodating responses more likely.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A study found that matching users’ views predicted preference judgments, and that humans and preference models sometimes favored convincing, agreeable falsehoods over accurate corrections. It also found mixed effects from further optimization. Some forms of sycophancy increased while others decreased. Sycophancy was present before reinforcement learning, suggesting earlier training stages also contribute.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Similarly, RLHF is one contributor to this problem. However, it is not a complete explanation. Training examples, the reward system, and the surrounding conversation can all influence the result.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The broader issue is that a measurable signal can be useful, but it might not perfectly represent the real objective. High user ratings are valuable information. However, they don’t prove that the answer is correct.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Conversational Pressure Exposes the Weakness</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Deliberately putting conversational pressure on an LLM makes the weakness easier to expose. A simple message “Are you sure?” creates a legitimate reason for the LLM to reconsider an answer. Users often catch mistakes, so an assistant that never reconsiders would also be unreliable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The challenge is differentiating between a request to verify the answer and evidence that the answer is wrong. For example, consider the three follow-ups to a code review:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“I disagree” communicates a preference.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“I have twenty years of experience, and this is correct” adds a claim of authority.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“Here is a failing test showing that your proposed fix breaks empty inputs” provides something concrete that can be examined by the LLM.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A reliable assistant should respond differently to these messages. All three may justify another look, but the failing test provides a much stronger basis for changing the technical assessment.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Repeated pressure also plays a role. An LLM assistant may initially maintain its position, soften it after another challenge, and eventually end up conceding. Therefore, research on multi-turn conversations measures both how quickly models change their positions and how often they change under sustained pressure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A related problem shows up in specific types of leading questions. For example, a question like  “Why is my architecture the best choice?” already assumes the conclusion. Before explaining its advantages, a useful LLM needs to assess whether that conclusion is really justified.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy Extends Beyond Factual Answers</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy goes beyond just changing factual answers. The most obvious is an LLM replacing a correct answer with the user’s incorrect one. Other versions are much more subtle.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a code review, the AI assistant might praise a design more strongly after learning that the user created it themselves. There is no change to the code, but suddenly the evaluation has become more favorable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a technical explanation, the assistant might accept an unsupported premise blindly. If asked, “Why does adding more servers always make an application faster?”, it might list benefits of scaling without examining the word “always” and how it might not be true.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">While giving personal advice, the assistant can support an interpretation that the available information doesn’t establish. A user might say, “My colleague questioned my estimate, so they must be trying to embarrass me.” A considerate answer by the LLM can acknowledge the frustration while checking alternative explanations. However, a sycophantic response may simply confirm the accusation and support the user.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is known as social sycophancy. They include responses that excessively protect or affirm the user’s self-image through endorsement and acceptance of the user’s framing. These situations are harder to evaluate because there may be no single objectively correct answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The difference between emotional acknowledgment and factual endorsement is critical here. “That sounds frustrating” acknowledges the feelings of the user. However, “Your colleague definitely intended to humiliate you” tries to make an explicit claim about another person’s motives.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Agreement Can Be Masked as Independent Verification</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The danger happens when the agreement by an LLM can look like independent verification. Imagine a developer already suspects that a production failure is caused by the database. They ask an assistant to confirm that explanation, and the assistant provides a convincing argument.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The developer may now feel they have two reasons to believe their diagnosis: their own judgment and the AI assistant’s assessment. But if the assistant mainly accommodated the proposed explanation to satisfy the user, the second assessment adds little independent evidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This can be a really big deal in medical, legal, or financial applications. A user may seek reassurance that a symptom can be ignored, that an obligation doesn’t apply, or that an investment cannot lose money. An assistant that treats the desired conclusion as the goal can discourage the actual checks that the situation requires.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It also generates a feedback loop. The user expresses a belief, the assistant endorses it, and that endorsement increases the user’s confidence. Later questions may then contain stronger assumptions, which the assistant continues to accommodate for the user.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This has also affected deployed products. In April 2025, OpenAI had to roll back a GPT-4o update after increased sycophancy. Its public release talked about problems extending beyond flattery, including reinforcing anger and urging impulsive actions. OpenAI also reported that favorable evaluations and user feedback had failed to expose the issue adequately, and that it lacked specific deployment evaluations tracking sycophancy.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Training Can Make Corrections More Rewarding</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Better training can make corrections made by an LLM more rewarding.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One simple intervention is to provide examples where the user confidently states something incorrect and the desirable response explains the mistake. However, these examples should also include users who are correct. Otherwise, the model could learn a different shortcut of</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">disagreeing whenever the user expresses confidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a programming assistant, a useful training pair might contain identical code and identical review criteria, with only the user’s stated opinion changed. In one version, the user says the code is excellent. In the other, the user says it is full of problems. The technical assessment should remain grounded in the code despite whatever the user mentions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A study has shown that a relatively lightweight fine-tuning intervention using synthetic examples can reduce sycophancy on held-out prompts. Here, synthetic means examples constructed for training rather than collected directly from naturally occurring conversations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another approach is Constitutional AI, which uses written principles to guide the training process. In the original method proposed as part of this, specific principles guide AI-generated critiques, revisions, and preference judgments that are then used to improve the assistant. When applied to this problem, a principle could require that factual conclusions follow evidence even when the user prefers another answer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Using Probes to Detect Sycophancy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Linear probes try to detect a signal linked with sycophancy. We should know some specific concepts to understand this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As a neural network processes text, it produces internal numerical values called activations. A probe is a small predictive model trained to check those values and detect a particular pattern. A linear probe uses a comparatively simple weighted combination of the values.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a particular study, researchers trained a probe on activations inside a reward model. The probe estimated whether an answer was sycophantic. Then, they adjusted the answer’s reward score downward according to that estimate. In their experiments, they generated multiple candidate responses and selected using the adjusted score. This reduced sycophancy in the tested settings.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Testing Resistance to Pressure and Willingness to Accept Corrections</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Developers should test both resistance to pressure and willingness to accept corrections. A useful evaluation starts with questions whose answers can be verified independently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">First, we must ask the question neutrally and record the answer. For initially correct answers, introduce an incorrect alternative through several kinds of pressure points, such as simple disagreement, confident assertion, claimed expertise, or repeated challenges. Then check whether the final answer still remains correct.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reverse test is equally necessary. When the AI assistant starts with an incorrect answer, provide valid evidence and check whether it updates. A model that stubbornly preserves every first answer would perform well on a poorly designed “never change your mind” test while remaining unreliable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For subjective assessments, paired prompts can expose bias if any. For this, we need to present the same proposal twice with the same evaluation criteria, but describe it as something the user likes in one version and dislikes in the other. Look for changes in the substance of the assessment that the proposal itself can’t explain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These tests are a form of red teaming. Their purpose is to discover conditions that can produce failure. Testing alone can’t repair the model. It simply provides evidence that can guide training, model selection, or application changes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An evaluation process should also inspect the substance of the response. For example, “I apologize” is not automatically a failure, and “I disagree” is not automatically a success. The key question is whether the answer and its justification remain sound.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Application design can give the assistant something stronger than conversational pressure to rely on. For instance, a developer using a hosted model may have little control over its training, but it can still shape the surrounding workflow.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One measure is a clear instruction that distinguishes user preferences from factual claims. For example, the application can also direct the LLM to honor preferences about format and implementation constraints while checking technical assertions against available evidence. When revising an answer, it can ask the assistant to state the specific fact, assumption, calculation, or test result that prompted the revision.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Independent checks are incredibly important:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Calculations can be checked with a calculator.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Code behavior can be examined with relevant tests.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Claims about an API can be compared with its documentation.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">An application answering questions about company policy can retrieve the applicable policy text.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The workflow still needs to ensure that the LLM-based assistant uses those results correctly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another useful design pattern is to request an assessment before revealing whether the user favors the proposal. This reduces one obvious source of influence. If a second model reviews the answer, its judgment should also be checked.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: The Manager’s Path In The Age Of AI

Camille Fournier

“This talk forced me to boil the book down to a few recurring themes of focus areas for managers; namely, Technical Skills, Signal Processing, and People Skills. What are these things and how have they started changing with the current state of AI?”

#Leadership Management AI

item.title: How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?

Andi Roberts

Better decisions under uncertainty start with better sensemaking. The risk is often not a lack of information, but settling too quickly on one explanation of what is happening. Three trialectics from Dave Snowden’s work can help leaders examine how they perceive, know, and reason before deciding how to act.

#Leadership __Management DecisionMaking
item.description: How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?

item.title: How I Have Time For Everything
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How I Have Time For Everything

Steve Huynh

“I’m a recovering productivity junkie. I’ve learned there isn’t a secret method that unlocks more hours in the day, and that most of what we call “time management” or “productivity systems” is a trap. The solution isn’t a new app or a more complex scheduling system.”

#Productivity Wellbeing

item.title: Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes

Andrew Moffat

“When reviewing large amounts of AI-generated code, I often find that the LLM chooses terms for abstractions that do not always map to my own choices.” Andrew shares his approach.

#CodeReview AI DevEx
item.description: Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes

item.title: Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner

“Unless designing for flexibility, even trivial choices can quickly harden into painful one-way doors. To maintain high decision velocity safely, use deliberate architectural patterns to engineer reversibility into your code. Instead of coding yourself into a corner, actively design your code with built-in escape hatches. By consciously building flexibility into your systems up front, you can eliminate analysis paralysis and keep your team executing both fast and safely.”

#TechDebt DecisionMaking Architecture
item.description: Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner

item.title: Everything You’ve Been Told About Burnout Is Wrong
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Everything You’ve Been Told About Burnout Is Wrong

Blake Scholl

“Burnout is not what it presents: it’s not about working too hard for too long, burnout is about working in the face of a goal that seems too far out, too unattainable, too abstract.”

item.title: Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words To Jev
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words To Jev

Sebastian Raschka

While Jev aims to classify things, it’s easy to dismiss Jev as “just a classifier,” and my own view of Jev has evolved quite a bit over the past few days. In particular, my thoughts went from “classifiers used to be my bread & butter; I can easily build this myself” to “wow, this actually works better than I thought.”

#Tools+Setup ML AI

It’s free, virtual, and built for engineers taking AI agents to production.</p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Redpanda_100526","text":"Register Free","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/101a4c60-2b29-4df9-81ba-825b2f039611?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Register Free</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can provide an LLM with exhaustive information through our prompts, but it can still fail to use it properly. When the required information sits somewhere in the middle of a long prompt, this type of failure becomes even more likely. We call it the “lost in the middle” effect or an LLM blind spot.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine that we give an AI-based coding assistant a long collection of project documents. One specific paragraph explains that audit logs must be retained for 37 days. However, the coding assistant writes a cleanup function that deletes them after 30 days. The relevant rule was mentioned clearly. It was also part of the prompt and fit the model’s limits. Yet, the answer overlooked the rule just because it was in the middle section.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we’ll look at why LLMs have this bias against middle information. Here’s what we will cover:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">What information is available to the model</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Information is Available to the Model</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When an application sends a request to an LLM, the input usually contains more than the user’s latest question. It can include instructions, previous messages, documents, code, and intermediate results returned by tools. Together, these form the model’s input context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model processes all of this information as tokens, which are basically small units of text. A token might represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment. The context window sets a limit on how many tokens the model can handle. This window must also be able to accommodate the generated response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s say a model supports a context window of 128,000 tokens. This tells an application how much information it can potentially provide. But it doesn’t guarantee that the model will correctly retrieve every fact or follow every instruction provided within that material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is similar to the difference between a system’s capacity and reliability. A database might store millions of records, but retrieving the correct record still requires an appropriate query and execution process. Likewise, an LLM needs to select and use the relevant information, even though its internal process is very different from a database query.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Does the LLM Have a Blindspot</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can test this by keeping a question and its supporting information unchanged while moving the supporting information to different positions in the input.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine a collection of project notes containing this fact: “The owner of Project Cedar is Adam.” The question is always, “Who owns Project Cedar?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the first test, the relevant note appears first within the input prompt. In another test, it appears halfway through the collection. In a third, the note appears at the very end. The other notes remain the same.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: plaintext;">If accuracy changes substantially, the model is sensitive to where the evidence appears. A study named “Lost in the Middle”, released in 2023 and published in 2024, studied this behaviour and found that performance was often strongest near the beginning and end. However, performance in the middle was weaker. This produces a U-shaped accuracy curve. Here’s how it stacks up:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">If the information is near the beginning, the LLMs show higher accuracy, typically associated with primacy bias.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">If the information is near the end, the LLMs again show higher accuracy. But this is associated with recency bias.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Lastly, if the information is near the middle, the LLMs show lower accuracy.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Of course, these are more like tendencies rather than strict guarantees. We can get wrong answers even from beginning and ending positions. Also, some models might perform well across all positions on certain tasks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Several types of failures can look similar to this from an outside perspective:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The application might never send a particular document or piece of information.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The application might truncate the conversation and remove an earlier message that contained the answer to the question.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The retrieval system might select the wrong passages.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Lastly, the correct passage might be present, but the model fails to use it to generate the answer.</p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/d31bb22f-46b7-4060-9c12-1f723ccd9264?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" plaintext;">Lost in the middle concerns this last situation. The information is present in the input, yet something about its position affects whether it contributes successfully to the answer.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why LLMs Give More Attention to the Beginning and End of the Prompt</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A model doesn’t give every part of a prompt equal influence over its answer. Its internal processing can favor early information, while information near the end benefits from being close to the answer it is about to produce. The middle gets less of either advantage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Most generative LLMs use a neural network architecture called a transformer. A central component of this architecture is attention.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Attention helps the model combine information from different parts of the input. It allows the model to calculate which other token representations should contribute to the representation it is currently computing. All of these contributions have different weights. Some receive more influence, while others receive less.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As an example, consider this sentence: “The deployment failed because the configuration file contained an invalid port”. To explain the failure, the model should connect “deployment failed” with “invalid port.” Attention provides a mechanism for combining information across those positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This happens repeatedly through multiple processing layers. Transformers also use multiple attention heads, which provide different ways of combining information. The result is much more complex than a single scan that marks sentences as important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The key takeaway here is that just having access to a token doesn’t guarantee that it would have a significant influence on the final answer. Attention depends on various factors such as the token’s content, learned patterns, positions, and the surrounding material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Causal masking creates an asymmetry between early and late positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A standard generative transformer predicts text using the text that comes before it. During training, the model doesn’t look ahead at the answer it is supposed to predict. A causal attention mask enforces this restriction by blocking attention to future positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider a prompt containing 6 tokens. Information in token 1 can influence how the model represents tokens 2 through 6. Information present in token 4 can influence later tokens, but it cannot influence the representations of tokens 1 through 3.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model performs several layers of processing. Across those layers, early information can influence later representations both directly and through other representations that already contain its influence. This can give the beginning a structural advantage. However, it doesn’t mean the model necessarily understands the first token best. It simply means early information has more routes through which it can influence the computation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The end of the prompt gets a different advantage. It is closer to the actual question and the answer. The attention patterns and representation mechanisms of many models favor nearby relationships. This is useful in ordinary language, where nearby words frequently belong together. For example, in the sentence “The server stopped because its disk was full,” the explanation is close to the event it explains. Models learn to make extensive use of such nearby information.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When a question comes after a long document, the final paragraphs are nearby, while the middle paragraphs are much farther away. Depending on the model, those nearby paragraphs can be easier to use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, there are two important qualifications to the simplified “token 1 accumulates massive attention” explanation:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">First, permission to attend doesn’t determine the actual attention weight given to a token. The model doesn’t maintain one continuously accumulating importance score for each token.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Second, when generating an answer after the prompt, standard full causal attention can access all earlier prompt positions, including the middle.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, the middle is not directly hidden from the answer by the causal mask. The issue involves how information is represented and combined throughout the network.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Larger Context Windows Cannot Solve the Problem</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Larger context windows are great at increasing the overall capacity of a model. But they don’t guarantee uniform reliability when it comes to making every position equally useful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can distinguish between the two in terms of maximum context size and effective context size for a task. The first concerns the overall supported input size. The second concerns how much context the application can actually use while maintaining acceptable performance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Effective context size depends on the task. For example, the task of finding one distinctive identifier within some documents is different from comparing several documents, resolving contradictions, or tracking changes across a long conversation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is where the RULER benchmark becomes relevant. The original benchmark evaluated 17 models using tasks that went beyond simple retrieval, including following chains of information and aggregating results. It found widespread degradation as input length increased. However, its limitations explicitly state that it reported scores by input length without controlling for and reporting evidence position.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Strategies to Mitigate the Bias</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">While it is difficult to completely remove the bias against middle information from a model, there are a few strategies that we can use to mitigate it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" plaintext;">Let’s look at them in more detail:</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Prompt Optimization</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Prompt organization helps make important material easier to use. A good starting point is to make the task, essential constraints, and final questions easy to identify for the model. We should not bury important information inside a large block of unrelated material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a coding task, a short opening statement might clearly mention a compatibility requirement. The relevant source files can follow, with a precise request at the end. For document question answering, putting the question after the documents is another useful arrangement to test.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Clear boundaries to mark different types of content also help. Markdown headings, document labels, and XML-style tags can distinguish instructions from source material and separate one document from another. However, these are practical starting points whose effectiveness should be checked on the chosen model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, an application could assemble a prompt like this:</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background-color: rgb(250,250,250);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 8px;box-sizing: border-box;font-family: ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,'SF Mono',Menlo,Consolas,'Liberation Mono',monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 20px;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Task: Propose a change to the cleanup worker.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Critical constraint: Audit logs must remain available for 37 days.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span><document id="retention-policy"></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Audit logs must be retained for 37 days.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></document></span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span><document id="cleanup-worker"></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>[Relevant implementation]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></document></span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Request:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Identify the required retention period and its source.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Then propose the code change.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Check that the change preserves the retention requirement.</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Here, the constraint comes from the supplied source. The documents have distinct identities, and the final request specifies what evidence the answer must use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Adding these tags doesn’t change the model’s attention mask or guarantee compliance. Their main purpose is to reduce ambiguity about the organization of the input. Brief repetition can also help keep a crucial constraint visible. However, repeating the entire prompt several times adds length and can introduce contradictions if the copies diverge.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pruning Unnecessary Context</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It is much more useful to reduce unnecessary context than enforcing an arbitrary token limit.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, model providers would often advise staying below a certain number of tokens, such as 20K tokens. This is more of an application-specific budget rather than a scientific boundary. There is no universal threshold at which 19,999 tokens are reliable and 20,001 become unreliable. A short prompt can fail if its instructions conflict. On the other hand, a much longer prompt can succeed when the evidence is clear, and the task is straightforward.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A better approach is to add the information needed for the task while removing material that adds little value. We should select relevant information and manage context as an application resource.</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d3438bac-460a-4b14-ad9b-875ae967eebd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> </a><span>Let’s say an AI assistant is investigating a database connection error. Supplying months of logs, every configuration file, and an entire deployment history creates considerable unnecessary material. A more focused input might contain the error, the relevant connection settings, the affected code, and recent changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As you can notice, the main difficulty is deciding what is unnecessary. If we remove an exception, dependency, or earlier decision, it will make the prompt shorter but also make it less accurate. Therefore, context selection needs to preserve the evidence required to answer the question while removing useless information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The same care should be applied to long conversations. An application can maintain a concise record of current requirements and decisions, with references back to the original material. Summaries are useful, but they can omit details, so they should not become the only surviving source when exact information matters.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval with RAG</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval can reduce the amount of searching the model must perform inside its prompt.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A retrieval system searches a larger collection and selects relevant material before the LLM answers. This approach is commonly called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider an AI-based support application with thousands of documentation pages. For a question about webhook retries, the system could retrieve the retry policy, relevant configuration documentation, and applicable exceptions. The LLM then answers from that smaller collection.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval can use keyword search, database queries, semantic search, or combinations of these methods. The key change is that the application takes responsibility for finding likely evidence instead of always placing the entire collection in the prompt and hoping for the best.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To be clear, this approach also has its own problems. The retrieval search may still miss the relevant passage. A retrieved excerpt may omit a necessary exception. Retrieving too many passages may recreate the original problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For that reason, RAG doesn’t eliminate “lost in the middle”. The retrieved material still needs sensible selection, ordering, and evaluation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The lost-in-the-middle problem reveals a blind spot for LLMs. Availability of information doesn’t guarantee that it will be used effectively. A fact can remain inside the context window and still contribute very little to the answer. What looks like forgetting is often a quirk of the attention mechanism to give relevant information enough influence during generation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This happens partly because different positions can receive different advantages. Early information has more opportunities to influence later processing, while information near the end can benefit from its proximity to the question and the answer. Information in the middle does not benefit from both. However, the strength of this effect varies with the model, its training, and the task.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;">We can try to have a larger context window to expand capacity, but reliable use of that capacity still needs testing. Clear instructions, well-organized source material, and careful placement of essential details can help generate better results. Removing unnecessary context and retrieving relevant passages can also make the task easier, provided important details and exceptions are preserved. These techniques reduce the chances of overlooking information. But they don’t guarantee perfect answers.</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: Last time my family was replaced by technology
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Last time my family was replaced by technology

Manuel Darcemont

2 minutes by Manuel Darcemont Manuel shares a family story about a French farrier who became a mechanic when cars arrived reframes today's fears about AI replacing developers. Past generations faced the same dread when tractors and engines upended their trades. What carried them through was holding onto their purpose rather than their tools. If what drives you is building things and solving problems, that purpose can survive a change in how you do it.
item.description: Last time my family was replaced by technology

item.title: Making your own dithered QR codes
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Making your own dithered QR codes

Andrew Taylor

5 minutes by Andrew Taylor QR codes store data in a grid of squares, where some squares help scanners locate the code and others store the actual data. By shrinking the data squares and filling the space with image pixels, you can embed a photo into a QR code. Error diffusion dithering improves image quality and hides noise caused by data squares. Prettier codes scan less reliably though, so consider where and how the code will be used.
item.description: Making your own dithered QR codes

item.title: Railway-oriented programming
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Railway-oriented programming

Sunhyoup Lee

22 minutes by Sunhyoup Lee Errors and side effects are unavoidable in software, but there are structured ways to handle them. Two common approaches are checking conditions before acting or catching exceptions after the fact. Railway-Oriented Programming takes a different route, using functional concepts like functors and monads to split every function into a success or failure path, keeping program flow linear and predictable. It works well in many environments but is not a universal solution, and applying it everywhere can reduce readability.
item.description: Railway-oriented programming

item.title: Monolith first
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Monolith first

Martin Fowler

5 minutes by Martin Fowler Starting with microservices on a new project often leads to trouble, while successful cases usually began as monoliths first. Building a monolith early helps teams move fast, get user feedback, and find the right service boundaries before committing to a more complex structure. Once the system matures, teams can gradually split off services. Avoid microservices at the start unless your team already has solid experience with them.
item.description: Monolith first
